43300.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43300.heading: Chapter 3 76
43300.content:
Chapter 3 76
Figure 3.2 – API rate limits are a good example of static thresholds as these are well-known system boundaries
Baselining: where static thresholds are impractical
In highly dynamic idx_a86ee90c systems that also leverage dynamic scaling techniques, such as Kubernetes
Event Driven Autoscaling (KEDA) and idx_34c0018d Karpenter (open source cluster autoscaler), we need to
think about alternatives to static thresholds. Various baseline approaches exist that allow us to
adapt to the dynamic nature of our workloads and environments, such as the following:
Auto-adaptive baselining: Automatically adapts the threshold based on a rolling
window of historical data, for example, the last seven days
Multi-dimensional baselining: Calculate baselines on various data dimensions, such
as service endpoints or geographics
Seasonal baselining: A baseline that understands distinct seasonal behavior, such as
business hours or holidays
The following figure shows that dynamic baselines are typically visualized with confidence
bands, and most tools also allow adjusting the baselining methodology depending on the use
case:
•
•
•
77 From Observability to AIOps and the Use Cases it Solves Today
Figure 3.3 – Baselining on certain data eliminates the need to define and manage static thresholds at scale
(source: https://grafana.com/docs/grafana-cloud/monitor-applications/application-observability/manual/
automatic-baseline/)
While static thresholds will always have a role in observability, we need alternatives in our
modern, highly idx_11a0a073 dynamic environments. It's not only the way we set thresholds that needs to
change, but also the data on which we are setting thresholds.
Beyond CPU and memory: cloud-native golden signals
CPU, memory, disk, and idx_a8c050e1 network have always been great metrics to get alerted on, or as a
trigger for infrastructure scaling. Expanding on that, many site reliability teams follow the
Google SRE handbook's definition of the " four golden signals " (latency, traffic, errors, and
saturation). SRE and ITOps teams, therefore, typically know the limits of their system very well
and can take corrective actions to remediate the situation, for example, resizing a virtual
machine to meet current memory and CPU demand, restarting a rogue or hanging process that
stopped handling requests, or distributing incoming load across multiple virtual machines
behind a load balancer to ensure faster individual response times.
Modern cloud-native architectures, especially container orchestrators such as Kubernetes,
introduced new components, layers, and built-in automation that automate or simplify those
tasks. The Kubernetes operator pattern, for instance, with its built-in control loop, automates
some of those tasks that ITOps teams had to implement themselves, changing the focus for the

43301.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43301.heading: Chapter 3 76
43301.content:
ITOps teams:
Automated restarts of hung processes: Kubernetes takes care of restarting unhealthy
Pods for us. Alerting, therefore, shouldn't necessarily be on unresponsive Pods, but
more when certain Pods get restarted very frequently, when restarts start having issues,
or if they impact other components.
•

43302.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43302.heading: Chapter 3 78
43302.content:
Chapter 3 78
Automated resizing and scaling of Pods: Kubernetes can resize (vertical scaling) or
deploy more instances of (horizontal scaling) Pods based on changed resource
requirements or a change in workloads. Alerting, therefore, must focus on detecting
when those resizing and scaling tasks are running into issues or cause service
disruptions.
Automated scaling of clusters: Like any system, Kubernetes is limited to the amount
of CPU, memory, and disk of all its nodes. Cluster autoscaling, however, can provision
new nodes from the underlying infrastructure virtualization. Alerting, therefore, must
focus on whether scaling of the cluster itself works as expected, and whether it finishes
in a timely manner to avoid any disruption of the Pods that are deployed.
With some of the automation moving into the various layers of our cloud-native platform
(Kubernetes, OpenShift, or managed cloud services), we need to focus on the new health
indicators and then decide how to best alert on them and which ones to use for scaling
decisions.
When it comes to cloud native, we—the authors—feel it's time to redefine the golden signals
that help us monitor health and get alerted on and scale every layer of our dynamic stack. The
following figure idx_98c421a6 depicts a modern platform, including the indicators for each layer:
Figure 3.4 – Golden signals redefined for cloud-native platform layers
•
•
79 From Observability to AIOps and the Use Cases it Solves Today
Let's look at idx_9ee1f86f some of those metrics across the cloud-native stack, starting from the
infrastructure layer (bottom) to idx_dbac8161 the application layer (top), as well as the observability layer
(across).
Resource layer
Without a doubt, we need idx_42ab6e7f sufficient resources to handle idx_f28bfe64 all workload requests. Doing proper
testing and capacity planning and then setting up alerting and scaling based on compute,
storage, and memory doesn't change all that much.
In cloud-native architectures, we see more components that communicate via various
channels. More than ever, network latency, throughput, and quality of service play a critical
role in overall stability and performance.
Orchestration layer
Kubernetes is the idx_89994060 leading container orchestration idx_515d9f3f layer and provides a lot of important health
indicators. If you are not using Kubernetes, then your orchestration layer of choice
(homegrown or an offering from a vendor) will have similar indicators that allow measuring
health. Key indicators are around the availability of the orchestration layer API as well as how
fast the orchestration layer can fulfill requests to schedule and deploy new workloads.
Cloud-native observability tip for infrastructure
We recommend baselining Ingress and Egress traffic volume. A significant spike or drop

43303.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43303.heading: Chapter 3 78
43303.content:
could indicate a misconfiguration, for example, a developer accidentally turning on
debug logs in production or the SRE team enabling a 100% sampling rate for
distributed traces. As all this data needs to be sent over the network, any change in
expected behavior has the potential to impact network health for your business-critical
services. The same baseline will also detect whether a misconfiguration on DNS or
firewalls blocks traffic from reaching the desired destination.
Tip

43304.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43304.heading: Chapter 3 80
43304.content:
Chapter 3 80
Workload layer
A workload is a set idx_cb1ec250 of Pods and containers that run an idx_c04d2a64 application or a service on a Kubernetes
cluster. It defines the Pods and containers, how they should be deployed, how they are sized,
and how they communicate.
The most important thing is that workloads can be started in a timely manner, keep running,
or restart successfully when needed. Keeping an eye on Pod failure rates, the reasons why they
fail (for example, running into limits), and the number of failed restart attempts is essential.
Cloud-native observability tip for Kubernetes
We recommend baselining the scheduling latency and deployment latency of new
workloads. That's the time it takes from kubectl apply until Kubernetes finds the
proper node to deploy it, and how long it then takes until the Pod is deployed. An
increase in pending Pods will ultimately lead to slower deployments and is an indicator
that your clusters are not healthy or don't have enough resources to fulfill all those
incoming schedule and deployment requests.
Tip
Cloud-native observability tip for container workloads
On top of that, we recommend baselining the time it takes to start a workload and how
long workloads are running. The startup time depends greatly on the type of workload.
A database-like workload will most likely take much longer to start and run much
longer than a small microservice that is only needed for certain use cases and otherwise
spun down. Init containers or dependencies, on the other hand, can also impact small
workloads. We therefore recommend baselining the workload start time and workload
lifetime by the type of workload. Any change in timing behavior deserves to be looked
at more closely!
Tip
81 From Observability to AIOps and the Use Cases it Solves Today
Platform service layer
Platform idx_0abf05f4 services idx_1a106c3b are typically shared services that are used by business services and
applications. Examples of those are message queues, service meshes, databases, and other
storage services, as well as critical shared business services such as an authentication service
or Single Sign-On (SSO). All of these services provide some type of API to their consumers
and, therefore, we see that the four golden signals (latency, throughput, errors, and saturation)
are used to monitor and alert on health.
Figure 3.5 – Key technical indicators for ensuring Kafka health
Cloud-native observability tip for queues and critical services
We recommend baselining key health indicators of queues, such as wait time, queue
length, message sizes, compression, and processing time. A queue that keeps growing
or where wait time increases over a period of time is a warning signal that needs to be
addressed to avoid impacting dependent services. As most critical services also have

43305.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43305.heading: Chapter 3 80
43305.content:
API rate limits, it's good practice to monitor and alert on rate limit usage or burst usage.
Those can indicate a misconfiguration on the caller side or a need to idx_58541806 adjust the idx_2bfee49c limits
for certain callers in case of overall increased volumes of transactions.
Tip

43306.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43306.heading: Chapter 3 82
43306.content:
Chapter 3 82
Service layer
With services, we mean all idx_7a3839ff business services that power the idx_0c33fa4a applications that run on your
platform. For a financial services organization, those might be services such as account-
service, trading-service, transfer-service, or currency-service.
SLOs around availability, performance, and failure rate for those services are a good idea as
they give a good indication of whether the services are delivering on their promise. While SLOs
and their error budgets and burndown rate are great tools, they also come with management
and operational costs when not done right, hence the following tip!
Application layer
Most services provide idx_12c11124 critical APIs for business applications idx_f912aa12 and their critical business
transactions. Examples are the number of users that are logged in to their online banking
system, creating a new bank account, or transferring money between accounts.
For any organization, this is the most critical layer, as this is where your business generates
revenue or where you enable your employees to do their job!
At a high level, you want to make sure that those systems and critical transactions are
available. At a minimum, we suggest using synthetic tests to validate that those key
transactions work from end to end and then alert on any availability or performance
degradations.
Cloud-native observability tip on SLOs
Too often, we have seen organizations define SLOs for every single internal and external
API endpoint of every service. That results in thousands of SLOs without any consistent
thresholds across the organization. A better approach is to define SLOs only for end
consumer APIs along the critical path of your business transactions. Even then, it's best
practice to provide templates for gold, silver, and bronze or tier 1, tier 2, and tier 3 APIs
with predefined company-wide standards on thresholds and alerts. For all other APIs,
we suggest using anomaly detection and then seeing whether the idx_e41815fc anomaly of an
internal API is really impacting the upstream idx_a48c3d10 SLO. More on that topic later in this
chapter, in the From ops to business: SLO-based impact analysis section.
Tip
83 From Observability to AIOps and the Use Cases it Solves Today
Observability layer
There is a idx_b65e4653 saying: the best comes last. No alerting or scaling idx_952023e7 would be possible if we didn't have
any observability data. Therefore, it's important that we also apply the same health principles
to the observability stack. This includes the health of the instrumentation, collection, storage,
and analysis. When using OpenTelemetry, for example, we need to make sure that all collectors
are properly sized, all receivers are healthy, no data is dropped, and all observability signals are

43307.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43307.heading: Chapter 3 82
43307.content:
forwarded to the backend analytics platform.
Cloud-native observability tip on business
We also suggest baselining key indicators on whether your business is healthy. That
includes the number of concurrent active users on your system, the throughput of
business processes and transactions, how long critical transactions take, and the
number of transactions per user or session. If those numbers start to deviate from
normal behavior during a regular day or work week, then you should act. Focusing on
the business impact has become key in modern observability, which is why we cover
this in more detail later in this chapter in the From ops to business: SLO-based impact
analysis section.
Tip
Cloud-native observability tip for your observability stack
Besides following the best practices around self-monitoring of your observability
tooling, we suggest baselining the received, processed, and ingested volume of all your
observability signals. The baseline will show you whether you have a sudden spike or
drop in observability data. Root causes could be misconfiguration or an unexpected
change in manual or automated instrumentation. We have seen examples where the
number of spans increased 100x because of a coding mistake using manual
instrumentation.
A key indicator where a static threshold can be used is the percentage of dropped
signals, as ideally, you don't have any dropped signals unless it's intentional.
The time until analysis indicator defines how long it takes from data collection until
that data point is available to be charted in a dashboard or available for alerting. The
longer this time, the more reactive rather than proactive your responses to issues will
be.
Tip

43308.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43308.heading: Chapter 3 84
43308.content:
Chapter 3 84
These discussed indicators and metrics should give you a good starting point when it comes to
understanding the health of your cloud-native platform. As not everyone runs on Kubernetes,
OpenShift, or other container orchestration platforms, it's important to understand the layers
of your specific idx_50923142 environment. Make sure to consult the idx_d9929b36 best practices documentation of the
vendors you use. A great additional and recommended way to choose the right metrics is by
conducting some load and performance tests.
Choosing the right metrics through proper load testing
Every application idx_962b6ed0 and distributed system is unique. Therefore, it's not possible to provide a
golden rule template that includes all metrics one should keep an eye on. While the metrics we
discussed previously will be important for most systems, it's important to understand the
characteristics and dynamic behavior of your system under different conditions.
Load and performance testing is a key practice that helps you understand the dynamic
behavior of your application. It allows you to identify the critical components in your
architecture, for example, which queues or shared services are causing ripple effects when they
start slowing down or failing, or what the expected maximum throughput a critical
component can handle is before it starts breaking.
Going into all of the relevant details about setting up proper load testing is beyond the scope of
this book. We do, however, want to give you some guidance on what the key steps are and give
you pointers on where to find more information.
Step 1: setting up a test environment
We could stop right here if you can test in production. For very bold people, that means you don't
do any upfront testing at all and just deploy and react to whatever happens. For those who are
less adventurous, it may mean using the failover production environment for load testing.
Some organizations also use the live production system during low traffic times. Both scenarios
depend heavily on how your production environment is set up and whether it's possible to
deploy a different version of your software in those environments. For those who can't do that,
please keep reading.
Ideally, test environments reflect production environments as closely as possible. This,
however, is not always possible due to the costs of running those large systems and the time it
takes to set up and operate such a system. While standing up the required infrastructure for a
short period of time has gotten easier, thanks to automation and on-demand available cloud
resources, it's most often very challenging to replicate production-like datasets of your systems
of records.
There is plenty of material available online about how to overcome some of these challenges,

43309.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43309.heading: Chapter 3 84
43309.content:
such as generating representative production data without running into any compliance issues
or even considering mocking or simulating those data layers.
85 From Observability to AIOps and the Use Cases it Solves Today
If a production-like system is not achievable, we suggest setting up a scaled-down version that
you can stand up idx_0fd37ec8 and operate within acceptable costs, because it helps you understand which
indicators across your layers are leading indicators for problems at scale. And remember, that's
really what this exercise is all about.
Step 2: defining realistic scenarios
When testing a sports car, you would not just test it by driving in first gear at 20 miles per
hour. That would not reflect how the car will be used by a real driver. The same is true for
software testing. Before creating any test scenarios, you need to understand what the top real
end user scenarios are. Ideally, you would get this information from the owners of the
applications and services you are testing. Also, ideally, you would simply look into your
observability stack and extract this information from there; for example, what are the top hit
APIs, or what are the most common click sequences in your web UI or API call chains? Also, you
can get a sense of how this load is distributed across those scenarios and in the course of a
regular 24-hour day. These are all insights that allow you to best model your load test to be as
close as possible to production.
Once you have this, you can pick your load-testing tool of choice and create your test scenarios.
There is no shortage of available tools, including lots of open source options, such as JMeter,
Gatling, k6, and Locust. Pick the one that works best for you and allows you to easily create and
maintain your test scenarios.
Step 3: expand-left observability
The term shift left has been used quite a bit over the past years. Typically, this means that we
shift tasks and responsibilities earlier idx_990e158e in the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). A
better term for our case is expand left because what we really want to do is expand the usage of
tools and practices from production earlier into the life cycle. For testing, this means we simply
use the same observability tools and practices for our load-testing environment. This not only
allows us to capture relevant data to identify our critical indicators for production monitoring
but also allows us to validate that our observability setup works as expected. For example, are
you capturing all your logs, metrics, and traces? Can you access them in the way you expect to
in production? Does your observability setup alert you on bottlenecks during your load testing
automatically because you have set up some dynamic baselines or use machine learning to
identify anomalies?

43310.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43310.heading: Chapter 3 84
43310.content: We hope you can see how powerful the concept of "expand left" is.

43311.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43311.heading: Chapter 3 86
43311.content:
Chapter 3 86
Step 4: running tests
Ideally, you would idx_32ccaf8b run your tests continuously, kind of like simulating production load all the
time. This allows you to continuously validate that your test system can be run. It also allows
you to identify how the system behaves under continuous load. For example, this approach is
great to identify any memory or connection leaks that only materialize after a certain time. If
you have such a setup, you can also validate how a running system behaves under load when
you deploy a new version of a component while it's still under load. That's a great test as this is
what will happen in production when you have to roll out a new change.
Now, if such a continuous test is not possible, then we suggest running shorter tests at a
regular cadence, maybe once a day or a couple of times per week. This provides continuous
feedback to your engineers and gives you continuous insights into how changes affect the
internal behavior of the system.
There are also different types of tests with different load behaviors, such as increased load,
steady load, spike tests, and stress testing. You can find more information about different
simulated behaviors and their goal in many online resources. You can also apply chaos testing,
where you simulate failures throughout the load test to bring the system into a critical
situation, for example, artificially slowing down a network connection, killing Pods, or turning
off a critical service such as your database.
All of these tests and the simulated chaos should give you plenty of observability data to
analyze and identify new technical indicators that you can apply to your production
monitoring and alerting. This brings us to the next step.
Step 5: identifying critical indicators
Load tests fulfill several purposes. On one side, they tell us whether the system behaves as
expected under the simulated load. On the other side, they allow us to optimize system
parameters and configuration to optimize the system's output under load, for example,
tweaking our connection pool sizes or adapting resource and request limits on our containers
for optimal resource usage. It also allows us to validate that our observability captures all the
data we need to identify problems, performance bottlenecks, and their root causes. This gives
us more confidence that, once we deploy in production, we can also find those root causes if
there is an issue in production that we need to fix. If we didn't find any indication of an issue
when we should have, then it means we need to think about what additional metrics, logs, or
traces we need our developers to put into their system for better insights!
The other benefit is that we can look at all the data collected after the test is finished and see
whether there are certain metrics, logs, or traces that contain information that serves as early

43312.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43312.heading: Chapter 3 86
43312.content:
warning indicators of a performance or availability problem that was uncovered during the
test.
87 From Observability to AIOps and the Use Cases it Solves Today
Once you have those indicators, make sure to monitor them in production as well. Use them as
early warning health indicators, as we discussed earlier in this chapter. Also remember that as
systems constantly change with every release, you want to continuously validate and update
those critical indicators as they may change over time.
Now you should understand that modern observability is about looking beyond CPU, memory,
and disk. While those metrics still play an important role, we have new indicators of system
health, for example, how fast a Kubernetes cluster can deploy Pods. We also discussed that
setting and maintaining static thresholds for alerting doesn't scale when we have to deal with
thousands of cloud-native components compared to traditional architectures. There are simple
and sophisticated baselining algorithms that modern observability platforms provide as an
alternative idx_4278d2b0 that automatically adjust their alerting based on historic behavior.
To conclude this section, let's look at a specific implementation scenario from one of the
organizations we have worked with.
Use case: baseline alerting on Kubernetes health
There are various idx_836c9cb4 ways to define the health of a system, and the same is true for Kubernetes.
One method to observe health is to look into how well and successfully Kubernetes provisions
the requested resources. The nature of Kubernetes is that it retries failed attempts, thanks to its
implementation of the controller and operator pattern. Therefore, just alerting on a failure is
not a good thing because the system will retry upon failure. A better way is to analyze trends
and alert on abnormal behavior. This is where a baseline is a perfect fit. The following
screenshot shows using a baseline on the number of Kubernetes Provisioning Failed events.
When we ingest these events, we can baseline what "normal" looks like and then alert on
"abnormal" or "out of baseline" situations, as shown in the following graph:
Figure 3.6 – Baseline-based alerting on the number of Kubernetes Provisioning Failed events is better than using
static thresholds
The preceding graph shows that at 7:00 a.m., there was an unusually high number of
provisioning failed events. Using a static threshold would potentially lead to too many false

43313.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43313.heading: Chapter 3 88
43313.content:
Chapter 3 88
positives, as we can see that there are constant failed events happening. Using a baseline here
also means our alerting will automatically adjust if the "base error events" decrease or increase
over time. What we are really after is abnormal, out-of-baseline behavior.
Now that we have seen practical cases of how to elevate monitoring from static threshold
alerting on well-known infrastructure metrics to leveraging baselining across the different
layers of a modern platform, it's time to think about how we can fundamentally change the
approach to observability.
We need to move idx_4d300aca from trying to understand a system once it's running in production toward
having software engineering teams including observability as a key software requirement
before even starting to write a line of code.
Observability-driven development
" Here is the new software package from development. Now, you in operations take it and figure out
how to run it in a stable way." This is the classical " throw it over the DevOps wall " mentality that
many idx_6d3a69da organizations applied in the past.
We can debate whether the term shift left or expand left is a better description for embedding
observability as a requirement earlier in the software development process. We, the authors,
prefer the term observability-driven development because it describes the mental shift that
needs to happen within an organization to treat observability as a software requirement.
Similar to test-driven development, which idx_5c142136 focuses on creating tests before writing the
business code, observability-driven development focuses on defining what and how to observe
software before it gets deployed for the first time in a testing or production environment.
Transformations such as this don't happen overnight or because somebody mandates it. As
with many other transformations, it has proven successful to start idx_3f9e74ac with a lighthouse project
that executes on the new way of embedding observability in the development process. If that
project succeeds, others will follow. Let us walk you through the key ideas and steps for such a
lighthouse project's implementation.
Step 1: defining internal and external system health
indicators
When you look at your idx_05acaea3 mobile phone and see the battery charge turning from green to yellow
and eventually red, you know that you must act quickly, otherwise your phone will die. The
same is true when driving a car and the dashboard shows the engine's heat moving toward the
red zone. This means the engine is moving to an unhealthy state that could result in
unrepairable damage. The root cause can be bad driving, such as putting the motor in constant
high RPMs, or it could be a leakage of cooling water.
89 From Observability to AIOps and the Use Cases it Solves Today

43314.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43314.heading: Chapter 3 88
43314.content:
Just like those simple health indicators, we need to define how to measure the health of our
software systems and components. We typically start with measuring health from how the
system is perceived by the caller or consumer of the system. When the system is called through
an API, we can follow the best practices around the four golden signals:
Throughput: Can our system process the number of requests per time interval that we
designed it for?
Latency: Can our system finish processing the request in a time acceptable to our end
users?
Errors: Is our system returning valid responses for valid inputs most of the time?
Saturation: Is our system using the expected resources based on our capacity
planning?
But as with our example of the car engine overheating, we must define additional technical
leading indicators to get alerted before the system becomes unhealthy for the user. We need to
define metrics that give us an early warning signal and can also be used for root cause analysis.
Here are examples:
Cache hit ratio: For systems that have internal caches, this metric is a great indicator
of whether the cache works as expected or needs an update before it impacts overall
performance and stability.
GC: For memory churn-intensive systems, GC runs and GC time are good internal
health indicators. A change in behavior suggests that there might be some memory
leak, or that the memory behavior has changed, which may require adjustment to heap
sizes or GC strategies.
Incorrect request format: For any request/response systems, it's important not to
waste too much time on incoming messages that have an incorrect format. It's typically
a sign of wrong usage by the caller or could also indicate some type of denial-of-service
attack. Knowing the percentage of incoming request messages that are invalid by
nature can be a good health indicator as it allows us to react to the problem before it
impacts the processing of correct messages.
Once we know what good external and internal health indicators are, we need to make sure
these indicators can be measured.

43315.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43315.heading: Chapter 3 90
43315.content:
Chapter 3 90
Step 2: defining how to measure health indicators
For most health indicators, there might already be an existing way to extract them from logs,
metrics, or traces. The response time of an API, for example, is something we can measure by
enabling a Prometheus exporter on the Ingress controller or extracting it from the HTTP
request logs. If none is available, developers can export additional data using Prometheus or
OpenTelemetry, or write it as a log that can then be converted into a metric in the data
pipeline, for example, through the OpenTelemetry Collector. When using an agent-based
observability approach, chances are high that you get those metrics out of the box without any
additional development involvement.
For system-specific internal indicators, such as incorrect request format or roundtrips to the
database, or any business indicators, such as number of opened bank accounts, it will be necessary
to define how to measure idx_447b62ae them and how to expose this information to the observability tool
(Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, logs, and so on). You also need to specify what value ranges of
those metrics indicate healthy or unhealthy; otherwise, nobody would take action if those
indicators fall outside the expected value range.
Step 3: providing easy access to this data for engineering
Capture everything, everywhere, and make it easily accessible! This is the only way observability-
driven development has a chance to become adopted as it avoids an additional step for
engineers to find the data they are looking for.
For this to work, we need to answer two critical questions.
Where was the data captured, and who needs it?
Later in this chapter, in the Context is king: the quality of observability data section, we will dive
deeper into how we can enrich observability when it gets captured with all this additional
metadata. This metadata is needed to answer the following question.
Where and when does this data need to be made available, and
to whom?
First, we need to learn which tools our engineers use on a day-to-day basis and where they
spend most of their time for certain tasks:
Which IDP is used for self-service, for example, Backstage, Kratix, or Confluence?
Which IDE is used for coding, for example, Visual Studio Code or IntelliJ?
Which Git platform is used for commits, for example, GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket?
•
•
•
91 From Observability to AIOps and the Use Cases it Solves Today
Which chat platform is used for communication, for example, Slack, MSTeams, or
Discord?
Which ticketing system is used for task management, for example, Jira or ServiceNow?
Next, we need to analyze what decisions engineers need to make in these tools for which tasks
and how observability data can help. For example, when troubleshooting problems, would

43316.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43316.heading: Chapter 3 90
43316.content:
engineers benefit more from viewing the latest critical logs of their components in their service
catalog, or would it be more efficient if they got this information presented in a new Jira bug
ticket?
A good example of how these thoughts materialize is explained in the following self-service
use case that was implemented by an airline to improve software quality and performance
based on observability data without having engineers identify hotspots themselves.
Self-service use case 1: providing the top three database queries
for team standup
Most development idx_84074bdc teams have daily standups to discuss their daily tasks and get advice from
their colleagues on things they are blocked on right now. This is a perfect opportunity for
observability as a self-service.
By leveraging distributed traces that include calls to database queries, the team can build
automation that identifies the top three database queries per service in the last 24 hours
running in production, similar to what we discussed in Chapter 1, in the Observing databases
section. With the additional context-enriched information about which teams own that
service and in which version that service is currently deployed, they can also send this
information directly to the team's internal chat channel just in time for their 8 a.m. standup.
This is an immediate value moment for engineers as they get actionable insights provided in
the tools where they spend their time discussing issues, such as Slack or MSTeams.
Step 4: refining, enriching, and automating toward
production
" Is this data really useful? Can you take action on it? Would this help you to troubleshoot a problem if
it happens in production? "

43317.heading: Chapter 3 92
43317.content:
Chapter 3 92
If the answer to these questions is no, then it is time to refine the definition of health indicators
and update what data you are capturing and what you do with this data.
As software moves closer to production, you also want to ask these questions: " Is there a health
indicator that you want to get alerted on? One that should trigger scaling? Or one you need to access
when troubleshooting a problem? "
The answers to these questions will allow you to set up alerts—using either custom thresholds
or baselines, as discussed earlier in this chapter. Those alerts can then either create a problem
ticket for troubleshooting or trigger a self-service GitOps process by opening up a pull request,
as explained in the next self-service use case.
Self-service use case 2: right-sizing container recommendations
as a Git pull request
Specifying good requests and resource limits is a very challenging thing. That is why most
workload definitions on Kubernetes do not have any limits at all or just rely on defaults.
Having metrics for the actual CPU and memory consumption of containers and comparing that
with the current set limits allows us to build automation that automatically opens up a pull
request with suggested limits that are aligned with actual resource requirements from a
production system.
This is an immediate value moment for engineers as they get actionable insights provided in
the development process they are following, for example, a pull request with suggestions on
how to modify the workloads.
We will cover this use case in more detail in the AIOps: reducing the noise with anomaly and root
cause detection section, as it idx_e483165a requires both automation and some GenAI to correctly open a pull
request with proper formatting of those Kubernetes workload definitions.
93 From Observability to AIOps and the Use Cases it Solves Today
Figure 3.7 – Automated pull request with suggested request limits based on observability data
These two simple yet powerful self-service use cases highlight how important ingesting
context-enriched observability data across the full stack is. We will cover more use cases
throughout the book, especially when we talk about how those use cases align with self-
service platforms.
When following these steps, there is a high chance that both operations and development will
see the benefit of this approach; operations gains insight into what observability data is
important for a new software component, eliminating the need for their own research or
identifying it during an outage as part of a triage session. Development, on the other hand,
defines what information is important for them and gains access to this data whenever they
need it, making the troubleshooting and fixing issues process faster and easier.
The more software teams that adopt this new approach, the more observability data will be

43318.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43318.heading: Chapter 3 92
43318.content:
captured. But more is not always better, especially when data is captured without the right
context about the software component, version, and team. To scale modern observability that
starts in development, we must therefore define a good strategy for enriching our data with
more context. This enables many new use cases, such as those already discussed earlier, for
example, sending the top database queries to the responsible team. It also ensures that the IT
operations team idx_2b634609 is not drowning in data and potential alerts without knowing who is
responsible for this and who the data should be sent to.

43319.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43319.heading: Chapter 3 94
43319.content:
Chapter 3 94
Let's dive into the details!
Context is king: the quality of observability data
We've said it before and idx_c3c35d33 we'll say it again: observability data is growing and will continue to do so!
The challenge is how to deal with that growth and ensure that it provides valuable insights,
rather than just letting it sit in a big lake of data that accumulates costs for storage.
We know that we need the help of AI to manage this data, but AI can only help us if the data is
of the right quality and is enriched with enough context about where it comes from, how it
relates to other data, and which part of the data is needed for decision-making.
We will walk through best practices around how and where to enrich data and the use cases
where this enriched data enables us to get more value out of our observability implementation.
Let's start with the challenge of scale and the need for semantic conventions.
From pets to cattle: semantics for observability
If you have managed idx_2de8f376 infrastructure before, you have probably heard about the pets versus cattle
analogy. Instead of treating every server like a unique, cared-for pet with a lovely name and
even a remembered birthday, we need to think about infrastructure more like cattle. Cattle
thinking means idx_651158a1 that we have a potentially unlimited number of components that we treat as
disposable and replaceable when problems occur. For that to scale, we also need to think about
automating tasks versus manually taking care of every individual component.
In cloud-native architectures, there are no pet names by default. But there are certain semantic
conventions when naming entities. Objects in Kubernetes, for instance, get a new Unique
Identifier (UID) when idx_2076e07e the resource gets created and a generated name that will be different
for every new object instance even though the object may have been created before. Take a Pod
as an example. If you create a workload with the name my-critical-svc, then every Pod for
that workload (can be a single replica or multiple) will have a unique name, such as my-
critical-svc-1694 and my-critical-svc-4352, whenever the Pod gets restarted or scaled up.
This also means that in observability, we need to adjust the way we think about monitored
entities: a host, cluster, node, workload, Pod, service, serverless function, or database. All of
these entities might no longer just have a unique name throughout their lifetime, especially
when they are restarted, scaled up, or scaled down. Gone are the days of creating a dashboard
for servers named Joe, Sally, and Hugo. Instead, we now create dashboards that are specific to
certain use cases and idx_045cf6f8 tech stacks, which can then be filtered based on agreed-upon metadata
with standardized semantics. This metadata can be extracted from labels, annotations, or tags

43320.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43320.heading: Chapter 3 94
43320.content:
applied to the cattle infrastructure we are observing.
95 From Observability to AIOps and the Use Cases it Solves Today
Figure 3.8 – Observability dashboard that can be filtered by metadata such as service name, server, cluster, or
cloud region (source: https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/dashboards/variables/)
Let's dive into modern best practices around organizing observability data that scales with our
organizational idx_d615a91c and operational needs.
Enriching observability data across the stack
When it comes to idx_ca5201b7 organizing our observability data and enriching it with context, we need to
look at all metadata across the full stack (from host to namespace, to container, to service, to
endpoint). A log line, for example, must not just be enriched with the information from which
API call it was generated from. It should also contain information about the Pod, workload,
namespace, Kubernetes node, and cloud region. This is essential for troubleshooting and root
cause analysis, as we can answer critical questions:
Does this error happen across all our cloud regions?
Does it happen across all of the various versions of our Kubernetes clusters?
Is it limited to a specific deployment with a very specific configuration?
Let's discuss the best practices for context enrichment from the top to the bottom of the stack.
•
•
•

43321.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43321.heading: Chapter 3 96
43321.content:
Chapter 3 96
Enriching with tags from your infrastructure
Most infrastructure teams have worked out a good way to tag their infrastructure. When
creating new virtual machines through IaC tools such as Terraform, Ansible, Chef, or AWS
CloudFormation, the individual server instance typically follows a naming scheme but is
enriched with tags that indicate why this infrastructure exists, what its purpose is, and who
owns it. Here's an example:
Name: foneacme_p_w_csp_web3
Environment: Production, Dev, Staging
Group: Web, DevTools, BusinessApps, Backoffice
Application: CustomerServicePortal, OnlineBanking, TimeManagement, Salary,
SalesPortal
Project: Project-A, Project-B, Project-C
Owner: CustomerService, Engineering-TeamA, LOB-OnlineBanking, SalesUSEast, CFO
CostCenter: Dev, Sales, Finance, LOB
To learn more about good tagging strategies, please consult the available white papers and
best practices documentation of your cloud partner, such as the Best Practice for Tagging AWS
Resources[1].
When ingesting logs, metrics, traces, or any type of events (deployment, configuration,
security, and so on), the best practice is to enrich those signals with the same tags. This
ensures proper filtering, alerting, and access control, which is all managed through all the
already-available tags and doesn't need to be configured on top of the metadata that already
exists. To continue the previous example, let's discuss two scenarios.
Use case: logs only accessible for sales
If logs from the sales portal backend are ingested with the Owner:SalesUSEast tag, then these
logs are most likely only for the eyes of the sales organization of that region, as well as for the
global sales team. The backend observability storage can be set up so that all logs with that tag
can only be seen by those team members by specifying what some observability vendors refer
to as the security context.
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
97 From Observability to AIOps and the Use Cases it Solves Today
Use case: traces from development only kept for two sprints
When ingesting traces in the lower-level development environments, and those traces are
enriched with the Environment:Dev tag, they may only be stored for two sprints. Why?
Because traces captured during a development cycle are typically only relevant for the time
when active development is done. Most developers don't need traces from their development
environment at a later time. So, retention of those traces can be set to a shorter timeframe, and
with this, the organization can save on observability storage and retention costs.
Think about your own current tagging strategy for your infrastructure and make sure that
those tags can be used to enrich any ingested observability signal, including logs, metrics,
traces, events, real idx_10abe610 user data, and profiling.

43322.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43322.heading: Chapter 3 96
43322.content:
After looking at these use cases, let's move a level up the stack: from infrastructure to your
application deployments!
Enriching with tags, labels, and annotations from your
deployment
Infrastructure allows us to deploy applications and services. When deploying workloads on
Kubernetes, serverless functions, or any other cloud SaaS services, such as load balancers or
database services, we can specify additional metadata about those deployments in the form of
more tags, labels, or annotations.
Here is a snapshot of a Kubernetes Deployment definition template with additional metadata
around the version, environment, service dependencies, and environment:
template:
metadata:
labels:
dt.owner: "engineering-team1"
app.kubernetes.io/name: authentication-svc
app.kubernetes.io/part-of: customer-service-portal
app.kubernetes.io/version: 4.0.2
dynatrace-release-stage: "preprod"
backstage.io/component: "default.authentication-svc"
Similar to the tags on your infrastructure, these labels can be used to enrich any ingested log,
metric, trace, or event from the Kubernetes Pods that run based on this deployment. This will
then enable use cases such as the following.

43323.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43323.heading: Chapter 3 98
43323.content:
Chapter 3 98
Use case: is version 4.0.3 good enough to keep, or do we need to roll
it back?
When analyzing metrics, logs, or traces, we can now compare the difference in response time,
execution behavior, memory consumption, or error logs between different versions of a service.
If the team decides to push a new version to a group of customers, they can now selectively
analyze and compare those signals. Additionally, we can leverage AI and automatic anomaly
detection between data on different metadata. This allows the development team to get an
automated alert if a newly released version sees a higher failure rate than the previous one.
This allows the team to quickly roll back to the more stable version.
Use case: is the quality of customer-service-portal in preproduction
good enough for production?
Ingesting deployment signals enriched with metadata from all environments (development,
quality assurance, preproduction, and production) also makes it easy to compare versions. Too
often, the question comes up: " Will the new version we have in preproduction be better than what
we have in production? " By having the metadata on logs, metrics, and traces, you can actively
compare idx_b1fa3ee6 performance, errors, and runtime behavior to make a more informed decision about
promoting a new version from preproduction to production.
Enriching observability data across the SDLC
We talked about idx_adb971b6 enriching our observability data with information idx_2da8a5fa across the stack so that we
know that a log, metric, or trace comes from a specific data center region, cluster, namespace,
workload, pod, or service. We can even enrich it with information about our release version or
deployment stage.
The enriched observability data is already the basis for what we call SDLC observability. Let's
dive deeper and explain what problems it solves.
Tracking the SDLC
" Where is my build? How long does it take to get a code fix into production? Which Git commit just
broke production? " These idx_b7a2a6dd are some of the questions we briefly discussed in Chapter 1 in the Three
pillars and beyond – use cases for logs, metrics, and traces section. It was about ingesting events
from any tool that is involved in the SDLC when creating, building, testing, or deploying
software artifacts. This might include tools such as Backstage, Jira, GitHub, SonarQube,
Jenkins, Harbor, Argo, or any other tool you have in your DevOps toolchain.
The following figure gives an overview of such representative SDLC events and from which
tools they can be ingested (typically through webhooks, notifications, event logs, or traces):
99 From Observability to AIOps and the Use Cases it Solves Today
Figure 3.9 – SDLC as a standard to track the life cycle of artifacts
Ingesting these events into the observability backend and connecting them with the logs,

43324.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43324.heading: Chapter 3 98
43324.content:
metrics, and traces from the running processes or Pods of those artifacts enables the following
use cases.
Use case: automated real-time artifact inventory and software catalog
By ingesting events from every delivery pipeline run (GitHub Actions, GitLab pipeline, Azure
DevOps, Jenkins, Argo, Flux, and so on), including information about which artifact was
deployed in idx_ef0d4f8e which environment, we can provide an idx_26ccf58a automated real-time overview that
answers questions such as: Which service in which version was deployed where, and by whom?
In most organizations, answering this question is very hard. Observability across the life cycle
provides these insights out of the box.
Use case: tracking DORA and other DevEx efficiency metrics
By ingesting events from Git commits, pull requests, pipeline runs, and deployments that
contain the same metadata about the artifact (for example, which image version was built), we
can provide automated real-time information such as lead time for change (time from
commit to deploy) or deployment frequency (how often a component gets deployed).
Most engineering leads try to capture these metrics in a consistent way across the organization
to provide engineering efficiency insights. Using SDLC events allows you to provide those KPIs
and more to your engineering leads.

43325.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43325.heading: Chapter 3 100
43325.content:
Chapter 3 100
Use case: automated correlation of deployment changes with problems
When ingesting deployment or configuration change events into the same observability
backend that monitors the health of the deployed components, we can automatically correlate
those changes to detected problems. This allows us to automatically answer the question: " Did
my Git commit break production? "
Besides automatically correlating the event to a problem and identifying it as the potential root
cause, we can also set up automation that can immediately open up a new pull request that
suggests rolling back the change that is currently causing an issue. Mature organizations often
adopt this as a standard approach to automated remediation.
A side benefit of integrating our DevOps tools into observability by having them send events on
critical life cycle idx_01482f12 stages is that we can expand on this and also idx_7c58e748 observe these tools in terms of
health and activity. After all, nothing is worse for a development team than having the
supporting tools fail when they are most needed.
Observing your DevOps tools
" Why is Jira so slow today? Why is my latest code change still not running through our build pipeline?
Why do I keep getting errors when using our Visual Studio Code AI agent for code reviews? "
Sometimes the idx_5cdb5aa0 answers to these questions are idx_cbe7735c straightforward. It could be that Jenkins
pipelines are taking longer to execute because of a shared infrastructure issue. Jira might be
unavailable because of a misconfigured network route, or a misconfigured MCP server might
have executed too many GitHub API calls, causing your other users to run into rate limiting.
While those answers sound simple, they are typically not identified automatically, but only
when people have been impacted and started to complain.
Thanks to the broader adoption of open standards such as OpenTelemetry, we see better
observability support built into all those tools. This allows us to apply the same observability
practices on those tools as we apply to our business-critical apps.
Ideally, you should also set up observability with proper alerting for your Jira, GitHub, GitLab,
Argo, Harbor, and similar tools. This gives you the chance to fix problems before they impact
the majority of your engineers.
The following is a dashboard based on OpenTelemetry traces out of GitHub and GitHub
Actions, giving insights into activities across all repositories of a GitHub organization, with
indications on problematic repositories or workflows. Having this insight helps you keep your
tools running healthily.
101 From Observability to AIOps and the Use Cases it Solves Today
Figure 3.10 – Open standards such as OpenTelemetry provide observability into new use cases, such as observing

43326.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43326.heading: Chapter 3 100
43326.content:
your DevOps tools
As a thought experiment, think about all the tools that you have in your engineering
organization. How many of them have proper observability and alerting set up? Which ones
don't? And how many engineering hours could you have saved by having a proper alerting
setup to fix problems before they impact the majority of your engineering teams?
We hope that by now you have a good basic understanding of modern observability and how
high-quality context-enriched observability data enables automation and AI to produce better
actionable insights as you are developing, deploying, and operating your IT software systems.
In the AIOps: reducing the noise with anomaly and root cause detection section, we will see how all
of this fits together to make the day-to-day life of those engineers who need to keep systems up
and idx_78287137 running easier.
To conclude this section, we idx_658d5c8b need to address one question that has probably already occurred
to you: " This seems like a lot of data that also needs to be enriched with even more data points. How do
we ensure its quality and manage the quantity? "

43327.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43327.heading: Chapter 3 102
43327.content:
Chapter 3 102
Quality of data: where to enrich it and what to sample
We have talked a lot idx_0b81192c about how we need to enrich observability data by providing more
context across the stack and the SDLC. The remaining questions are about where to enrich our
logs, metrics, traces, and events, and how to strike the right balance between capturing
everything and capturing what we need, to control costs and make data analysis more
efficient.
How and where to enrich observability data with context
Enriching observability data close to the source, where it gets generated, is the best and most
efficient way to increase the quality of your observability data. Quality is what matters once we
start discussing how the observability data can be analyzed using machine learning or AI. As
the saying goes: garbage in, garbage out.
The same is true for observability data. Only if the observability data is of good quality and
enriched with additional context will we be able to leverage the full potential of AI. Why?
Because, like humans, AI will produce better outcomes on better observability data.
In other words: high-quality observability in, high-quality insights out.
Depending on the tooling used for collecting observability data, there are different options for
when and where to enrich it. Observability agents from vendors typically enrich the logs,
metrics, traces, and events right where the agent picks up those signals. For example,
Dynatrace's OneAgent has the option to enrich the data right at the cluster, host, or process
level. Dynatrace also has a public semantic dictionary that defines what metadata it looks for
and what it will do with the observability data once it gets analyzed[2]. A common alternative
is to use a data pipeline such as the OpenTelemetry Collector. The Collector provides so-called
processors that allow idx_9c975b86 defining rules of what additional metadata should be used to enrich logs,
metrics, or traces before they are sent to the observability backend. For best practices on
OpenTelemetry enrichment, check out the many available tutorials and best practices, such as
the GitHub tutorials from isItObservable [3].
Do we need all the data? Sampling strategies
While context-enriched idx_fa2d1ce5 data is higher in quality and easier to analyze, we also need to bring up
an important question: " Do we really need all observability data all the time? "
Think about a bank that wants to observe every single banking transaction from end to end
with logs, metrics, and traces. With potentially thousands of transactions per second, we are
talking about a lot of data. That's a lot of data that needs to be captured, enriched with context,
transmitted to the backend, stored, and later analyzed if a transaction fails. But what if only
0.1% of transactions ever fail? Do we still need the successful 99.9% in all of that detail? Or is it

43328.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43328.heading: Chapter 3 102
43328.content:
103 From Observability to AIOps and the Use Cases it Solves Today
enough to capture a representative sample of that data in detail and just create metrics for the
total number of transactions and the response time for reporting and alerting?
These are very critical questions that we need to answer that will have a major impact on the
size and cost of the observability backend where all this data gets stored.
If we decide that we do not need all the data in all its detail, we can idx_69dc8a9b apply sampling strategies.
As the name implies, sampling is about making a decision on which observability data should
be part of the sample that we look at and store, and which is ignored because it doesn't give us
any additional value.
The topic of observability data sampling is too big to cover as part of this book. There is plenty
of literature and best practices available from the OpenTelemetry community. Observability
vendors also provide good documentation about the sampling strategies that their agents or
data pipelines provide. Some of them provide basic percentage-based sampling, while others
provide highly sophisticated sampling by dynamically adjusting sampling rates based on
observed behavior in logs and traces of individual service endpoints, workloads, or
infrastructure components.
If you go down the route of implementing your data pipeline yourself and decide not to use
agents with built-in automated sampling strategies, be aware that you have to take care of
sampling yourself! For that, you need to become familiar with the available strategies in the
tools you are using.
As a reference, please review the following key sampling strategies and their approaches:
Probabilistic sampling: You idx_68dc1e9d define a certain percentage (e.g., 5%) of traces you want to
sample, meaning that you want to store them. It's efficient, and with a large volume of
data, there is a good chance that that 5% includes important traces such as those that
commonly fail or take long. If you have a small number of failed or slow requests,
chances are high that you don't capture the details for those outliers!
Adaptive sampling: The sampling rate automatically adjusts based on incoming
traffic. This avoids collecting too much additional information during peak loads and,
with that, causing any type of issues, either where the data gets captured, on the
network where the data gets transported, or in the observability backend where the
data needs to be stored and analyzed.
Rule-based sampling: You can configure what is important and what is not based on
attributes such as specific URLs, requests that tend to take longer than a certain time or
fail, or requests from specific IP address ranges. The challenge here is configuring and
maintaining the rules that also need to be evaluated on every single trace.

43330.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43330.heading: Chapter 3 104
43330.content:
Chapter 3 104
The next question is which idx_4b7fcc11 component decides on whether a certain data point gets sampled
or not. Head-based sampling decides at the root span (beginning), while tail-based sampling
decides when all spans of a trace are received. Tail-based sampling can make better decisions
because it sees the full trace and can analyze whether this trace is interesting, for example,
showing a problem or error or taking very long. The drawback, however, is that tail-based
sampling requires a lot of memory as first, all the spans need to be captured and analyzed
before a decision is made to sample or not. This can become very resource-intensive in large-
scale, highly distributed, and high-volume environments. Head-based sampling, on the other
hand, makes the decision at the start of a trace. This is low effort but is limited to making
decisions only based on information that is known at the beginning of a trace.
A good rule of thumb is to start with head-based sampling and then maybe combine it with
tail-based sampling for critical transactions where you need all the details for failed
transactions or where you need specific details for regulatory or compliance reasons.
To learn more, we highly recommend another tutorial from isItObservable: Sampling Best
Practices in OpenTelemetry [4].
The systems we need to manage will continue to get bigger. We need to apply the same
practice of treating our monitored entities as cattle and no longer pets, just like we did with
classical infrastructure. We need to leverage the existing metadata and enrich our observability
signals to provide a unified experience based on a well-understood semantic dictionary. Also,
we must go beyond just observing our applications; we must also observe the tools that make
changes to our software—ideally, from the first requirements definition, when the first code
gets written, tested, and deployed, until the software gets retired. This highly enriched data
will allow us to better leverage observability data for AI and machine learning. It will give us
better idx_32c1c0d5 and faster insights into ever more complex distributed systems, especially when they
don't operate as expected.
So, let's see how this can look in action.
AIOps: reducing the noise with anomaly and root
cause detection
What would it idx_52ac32d0 look like to live in a world where, without any human interaction, incident
analysis and remediation recommendations are fully automated? You've been focused on other
tasks when your AI agent says in Slack:
" The latest Argo CD sync triggered by pull request PR-342 has caused a higher-than-usual failure rate
in our payment service. We also see new logs containing java.lang.abcdException in the frontend
service as a result causing HTTP 500 errors for end user requests. The recommended action is to roll

43331.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43331.heading: Chapter 3 104
43331.content:
back this pull request to mitigate the issue."
105 From Observability to AIOps and the Use Cases it Solves Today
What sounds like science fiction can be a reality today. How? By building on the foundation of
context-enriched observability data, leveraging automated baselines and machine learning to
detect anomalies, and using trained models that can traverse connected observability data to
detect root causes. The following screenshot illustrates such an implementation.
Figure 3.11 – A problem card showing the impact (1,070 users) and root cause (high failure rate + Argo CD sync)
The last step is idx_8a42ff8b using an LLM to generate a human-readable description of the following:
The finding: What is the impact?
The root cause: What is the reason behind that impact?
The recommendation: What can we do about it?
