is a new concept to the group. Even better, the project provides a remote flag management
server called flagd that they could deploy to manage all the configurations. In theory, they
could even relatively easily switch to a different flag management server if, for some reason,
flagd doesn't work out.
OpenFeature also supports multiple languages for the client and server. The multiple
languages and remote flag management server mean they will be able to manage features
across application domains. They can even coordinate feature availability to their mobile apps,
which is beyond the scope of their original ideas for a solution.
Since flagd supports retrieving configurations from one or more remote resources, and that
source could be a Git repository, they have a very flexible flag configuration management
pattern. Using Git also enables change management and auditing functionality around the flag
configurations, which is something they hadn't originally considered. Given the highly
controlled environments they idx_51a39a30 operated in, this seems like a requirement that they didn't know
they had.
OpenFeature is open source as well, so it is a solution that should be easy to get approved. They
will have to do some designing and architecting around the flagd server and some training for
development teams, but this seems like a clear win.
The fraud group
The group looking for tools to help counter fraud is somewhat similar to the group looking at
the alert problem. However, while the alert group is looking at solutions that address a much
wider set of problems, this group is idx_7f100ca6 focused on how an observability tool can help address
fraud. To do that, they decide to come up with a wish list of functionality that could help detect
and prevent fraud and see whether there are any observability tools that can provide that kind
of functionality.
Before they start looking at tools, this group first looks at the fraud patterns that have been
addressed over the last year, how they were detected, and how they were countered. They hope
to look for general patterns that the group can turn into wish list functionality to assess in new
potential tooling.
ACME Financial Services already uses network traffic anomaly detection, and it has helped
detect some kinds of fraud. It can alert on things such as a spike in traffic outside of what the
company usually experiences. While it has helped, there is still a large amount of suspicious
activity that has to be manually detected.
After analyzing past fraud events, the team discovers a few patterns:
A user who has logged in and is trying random URL endpoints on the company's

metrics that the company has used to understand how a new method of fraud operates. Since

The group takes the findings from their research to the next progress meeting. They are

have discovered to the wider group.
With three of the four groups finding either open source solutions or functionality that is

Because observability has the data to tell us whether we have unusual behavior from certain

The alerts group
The group that is trying to solve the company's issues with alert fatigue has the largest and
most difficult problem to solve. Not idx_a2f94c24 only does the group need to find a way to reduce the
number of alerts, but they also want to come up with ways to make existing alerts more idx_88f1784e
actionable. With that in mind, they start by researching the causes of the problems they know

43375.heading: Chapter 4 146
43375.content:
Chapter 4 146
The SLO mess
It has long been the practice at ACME idx_88823d07 Financial Services for applications to create, monitor,
and alert on SLOs. With a growing number of applications across multiple business areas, the
number of SLOs generating alerts has exploded. Everything from a highly important interface
to a customer to applications that do processing in off-hours generates alerts when their SLO is
violated. They know that the number of applications will continue to grow, so this policy is not
going to be viable moving forward.
Knowing the policy isn't viable is one thing, but knowing what to do about it is something else.
They start researching SLO best practices and find that they need to change how they think
about SLOs. They decide to evaluate a practice of looking at SLOs from the outside in, which is
to say services and interfaces that the customer interacts with, and any systems used to
support those operations. This practice would focus on events that users would experience,
and those are the most important events to ACME Financial Services. Since they are acutely
aware of the company's reputation, this policy would help align the actions of the response
teams with the principles the company cares about the most.
Implementing this SLO practice would drastically reduce the number of SLOs being tracked
and generating alerts. It would require changing company guidelines that have stood for a long
time, but the working group is confident that they have a winning message that they can take
to senior leadership.
Static alerts
Another driver of alert fatigue is the idx_cd597862 common practice of using static alerts by the application
teams. When applications were relatively few and monolithic, this practice wasn't so bad. If an
application was low on CPU, memory, or disk availability, then the support teams would want
to know in order to take action before a failure occurred. Now that the application teams have
modernized and adopted cloud-native design principles, those same alerts are now being
generated by many more application Pods. Even worse, that same data is sometimes used to
auto-scale the Kubernetes cluster or application Pods, which means the alert is complete noise.
It seems obvious that a first step to improve the noise generated by these alerts is to remove
any alerts around metrics used to auto-scale the Kubernetes cluster or application Pods. While
that is a good start, it doesn't go nearly far enough to solve this problem. The number of Pods
generating alerts is enormous and only getting larger. These alerts also have much less utility
than they did in the past. If 1 Pod out of 100 is low on CPU, memory, or disk, that isn't as much
of a concern as when the monolithic application they replaced raises the same alert.
They decide to look into what other options exist for alerting practices besides static alerts. The

43376.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43376.heading: Chapter 4 146
43376.content:
working group discovers that this problem is one that ML/AI can help address. Instead of
setting static thresholds for each Pod and trying to maintain them, tools that utilize ML/AI are
147 ACME Financial Services: Implementing AIOps
able to automatically baseline an application and understand its unique usage patterns. This
can drastically cut down on the number of alerts generated. Those tools also have some other
potential benefits, such as automatically detecting relationships and anomalies, and can even
automate some response actions.
Improvement in this area would not only depend on choosing the proper tool, but also on
changing the culture and guidance for application development teams at ACME Financial
Services.
Siloed data
After talking with the response and application teams, they discover that the current processes
suffer from a problem called siloed data. The idx_32cf604a problem is that when an alert is raised, it only
provides information about a single piece idx_27cd5d17 of information. For example, the CPU utilization is
above 90%. However, once that alert has been received, there is no further indication about
what may be causing it. Prometheus has no connection to application logs or source code
repositories, so response teams and application teams have to search through logs and change
histories to try to discover what might be causing the alert. Once the alert is received, the
investigation teams have no way of knowing whether the alert was generated because of a
spike in traffic from normal usage, fraud, a long-standing bug, or a new feature that was
introduced. The lack of context for an alert means the mitigation investigation has no
definitive place to start. Some incidents benefit from tribal knowledge that teams have gained
about how an application functions and what may have caused specific problems in the past,
but that kind of information is fragile. If a person is on vacation or leaves the company, then
that knowledge isn't available when an alert is being investigated. Some teams have tried to
document this kind of knowledge in their runbooks, and while that has helped, it has not
replaced the idx_b12855e6 experience gained by those diagnosing the causes of events.
As the working group researches solutions, they discover that this is another area where
observability tooling that uses AI/ML can help. These AI/ML observability tools, combined
with OTel traces and logs, as well as source code repository commit histories, can provide a
rich set of context to response teams investigating an alert. It is exactly this kind of context
data that response teams have to go and discover on their own with the company's current
tooling.

43377.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43377.heading: Chapter 4 148
43377.content:
Chapter 4 148
Alerts from logs
Even before the cloud migration effort, ACME Financial Services was already on a journey to
improve alerting within the idx_5741d744 company. The first iteration of this was going from no alerts to
using their log aggregation service to produce alerts. While this was an improvement over
nothing, it eventually came to be the bane of application and response teams. Application
teams were given free rein to decide what to alert on and at what thresholds. The application
development teams have not been diligent in trying to address the cause of alerts in non-
production environments, and so the alert notices clog up email inboxes and are largely
ignored, even in production. Most application development teams use email filters to prevent
alerts from filling up their inboxes. This is the very definition of alert fatigue.
What makes the alerts from logs even worse is that they are delayed, usually by at least 15
minutes, from the time of an event occurring. This puts response teams behind in trying to
reduce the Mean Time to Resolution (MTTR). There is a type of alert where this delay may
not matter, but for anything idx_4c3f23dd customer-facing, this guarantees that the problem will be
experienced by customers for at least 15 minutes, if not more.
For these reasons, ACME Financial Services has already been encouraging teams to move off of
log-based alerts and to metrics-based ones. This has been a slow effort because it first requires
that the metrics exist in order to create the alerts. Up to this point, instrumenting an
application with metrics has been left up to the application teams, and the result has been that
the progress on migrating away from log-based alerts has been slow.
The team doesn't see how it will be possible to meet some of the objectives of the project and
still allow log-based alerts for customer-facing services. While the effort to migrate off of those
types of alerts has been slow, the team agrees that they will need to find a way to entice or force
the application teams to make the needed changes. Limiting the scope of this change should
help get the support needed for the effort from senior management, but the work will still have
to go into an application team's backlog and be prioritized with other work. They decide to
present a plan to senior leadership, calling for the completion of this work by customer-facing
applications only within a year.
149 ACME Financial Services: Implementing AIOps
Bringing it all together
The various teams continue to meet regularly to share information and discuss progress, and
over time, it becomes apparent just how interrelated the various issues are to one another.
OTel, first discussed by the traceability group, is not only relevant to that problem but also to

is a nice bonus.

After creating use cases to evaluate the various tools, they contact the vendors and plan
evaluations of their products. The working group evaluates each tool against the list of use
cases and documents how the use case is implemented, as well as information that they gather
about the tool, such as resource requirements and pricing. After this exhaustive evaluation

Plan of action
The result of the initiative to evaluate and improve ACME Financial Services' observability
practices has produced quite a list of changes, some of which are small and others are quite idx_e3a0f54c
large. The working group puts together a summary of the actions that they have determined
are needed:
Augmenting application deployments with metadata to address the lack of ownership
for deployed artifacts. This would be enforced with additional checks during the
deployment approval process and application team training.
Championing OTel to address company-wide traceability issues. This will require the
creation of some standards and training for application teams, as well as designing and
implementing OTel Collectors to route the data to Prometheus and the new ACME
Observability tools.
Using AI/ML in the ACME Observability tools to monitor and detect application-level
anomalies in order to enhance fraud detection capabilities.
Using OpenFeature to track feature usage and control feature availability in deployed

may want something done, they also still want new features, products, and bug fixes. Any work

already on their plate. Given the nature and importance of these improvements, and the level

The team knows that when they go to request work from the application development teams,

Let's look at how fraud detection and response could be enhanced with AIOps. Through this
AIOps user story, we'll identify places where the sociotechnical aspects of ACME Financial
Services may influence the implementation and success.
The use case: As a fraud specialist, I want automated alerting, incident response, and ticket
augmentation for potential fraud activity.
Definition of done:
An AI agent leverages observability data to flag potential fraud
An incident is created for the fraud department
The AI agent augments the incident details with the relevant data samples
The relevant standard operating procedure is executed, which may include the
following:
Notifying the account owner and asking them to call in
Deactivating online access or forcing a password change, and identity
verification
This is the user story that the fraud team wrote up to capture their requirements. Each of their
requests has dependencies on other idx_1a758608 teams and existing systems. The AI agent will need to
combine its unique capabilities with those of existing systems in order to meet the definition of
done for this user story.
There are a few other requirements here that may not be as immediately obvious. Most
financial companies use the Gordon-Loeb model to determine the appropriate amount of
monetary investment to make into security. That model sets the threshold for optimal
maximum investment at 37% of the expected loss from a breach (https://en.wikipedia.org/
wiki/Gordon%E2%80%93Loeb_model).
This means the team that is implementing the solution must try to ensure that the solution is
not overly expensive to implement and can demonstrably save human time to help offset its
costs.

First, the team needs to clarify several key aspects of the requirements:
What is the threshold for metrics to trigger a fraud incident?
What kinds of anomalies indicate potential fraud?
What is the necessary data for incident augmentation?
What are the security and compliance requirements for writing that data into the
ticketing system?
Where do the SOPs live, and how is the correct one identified?
For this use case, the AIOps system will have an immediate and measurable impact on the end
customer. Although they may not know that it's responsible for locking their accounts after
suspicious logins, they will be negatively impacted if it does so erroneously. Therefore, it's
critical to get this right, and use a crawl, walk, run approach.
The first step is working with all dependent teams to get the data needed by the fraud
department with the correct enrichment. This isn't an easy or overnight process. So, it may not
be completed until well into the run stage. Therefore, the team will have to work within the
processes of the company to ensure proper prioritization of the work. Demonstrating potential
cost savings, and any other value, can tip the scales of feature negotiation to free up capacity
for getting that work done.
While that data enrichment doesn't exist, it's possible to start satisfying the definition of done
by working in the confines of what does. The existing automation already does many of the
actions here. It detects fraud, creates an incident, locks an account, and sends a notification.
Those capabilities do not need to be rewritten, but they will eventually need to be made
accessible to the AI agent. If access is via an API call, then the agent will need to be given an
identity for using the API and knowledge of how to use it. This may call for a custom MCP
server, our first one.
Where the automation isn't doing a great job today is in augmenting the incident ticket with
all the relevant data. Financial systems data is highly regulated, so correlating it could be
challenging. However, if we consider a data model for event metrics, it's likely that there is a
one-way hash for correlating the idx_dab8451e metric to the account. Therefore, the AI agent can find
relevant metrics and logs, keying off that hash, and identify other potentially useful data
points to key off of, such as the typical time of day for user activity. It can combine raw data
with an analysis of that data and write it to the ticketing system.
Those writes will also need to be added to the AI agent's skillset, and that will be MCP server
number two.

A ticket is created by the AI agent.

AI runs the SOP.

Workflow 2:

Eventually, the confidence in the system will grow to the point that the human review aspect
may not come into play anymore. It's generally good practice to review incidents from time to
time, regardless of whether they were handled by a human or a machine, so we'd never
recommend cutting human review out entirely. Having the AI publish a summary of tickets,
their resolutions, and whether any were reopened on a regular cadence would also help
facilitate the surfacing of success metrics and general cost savings to the relevant business
stakeholders.
But wait, can that same incident workflow be applied to internal incidents? Yes! Although the
way the data is used is different and there may be some different incident management
tooling, a lot of the data and workflows are almost entirely the same.

At the heart of it, you have a source of truth for the incident, the observability data used to

Human checkpoints to ensure the AI isn't hallucinating or experiencing errors are still
necessary. But the capability to quickly narrow down the cause, parse logs, and send pull
requests makes AIOps a force multiplier in this space. One human can now work on an
incident far more efficiently with the assistance of AI. Remember, an accurate AI is an AI that
has the correct data, correctly idx_b263c354 enriched; the quality of the data it has to work with will
determine how well it can do the job.
It's finally done. What did we gain?
It's been a long journey for ACME Financial Services as they have worked to improve their
observability deficiencies after their cloud migration. It takes several years and lots of
planning, negotiation of priorities, and even some sacrifices, but they finally finish
implementing all of their planned improvements. All idx_68c0a91d applications are sending OTel traces and
metrics, as well as augmenting their application logs with OTel metadata. All new features are
gated behind OpenFeature, and metric information is collected and used by application
development teams to help prioritize work. Log-based alerts have been retired for all
customer-facing applications. ACME Observability is the new cornerstone of the company's
observability practices and is central to moving from static to dynamic idx_d0c6564b alerts with actionable
context. It is still early in the evaluation of the new practices, but a few improvements have
already been noticed:
Before After
Too many people were needed to help
troubleshoot incidents
Identification of relevant teams simplified

Alert fatigue Actionable alerts
Fraud detection limited Fraud detection and response expanded

159 ACME Financial Services: Implementing AIOps
The incident response teams are now much more efficient. Whereas before an alert would
arrive and the incident response team would gather a large group of stakeholders to diagnose
and mitigate an issue, now the response teams know exactly which teams need to be involved
in an incident and involve only those teams. Thanks to ownership metadata and traceability
information, the incident response teams now know not only which application is involved in
an incident but also which other applications are part of the sequence of events that caused the
alert. This has resulted in reduced strain on the application development teams as well, since
they are each called into much fewer incidents. The incident response teams are also better
able to document actions and drive resolution in an incident, instead of spending time trying
to make sure all the important stakeholders are involved.
Incident resolution times have also decreased by a noticeable amount. The appropriate
application development teams are involved in an incident sooner, and the alerts have context
to help them investigate the problem. Whereas before the application teams had to dig
through logs trying to understand what happened when and what sequence or change might
be relevant to the incident, now they have log, metric, deployment, and code change history
available in ACME Observability to help them diagnose the cause of an incident.
The number of meaningless alerts has dropped drastically. While it is still a battle to get
everyone to respond to every event, the culture is slowly changing as alerts prove themselves to
be more relevant. The number of alerts that are not acted upon is slowly starting to decline.
The changes are even helping to combat fraud. The AI/ML functionality in ACME
Observability's tools detects and alerts on usage patterns outside of normal activity. It has had
a noticeable impact on mitigating and countering new fraud patterns as they are encountered.
Because incidents are resolved faster and fewer people are involved in incidents, the general
atmosphere of the company has improved. Incidents cost less because they are shorter lived
and don't require as many people to resolve. The operations and application teams are much
less stressed, and therefore more efficient in handling incidents. Burnout that was so prevalent
before has been mitigated and even started to decline.
These outcomes are all measurable successes of the project. They matter not just for
engineering but also for executive leadership. When we think about DORA metrics, they don't
just map to engineering health. They also directly impact business health.
A decreasing change failure rate, lead time to change, and MTTR positively impact customers.
These metrics directly map to the success and delight of customers using the systems.

43401.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43401.content:
Increasing deployment frequency can mean customers are seeing features faster. When the
changes to systems are overall idx_9dd4d047 smaller and more frequent, they're often better tested and more
stable. The observability data that's already being collected can be used to calculate these

43402.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43402.heading: Chapter 4 160
43402.content:
Chapter 4 160
metrics and generate business reports, adding a key dimension to the overall picture of the
organization.
Most importantly, catching and preventing fraud more often reduces the risk of financial losses
associated with a successful breach. The same model that determines how much to spend is a
good investment can also be used to prove that the investment has paid off. If we track the cost
of the system and the cost of person-hours against the budget we needed to not exceed, and
we're still at or below that line, then the project would be considered a success by any measure.
Perhaps the best result of all the work is an improved reputation for ACME Financial Services.
With customers experiencing fewer issues and for shorter periods of time, they have more
positive and trustworthy feelings toward ACME Financial Services. More trust means more
customers, but in the financial services world, a trustworthy reputation is priceless.
Summary
In this chapter, we have followed our fictional company, ACME Financial Services, as they
found themselves in a difficult and unmanageable situation after completing their cloud
migration. Operational costs had jumped and their old observability practices were no longer
working. They had to find a way to address their problems before they resulted in serious
damage to the company. This required forming a group to investigate and learn about new
observability practices and tooling, evaluate new tools, plan company-wide improvements,
deploy new infrastructure, negotiate priorities, and get senior leadership support for the entire
plan. It was a herculean effort that affected the entire company and took many years to
complete, but the end result was a more efficient incident response process and, best of all,
improved company reputation.
This ended up only being the start of their journey. As with many complex problems, solving
one set of problems reveals additional problems that were hidden or not understood at the
start. One of the biggest drivers of the changes was cost control, and the observability working
group discovered that it is not as easy to reduce costs as they thought.
Cost was just one dimension of a much larger challenge. In this chapter, we discussed the
importance of making observability make sense by going from overwhelming data to
actionable information. In the next chapter, we'll look more at how an Internal Developer
Platform (IDP) helps organizations turn observability data into actionable information—a
lesson ACME Financial Services will also learn in future chapters.

Democratizing Observability: A
Primer to Self-Service Platforms
Many organizations are implementing internal development platforms (IDPs) as a central
self-service portal for engineers to idx_8810b028 get their daily tasks done without having a dependency on
centralized specialty teams that need to fulfill tasks on request. A platform in many ways acts
as the circulatory system for a company, supporting applications that serve all kinds of
purposes, both internal and customer-facing. In this chapter, we will dive into how
observability data can become part of self-service platforms, whether they are implemented
through Backstage, commercial offerings, or home-built solutions. We will highlight how we
can integrate observability into those platforms, how the platforms can help ensure the right
data is collected, and how observability data should be made available through those
platforms, rather than having users manually find the relevant data across the suite of
observability tools.
In this chapter, we're going to cover the following main topics:
What is a self-service platform?
How to bake observability best practices and context into templates
Bringing the relevant observability data to the end users
How to leverage and monitor AI
Beyond IDP: Other places to push observability data
Technical requirements
In this chapter, we will discuss model accuracy measurements.

https://www.python.org/downloads/.

What is a self-service platform?
A self-service platform is an IDP that enables the development teams using it to utilize features
or add capabilities without needing to idx_6aa37af4 wait for the platform engineering team to do it for
them.
Often just called the platform, an IDP provides centralized golden-path self-service to
standardize the way software is developed, tested, observed, secured, and operated across an

43407.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43407.heading: Chapter 7, ACME Financial Services: How to Move from AIOps to Agentic Platforms
43407.content:
organization. An IDP is considered the golden path when it's both opinionated and well
documented. A golden path doesn't just set the organizational standards; it enforces them and
provides quick and meaningful feedback to the end users when they have run afoul of those
standards.
For example, if we look at the platform engineering technology, Backstage developers of the
platform have a feature known as plugin support, allowing engineers to add capabilities either
from pre-written community plugins or by writing their own. https://backstage.io/

plugins/ has a series of plugins created by the community with various capabilities around
topics such as APIs and logging.
An IDP approach to software delivery is typically a business decision taken to accelerate
engineering velocity in addition to solving business cases, such as standardized deployments,
supporting security and compliance, and making scalability a central feature of the software
being developed. When software application developers need to move fast, a self-service
platform can provide them with the competencies to quickly start shipping a product, but also
the flexibility to address their own operational needs.
The purpose of an IDP is to unify the method by which highly repetitive tasks are accomplished
across the organization. Technology can replace people, taking dedicated release and
operations teams from individual development teams with duplicated repetitive tasks into a
central platform. This allows the development teams to spend their time focused on writing
software and not on the idx_5b35199f delivery mechanisms.
An IDP is often created as organizations go through the process of identifying how to make
developers more efficient. Often, the first step in the journey to creating an IDP is centralizing
functions that are repeated by many development teams into one central team.
Figure 5.1: Duplicate work and repeat functions are moved to a centralized team
However, this leads to scalability challenges, the central team pivots, and, ultimately, an IDP is
born.
It is also important to note that a portal, for example, Backstage, alone is not a self-
service platform. A portal is just the starting point that provides easy access to
templates, software catalogs, and similar resources.
Note

Figure 5.2: Platform engineering team creates an IDP
The IDP becomes the central hub for software development within an organization. This also
allows for the creation and enforcement of project norms and code style guides and the
utilization of templating technologies and linters to support these quality gates.
Similarly, an IDP can also support and dictate centralized logging systems, metrics collection,
and the methods by which observability data is made available to users of the platform. Those
users are not only highly technical but may also represent business and customer interests.
In Chapter 3, we discussed how the three pillars of observability—logs, metrics, and traces—
have additional use cases beyond just application health and runtime. Business insights such
as security and compliance or cost management are also supported through the collection and
analysis of observability data. However, in order for an organization to realize these benefits,
deployments must have some degree of uniformity. For many organizations, standardizing

43409.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43409.heading: Chapter 5 166
43409.content:
resource deployments is a key strategy for validation, security, and compliance; managing
costs; and assisting with idx_fff039f4 observability. In Chapter 3, we discussed the importance of
augmenting collected observability data with additional metadata. Templates and boilerplate
help to ensure that data is present, but also to standardize log levels and unify where and how
that data is pushed.
Democratizing observability data means making it available to everyone who needs it. This is
done by ensuring software systems are producing the necessary data, and pushing the right
data into locations that are accessible but also access-controlled.
You may be asking, " How can an IDP enforce these standards? " to which the answer, as always, is,
" It depends." When we look at the capabilities of a platform, one aspect of that is the
enforcement of a predefined maturity model for the workloads on the platform. The maturity
model is the definition of done for a workload to become a part of the platform. It includes
conformance to the golden path, which may include adherence to known best practices such as

43410.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43410.heading: Chapter 5 168
43410.content:
Chapter 5 168
logging levels, the use of feature flags, and well-tuned alerts with correct routing defined in the
observability stack. There can be several processes, both technical and sociotechnical, for a
platform and the platform engineering team to leverage to accomplish this goal. One such
process for ensuring the correct data is being collected is by leveraging templating and
boilerplate code to create a unified method of data collection and data organization—in other
words, codifying best practices around observability.
First, let's look at what technologies are leveraged for standardization. We'll look at options for
Kubernetes, serverless deployments, and traditional LAMP stack deployments, starting with
the least complex and working our way up to more involved options.
Kubernetes standardization
The Kubernetes API allows for object enrichment through the usage of labels and
annotations. Labels allow for objects to be idx_0b1934d1 selected by the value of the labels, effectively
making them a way of identifying related Kubernetes objects. Labels idx_a0d38e16 can be made available to
all cluster users via the app.kubernetes.io prefix and kept private to users if used without the
prefix. On the other hand, annotations are for storing non-identifying metadata and are
available to any user that has access to read the annotated object. In this context, identifying
means that the data can be used for searching and grouping objects. What would typically be
considered identifying data can be used in annotations, for example, to identify the pager
escalation for a workload, but it would need to be parsed by additional automation tools as
that is not the functionality of the Kubernetes API.
An example of a label is app.kubernetes.io/environment: staging, which could be used for
filtering or searching for all Kubernetes objects with the same labels. An annotation might have
information about the owning team or their Slack channel. The annotation can be used by
additional automation to direct idx_8fc21c19 data or alerts for the workload, and the staging label lets the
team know what environment the data belongs to. However, there are many other examples of
best practices. The following tables should be considered a source of ideas, not a

As discussed in Chapter 3, in the Context is king section, those labels and annotations can also
be used by the observability platform. For instance, when logs are ingested, they can be
enriched with information such as environment, team, or priority. This then allows a
development team to make requests such as: " Show me all the logs from the Tier 1 apps that my
team is responsible for." And thinking one step further, when the observability platform detects
new error logs that are tagged with Tier 1, it can action upon the alerting mode annotation. If
that is set to instant, an immediate message can be sent to the team that is set as the owner.
The next question is: how can we apply this metadata in a consistent way across the organization?
An easy way for a Kubernetes-based idx_1c050262 platform team to enforce the utilization of this data would
be via CI/CD pipeline checks, admission controllers, or a custom check on a pull request (PR)
merge into a Git repository. However, this still requires the labels and annotations idx_5794e9ce to be hand-
coded. That leaves an uncomfortable amount of room for human error and can cause
frustration and significant time waste if the point of failure is not until deployment is
attempted.
Therefore, a platform team needs to identify the user needs. From an observability perspective,
developers would benefit from several key capabilities:
Getting direct access links to the key observability dashboards relevant to their
software component, versus having to learn how to find those dashboards every time
they need them in the various tools
Getting presented with the latest critical logs that were captured by the observability
tool, versus having to find the logs themselves
•
•

43412.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43412.heading: Chapter 5 170
43412.content:
Chapter 5 170
Getting an overview of all SLOs for this component and what the current values are
versus having to find this information themselves
Getting an automated analysis of performance hotspots, for example, what are the
slowest requests and the worst database calls that the code is doing, versus having to
analyze logs, metrics, and traces themselves to find those patterns. Here, we also often
talk about automated observability scorecarding.
This is where templating technologies can make a big impact. By providing templates or
boilerplate code examples, a platform can support data quality and consistency during the
development cycle. While the use cases for templating and boilerplate exceed just ensuring
observability best practices are utilized in a consistent manner, this is the use case we're going
to focus on in this chapter.
Now that we understand the business cases and justification behind using templates and what
problems they solve for the users of a platform, let's dive deeper into the technologies available
today.
Kustomize
Kustomize is a configuration management tool included in Kubernetes by default that allows
users to generate idx_9fe9a9da configuration automatically.
For example, with Kustomize, you can idx_bcf19c19 use the annotation transformer to automatically apply
annotations to Kubernetes resources. This prevents mistakes or blocking of resource
deployment by ensuring the method for applying configuration lives on the cluster alongside
the workloads it is modifying. In the YAML for the Kustomize file, the methods for identifying
which workloads to select and modify are defined.
Kustomize's strength is its ability to crawl a directory and, with surgical precision, modify the
contents within.
Boilerplate code and templates
Boilerplate code is idx_379e9026 often supplied in a software development kit (SDK), typically as a
common library or function that developers can use to complete idx_a9f33dfb tasks. The Operator SDK for
building Kubernetes operators generates quite a bit of boilerplate to help fill in the basic
functions of an operator, and also includes the capability to generate observability
configurations by using boilerplate code to expose metrics that are considered a best practice;
see https://book.kubebuilder.io/reference/metrics-reference.html for more
information on those metrics.
Another example of boilerplate code comes idx_8180f2bf from the OpenTelemetry (OTel) SDK. This SDK
contains functionality to help developers quickly leverage the core functionalities. This SDK
supports best practices such as sampling and exporting data to a long-term storage solution,
•
•
171 Democratizing Observability: A Primer to Self-Service Platforms
and includes some capabilities for attaching metadata to the observability data being

43413.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43413.heading: Chapter 5 170
43413.content:
exported, such as hostname or some hierarchy information.
If you are using Backstage for your IDP, it natively supports software templates (https://
backstage.io/docs/features/software-templates/) as a core feature. When you create a
template, it is stored in the software catalog and can then be leveraged by the IDP users.
Prometheus templates
In Chapter 1, we discussed OTel and Prometheus for metrics collection, so we won't dive deep
into it again here. What's idx_1f5c230a notable for Prometheus is that unlike OTel's use of an SDK,
Prometheus leverages templates to codify best practices into the observability stack (https://
prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/configuration/template_examples/).
Prometheus's templating capability leverages the Go templates package of Golang. There's
more than one place where templating is idx_e29d45ab usable, but the most common use is likely in the
alerting rules. This allows you to write alert rules once, for every Kubernetes resource kind on
the cluster. For example, if you wanted to alert on Pods crashing, you'd write a rule like this:
annotations:
summary: "Pod {{ $labels.pod }} is crashing"
description: >
Pod {{ $labels.pod }} in namespace {{ $labels.namespace }}
is restarting frequently on node {{ $labels.node }}.
Prometheus templates can also be used to add the label and annotation metadata to metrics
and alerts, ensuring proper idx_eddde345 data enrichment during query and export. Typically, this idx_82d913b4 would be
done via Helm in combination with the Prometheus Operator, taking us to our final Kubernetes
templating technology.
Helm templates
Helm is called the Kubernetes idx_dea3b639 package manager and provides robust tooling for managing
Kubernetes deployments. A main feature of Helm is the templating engine, which, like
Prometheus, also uses Golang templates, with additional functionality written into the engine.
Helm manages inheritance idx_15018472 within the templating, allowing charts to have customizations but
also to inherit characteristics from parent charts, allowing developers to leverage the power of
templates while maintaining flexibility where needed.

43414.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43414.heading: Chapter 5 172
43414.content:
Chapter 5 172
Templates in non-Kubernetes architectures
While Kubernetes and idx_0d151e92 cloud-native architectures represent a large portion of the observability
landscape, other software architectures also benefit from the same principles and some of the
same technologies. For example, Prometheus idx_9e9a2f77 and SDKs are both available for use in other
architectures as well as Kubernetes. The following is a quick reference guide for architecture
types and observability solutions that either support templates or provide references or
boilerplate:
Architecture Platforms and Hypervisors Observability Tools

Table 5.3: Observability technologies for non-Kubernetes architectures
The configuration of these observability tools when you don't have Kubernetes environments
still looks more or less the same. You'll have a Continuous Integration and Continuous
Deployment (CI/CD) pipeline, such as GitHub idx_6e94e663 Actions, that executes the infrastructure-as-
code tool to apply these configurations. Major cloud providers have infrastructure-as-code
tools with templating, such as CloudFormation from Amazon Web Services (AWS),
Deployment idx_aad62148 Manager from Google Cloud Platform (GCP), and Azure Resource Manager from
Azure. However, these tools are idx_58e5d617 vendor-specific, so they lack flexibility for multi-cloud
environments or environments that idx_de732bba may have applications on-premises as well as on the
cloud. If your IDP doesn't need to be as flexible, then it's fine to use the cloud vendor's tool of
choice, but when it does, you'll need to idx_abc43616 look for more agnostic options.
A few of the most common infrastructure-as-code tools that work well for hybrid architectures
(where you have two or more flavors of infrastructure) are Ansible, OpenTofu, and Terraform.
These tools could be used together, with other tools, or standalone. These technologies, as well
as the cloud-specific technologies, also work for Kubernetes-based deployments, but that's not
their primary focus.
173 Democratizing Observability: A Primer to Self-Service Platforms
Terraform
Terraform is typically used for standing up infrastructure. It manages the low-level resources,
such as networking, virtual idx_a7bdb99a machines, storage, and security groups. If your idx_c1b042c9 infrastructure is
managed via Terraform, then the configuration of how to connect it to the appropriate
monitoring stack would be inserted into the Terraform .tf files directly. The " as code " portion
of " infrastructure as code " means that the deployment of the infrastructure is repeatable, and

43415.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43415.heading: Chapter 5 172
43415.content:
there's a single source of truth for how to do it. Terraform code is organized into modules,
allowing idx_69bfcd22 for small and independent changes within the code base, somewhat similar to Helm
charts. Modules support variables so that they're reusable across multiple teams within a
single organization. Modules are not templates, because Terraform tracks what piece of
infrastructure is owned by which module. In other words, it maintains a state for what it
manages and compares the actual state to the desired state before it takes any actions. On the
surface, this may not seem different from Helm, but Helm relies on the state management
provided by Kubernetes and does not maintain its own record of state, which is a key capability
of Terraform. Like many of the tools we've described, there's a large community around
Terraform, and there are many community-built Terraform modules available at https://
registry.terraform.io to help you idx_9c7c18ce get started.
OpenTofu
OpenTofu is a Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) sandbox project idx_f2a64639 that was
created from a fork of Terraform after idx_eabdff12 a licensing change was announced. OpenTofu idx_ce23342b seeks to
maintain backward compatibility with previous versions as it progresses, and is intended to be
a drop-in replacement for Terraform. There may be some use cases where they do not have
one-to-one capabilities, and as both projects evolve individually, that case count is likely to
increase. However, OpenTofu is still a fully functional and production-ready tool for
infrastructure as code.
Ansible
Ansible is capable of virtual machine or Kubernetes deployments, but its strength lies in the
robust configuration capabilities it idx_d663edf4 also has. Ansible will run its tasks against what it calls
hosts, or the infrastructure idx_6d12718b within its inventory. The inventory is user-generated by either
directly passing it into the run command or supplying an inventory file. Ansible organizes its
work into files known as playbooks. Playbooks idx_e304e182 are written in YAML but support Jinja2
templates. Playbooks idx_ef086720 leverage templates via template files. The templating capabilities allow
for the usage of loops and conditions in addition to variables and facts. This gives more
configuration flexibility and allows for efficient procedural operations—for example, only
installing a package on the host if it's not already present, or getting the IP of the host and then
plugging it into the rendered template during execution.

43416.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43416.heading: Chapter 5 174
43416.content:
Chapter 5 174
Now that we know more about templating and " * as code " technologies, let's look at how to
pick and choose a technology.
Choosing and using your templating technology
The best advice we authors can give you for determining which observability and templating
technology to adopt is this: do the idx_df2caacf needful; use what you need, not what you think you need. In
other words, solve the problems you have, not the problems you think you will have or don't
have yet. That doesn't mean completely abandon the idea of flexibility, but it does mean
prioritizing what you know you need when deciding what to integrate. To identify what the
needful is, first identify who your users are. Remember, the purpose of a platform is to provide
the correct set of capabilities to the end users, that is, the software developers building the
customer-facing or internal apps. A platform needs to be purpose-built, or else it is just more
infrastructure. For more on building a platform as a product, see Platform Engineering for
Architects, another Packt title by Max Koerbächer, Andreas Grabner, and Hilliary Lipsig.
Once you have your users identified, you can then conduct user interviews and create critical
user journeys. This will allow you to identify where your users can benefit from templates and
other platform capabilities, and what the needed capabilities will look like.
From there, use a crawl, walk, run approach. Start with the most straightforward use case and
the technology to match. Once that is in use, work on the more advanced cases. For example,
you may start with Prometheus templates and then later move on to having Helm manage
those templates, and finally, use Argo CD to manage the deployments and changes to them. Or
you could combine Helm and Kustomize to get the ideal user experience for the platform users.
Some quick decisions you can make based on our recommendations are as follows:
If you need multi-architecture-capable observability, choose Prometheus and Grafana
If you want to manage deployments with complex inheritance requirements in
Kubernetes, choose Helm
If you need multi-cloud infrastructure management, choose Terraform or OpenTofu
Most of these tools are not mutually exclusive, and with the open source options, you are not
vendor-locked. However, even across idx_2cfb98e3 observability SaaS vendors, you may find a mix-and-
match approach or the ability to migrate from one to another if it becomes necessary. Mixing,
matching, expanding, and migrating will all come down to how you decide to manage the
lifecycle of the templates your platform supports.
•
•
•
175 Democratizing Observability: A Primer to Self-Service Platforms
How to life cycle templates
If there is one truth in software engineering, it is that when you think you have finished, you

43417.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43417.heading: Chapter 5 174
43417.content:
have not. There's always a dependency that needs to be bumped for security patches, a bug
that needs to be fixed, or some other change coming down the pipeline. While some things
may change very slowly, or idx_4c0cc350 very rarely, it's still important to have a clear versioning strategy
and change management in place—in other words, a life cycle.
Templates are functionally the same as code; thus, the lifecycling of templates is a solved
problem. Treat them the same as idx_765fa847 your code. Like other code, they have a repository, and they
have to be cared for: stored, documented, versioned, and tracked.
In this context, your templates are no different from any other utility code. There isn't a hall of
AWS Lambda scripts; in fact, it isn't generally valuable to try to reuse such specialized code.
Perhaps it can be shared within a team or community, but the environment it lives in is ever-
changing. After version changes impact its utility, it must be adapted or decommissioned.
For boilerplate, it's even more straightforward. Release a new version of the SDK and let the
magic of libraries in software do the work for you and the engineers who consume your SDK.
Here you will find a comprehensive, but likely incomplete, list of all the ways you can approach
template life cycle management.
Change tracking
The key thing to know about templates is that when we in the industry talk about * as code,
templating is a cornerstone of that idx_10ce255f concept. Templates are typically stored in version control
such as Git and managed as source code.
For day-to-day management, the principles of GitOps apply. If a template is updated, your
desired state may not match the actual state; a GitOps tool such as Argo CD can help to ensure
that the changes you've made are populated to the correct locations—for example, pushing the
updates directly or making them available for pull models to catch the changes and bring them
in. Push is more event-driven, but pull is more secure, so both have their place in the
management of * as code.
There are automation-based solutions for catching changes between the base templates and
the rendered templates or repositories where the templates are invoked.
One such tool is the Renovate Bot. Renovate idx_863f4644 can be used to instrument GitHub repositories to
catch dependency updates and automatically make PRs to projects to bump the dependency
version. The repository that needs to inherit the changes is the one Renovate is configured
against, and the repository where idx_3a17863b the changes will come from will be listed in the data sources
configuration. For more information on the specifics of how Renovate works, we refer you to

43418.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43418.heading: Chapter 5 176
43418.content:
Chapter 5 176
the official documentation (https://docs.renovatebot.com/key-concepts/how-renovate-
works/).
This approach works for template changes, SDK updates, or boilerplate changes. The Renovate
automation tools catch differences between template versions (and they should be versioned)
and the version the rendered templates are using. When it catches drift, it will make PRs to
keep the two in sync. There are several ways to leverage Renovate, but the GitHub action is
where we recommend getting started (https://github.com/renovatebot/github-action).
If you've never used it before, Renovate can use a variety of data sources, and commonly will be
set to use GitHub releases as one of those sources. If you're publishing an SDK, when a new
version is released, if the release is created in GitHub, the Renovate Bot will catch the new
release for the repositories where it is a dependency, and similarly make a PR to bump to the
newer release version in that repo.
Renovate is also a great tool to use to manage Helm subcharts; the latest information on Helm
3 compatibility and eventual Helm 4 compatibility can be found in the official documentation
(https://docs.renovatebot.com/modules/manager/helmv3/).
To catch template differences for rendered templates in use, besides GitOps tools, a policy
engine such as Kyverno can also be idx_2d3da4bf used. This will help to catch whether changes are
attempted through an unexpected method, such as direct edits from a user. While the
existence of a platform and its capabilities should reduce instances of human intervention or
human-initiated edits, these things still do happen, and a policy engine can help to prevent
them entirely, or simply notify of the event, depending on the configuration.
Usage tracking
Another key part of lifecycling is knowing idx_31683b9e when it's time to deprecate a resource. Maintaining a
template or pieces of boilerplate costs time and money, so you need to be sure that it's worth
the investment; or, if you're removing a template for technical or business reasons, be sure that
it's safe to do so.
If you're removing boilerplate code, that can be more straightforward as it was directly cloned
into the end environment and can continue to exist without any need for upstream
management and maintenance. It becomes the responsibility of the implementing team.
However, for templates, especially for Helm charts, this requires more careful consideration.
That consideration should include whether or not the chart is in use. But how can you measure
usage and determine whether templates are in use?
If you're using Helm, Komodor has idx_d4323a0b created a plugin called Helm Dashboard, which can be
installed on your Kubernetes cluster and idx_a2fac1dc will show you which charts are currently in use:
https://github.com/komodorio/helm-dashboard.

43419.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43419.heading: Chapter 5 176
43419.content:
177 Democratizing Observability: A Primer to Self-Service Platforms
Finally, if you are using the Backstage idx_bce43075 developer portal as your IDP, and your templates are
registered to the software catalog, it has functionality that can measure the usage of those
templates, allowing you to make data-driven decisions. If you're finding that a template is
never or rarely used, it's a good candidate for deprecation.
What is the role of the platform?
It's up to the platform team to consult with stakeholders and ultimately define the standards
of observability tools and data collection. While individual development teams can also
leverage templates, the platform acts as a unification layer to ensure consistency and ease. By
providing the templates and standards along with enforcement, the platform ensures best
practices are followed. Templates idx_63f7c4a0 and boilerplate don't just assist in democratizing best
practices; they can also encourage and promote observability-driven development. This does
not shift left the accountability, but rather expands it left, providing the framework for
developers to incorporate observability as early as possible in the development cycle.
That enforcement and consistency treat all aspects of applications and tooling equally. From
the platform perspective, everything is an app (including parts of the platform itself). That is to
say, whatever best practices you apply to your customer-facing apps, you must also apply to
your AI and other applications.
Enforcement of the maturity models
In the Platform Engineering for Architects book, Hilliary defined maturity models as the
sociotechnical side of an IDP. These are going to be very subjective but essentially become the
minimum set of standards an idx_59f7977c application must meet to be onboarded to the IDP. Through the
use of policy engines and static analysis tools, a platform can shape the landscape of the
software being developed within an organization.
A simple maturity model for onboarding a new application to the IDP may look like a checklist
of tasks to be completed:
Kubernetes object definitions are labeled or annotated.
Prometheus alerts are configured.
SLOs are defined.
Alerts are routed to the appropriate service.
A Grafana dashboard configuration has been submitted.
Troubleshooting guides have been written and approved.
You may have other tasks to idx_ca0eb814 add to this list, but it's a starting point to help you develop the
standards your IDP defines, uses, and enforces.

43422.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43422.heading: Chapter 5 178
43422.content:
Chapter 5 178
The platform is the unifying layer
With the platform providing the golden path, it must also become the central hub for all truth.
This includes application definitions, access idx_9b3dfdc6 controls, and the observability data. The platform
needs to provide distinct value that brings users back and makes them happy to use it.
Centralized observability is just one example of the capabilities an IDP will need to have;
another is access controls.
Access controls are one of the most critical pieces of the platform capability. Democratization
of data cannot come at the expense of security and compliance requirements. The platform
must define and enforce least privilege for the observability data it stores and makes available
to users.
Most observability tooling idx_c6fdd1ea you would integrate into your platform supports access controls,
often called Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) or Identity Access Management (IAM). For
the idx_5552cd2b context of building an IDP with robust observability capabilities, you won't want to
manage access controls in multiple places. You will need to choose technologies that integrate
with the solutions already in place.
Grafana is an excellent example of this, as while you can manage RBAC directly, it supports
application plugins to leverage existing access control systems such as OAuth configured via
GitHub, GitLab, Okta, Google, and more. It has additional flexibility in that it can connect to
multiple data sources, such as databases, individual machines, or blob storage, allowing it to
act as a single point of entry for all data within an IDP. It's also architecture-agnostic, so if you
have a mix of architecture types, you won't need to have multiple data visualization tools. The
flexibility of Grafana makes it a good choice if you don't want your platform to be opinionated
on where observability data is shipped or how it's structured when stored, allowing teams to
self-service the Grafana configurations and plugins they need. Managing the Grafana
instance's availability would provide the flexibility your development teams need without
losing out on core platform functionality.
Grafana also supports the use of pre-made dashboards from templates, as well as allowing
user-defined dashboards. Here, we quickly used a template to visualize observability data
being collected from a developer's laptop:

Figure 5.3: Grafana dashboard with data
These configurations are stored as code—JSON for dashboards—and can be used and folded
into the software development idx_296bf538 life cycle just like any other templating technology.
The full JSON is too long to share, but here is a snippet from one of the many free templates:

Using or building the right tools to make the right data available, but only to the right people
or systems, will be core to your observability strategy. Any AIOps implementation will need to
be gated with appropriate access, which we'll cover further in later chapters as well. Now that
we've established how the idx_4e5c378e platform standardizes observability data collection, let's look at
how AI can augment the platform's enforcement capabilities and why the platform must treat
AI workloads with the same observability rigor as any other application.
Use cases for the integration of AI into the IDP
Where can an AIOps implementation help accelerate platform growth and offload tasks from
the platform team? While we idx_bf85010f can't possibly be exhaustive in our recommendations, we do
have a few places where we think AIOps can help, and it's not just acting as a user-facing
chatbot either.
The first is as part of the code quality enforcement arm. While traditional linters or even
custom GitHub actions can go a long way to ensure boilerplate code examples and platform
requirements for handling observability are met, they are still limited in their flexibility.
There are even products such as SonarQube that help idx_a0d736d8 platform engineering teams to ensure
quality gates are satisfied. But the same challenges we find with maintaining any automation
become readily apparent. Your automation is only as good as its programming and will be
limited in what it can do to what you've had time to write.
Here is where AI can find its time in the limelight. As we discussed in Chapter 2, an LLM-based
AI tool has far fewer limitations and can make inferences while also adhering to a set of
supplied instructions.
181 Democratizing Observability: A Primer to Self-Service Platforms
For example, AI can act as a multi-architecture bridge. It's almost impossible to apply the exact
same standards to observability for a virtual machine-based environment as for a Kubernetes
environment, so AI can act as the bridge between them to help normalize the data, or act as a
tool to sample or sanitize where other standard tools might not be so easily adaptable.
Data timeliness and quality are important, but no tool is entirely perfect. Prometheus can, in
some configurations, crash and lose data. Accepted idx_79242995 sources such as CloudWatch are known to
have strict rules for log timing, which idx_1b1b473d can create ingestion problems or omissions if time zones
are not properly accounted for in configurations. Serverless, low-code, and no-code metrics are
often shallow in scope and poorly communicated. And sometimes data may be lost due to

43425.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43425.heading: Chapter 5 180
43425.content:
events outside anyone's control, such as a natural disaster.
In these cases, AI may be very well positioned to handle unreliable or incomplete data but will
need to be given data and sources along with explicit constraints or instructions.
Instruction files and giving your AI direction
Instructions are provided via instruction idx_c21ebed5 files, and there are many ways to make instruction
files available to an AI system. For example, there's a project within the Linux Foundation
known as agents.md, which is a standardization effort around Markdown files added to code
bases with instructions that are useful to anyone, but specifically intended to help AI agents be
successful when interacting with a code base. There are no universally expected fields for an
instruction file, but there are best practices for writing a good one.
First, structure your file. Break it into topics and leverage Markdown formatting to break the
instructions into segments. For example, build instructions and test instructions should be
different headings.
Second, be as detailed and specific as possible. Just like when writing a README for a human,
the more details you provide, the less guesswork the AI needs to do. If you want your agent to
assume a certain role, task, or objective, be sure to include that information; that specificity can
help the AI to come back with better responses. If you want a specific output, such as what we
indicated with our data normalization use case, then that output format should also be in the
instruction file. Anything that is important for the AI to know, including your expectations,
belongs in your instruction file.
Third, let the AI know what it can and cannot do. If it can reach out to the internet, include
that. If it cannot reach out to the internet, include that in the instructions as well. Your
instruction files are the first line of governance for the AI system, and you can make it aware of
security and compliance requirements, as well as what data sources it has access to, in these
files.

43426.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43426.heading: Chapter 5 182
43426.content:
Chapter 5 182
Finally, when you are building out your instructions, you will want to test them and adjust
them. It's also important to keep them current with new information that your AI agent needs
to know.
For example, instructions for an idx_f6baff12 observability agent may look something like this rudimentary
example:
# AGENTS.md file
## Agent Persona
- You are a Site Reliability Engineer in a Kubernetes environment.
## Agent Constraints
- We are a SOC 2 Compliant Company
- You do not have external internet connectivity
## Desired Response Format
- Place investigation details into Jira
- Remove any data that could be PII
- When a solution is identified, open a pull request in GitHub following any
relevant contributor guidelines.
## Data Sources
- There is a Prometheus instance on the cluster
- There are logs being collected with Fluentbit
- OpenTelemetry is also in use
## Important Cluster Information
- All software has been installed with Helm charts
- All observability data should have labels and other metadata.
With proper instructions, AI agents can be more efficient and get to work faster. And by setting
expectations about the system it is working on, the AI can start detecting trends and patterns
in the data. From there, if you are in a situation where you have missing observability data, an
AI system can infer whether there's reason to suspect that there's a problem that extends
beyond the monitoring stack itself.
However, it's important to set your own expectations. If the data doesn't have strong
cardinality, such as labels and metadata, and the AI agent or assistant has never seen the
system before, the quality of the inference will be diminished; but once both of those are true
and the AI system is tuned, its judgment to identify and investigate large-scale issues can
generally be trusted. We will go over fine-tuning and its benefits in depth in Chapter 9.
A well-tuned AI system will bring insights to the users, which may often augment or extend
their existing expertise. For example, an AI can help with the following:
Best-practice recognition •
183 Democratizing Observability: A Primer to Self-Service Platforms
Misconfiguration detection
Data capture at preproduction through to runtime
Cost management
However, even with proper tuning, we can't let our AI run completely unattended. This is
where the platform must treat AI equally and apply the same security and access control
standards as it would to any application. The AI system must be observable and subjected to
governance; this is how we can idx_3f8c4d74 prove that the system is performing safely and meeting
expectations. Now that we've examined what observability looks like within the platform, let's
apply that to an AIOps implementation.
A reliable AI is an observable AI
A good IDP is customer zero to itself. The golden paths must be equally achievable for the

43427.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43427.heading: Chapter 5 182
43427.content:
product that provides them. AIOps is part of that customer zero model. It will be developed,
deployed, and monitored to the same idx_124f388e standards as anything else, with the goal of becoming
another capability of the platform for engineering teams to leverage. The capability to use and
benefit from an AI agent must be part of that centralized experience.
For an AIOps implementation to be useful, it must be accurate. Measuring the success and
accuracy of AI is a new challenge, but the concepts we have already discussed for observability
still apply. There are new standards when it comes to metrics for AI performance that are good
to keep in mind, and also new tooling, but at the end of the day, these purpose-built tools
recycle best practices.
In a Kubernetes environment, AI workloads are just Pods at the end of the day. So the usual
standards for Kubernetes workloads apply. You'll want to watch Pod health, such as CPU and
memory usage, as well as checking for crashes, restarts, or other general health problems.
Similar to most other applications, your AI applications will have performance metrics.
Request and response latency are key among them, but so are measurements of accuracy.
For AI workloads, these idx_a3df42e0 metrics will be critical to understanding whether your AI is providing
the right value to your organization:
Inference speed
Time to first token (TTFT)
System idx_9ce223b9 throughput:
Transactions per second (TPS)
Operations per minute (OPM)
Response accuracy

guardrails)

Knowing the metrics we need is great, but how do we determine what the measurements for
those metrics should be, and once we have those measurements, how do we make sure the AI
is performing as expected?
A good open source tool for benchmarking your AI system is GuideLLM (https://
github.com/vllm-project/guidellm), part of the vLLM project. GuideLLM is a platform for
evaluating how language models perform under real workloads and configurations. It can
operate on real or synthetically generated multimodal datasets and gives you clear insights
into performance, efficiency, and reliability before deploying LLMs into a production
environment. GuideLLM is a good starting point for benchmarking and optimizing your LLMs
as it also puts a focus on idx_3002317f the key metrics discussed previously: TTFT, inter-token latency
(ITL), output distributions, and dataset-driven variations. While there idx_2d7e912b are some industry
standards around what good metrics for performance look like that are emerging, there's not a
one-size-fits-all metric. Different models perform differently for the same task, and the same
model can perform differently across tasks of different complexity. This is because various
prompts can rightly need longer response times, more tokens, and more exchanges with an end
user. Time and tokens will be two aspects of performance and reliability to monitor as your
model processes prompts, and establishing a baseline and catching deviations from the
baseline will be critical to proper model observability. It's best to benchmark your model with
tests that mimic production, and evaluate the metrics of real use against those benchmarks.
You'll know what good looks like for your system over time with regular human review, and
ultimately, you'll be able to set up alerts and tune them. A good practice would be a weekly ops
review meeting to help define targets and alerts, instead of alerting right away and possibly
creating a signal that is no more than noise.
Whether you are using GuideLLM or other tools and frameworks, measuring that you're
maintaining the benchmarked performance is harder and requires putting some thought into
the system design for the AI system. Technically speaking, the LLM that powers your AI will be
accessed via an API. Functionally, once an API is in use for your AI agent, it stops being unique
and starts being the same as every other workload in your environment. TTFT becomes simple
math, subtracting the timestamp of the request sent to the API from the time the first token is
sent back. This can be measured with Prometheus rules or OTel.

43429.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43429.heading: Chapter 5 184
43429.content:
You can build a bespoke API and an AI serving engine, and the OpenAI developer docs have
great references to help do just that. However, there are open source options to save you the
•
•

185 Democratizing Observability: A Primer to Self-Service Platforms
trouble. If you're using vLLM to serve your AI agent, it comes with many metrics already
defined in the framework, ready for use: https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/usage/metrics/
#general-metrics. Also, you can always build out and define your own as needed.
Where most metrics are easily defined as numbers, accuracy may not immediately strike you as
a quantifiable metric. Up next, we'll show you how to measure accuracy and keep measuring it.
Strategies for measuring response accuracy
The challenge with measuring response accuracy is that responses need to be evaluated
regularly; it's not a one-and-done situation. As training data or other data the AI system has
access to increases, there's a reasonable expectation of drift between how the system
responded after initial training idx_5423debb and how it responds later on; however, that drift should be only
due to facts changing, not due to errors. We've identified the following practical strategies for
measuring response accuracy.
Natural language processing scoring
For natural language processing, there are many scoring systems for accuracy: BLEU, ROUGE,
BERT, METEOR, and Perplexity, just to idx_57611c93 name a few, and others may yet emerge. The most well
known are the BLEU and ROUGE systems. The BLEU scoring system is often used for use cases
where the output must be highly precise. If you've noticed that an AI chatbot uses a lot of
words to convey an idea but leaves little room for interpretation, it's likely scoring well against
the BLEU system.
ROUGE prioritizes recall and is intended as the scoring system for cases where summarization
and recall are more critical than output generation. It's a good scoring system for agents that
are parsing and distilling large amounts of observability data.
Of the other scoring systems we've mentioned, the most relevant for AIOps is BERT. It has a
similar scoring methodology to ROUGE but is computationally more expensive and may
provide a more accurate score. We'll spare you the math, but there's a link to a deep-dive article
on how scores for all three of these systems are calculated in the Further reading section of this
chapter.
For the purposes of observability and AIOps, we recommend using the ROUGE or BERT scoring
system to evaluate model performance, should you so choose. Both scoring models use a range
of 0-1. For production systems a score of around 0.8 on the BERT scale and around 0.4 on the
ROUGE scale would be considered on target.
Let's score the DeepSeek R1 model we've been using since Chapter 2 using Python scripts.

43430.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43430.heading: Chapter 5 186
43430.content:
Chapter 5 186
In an ideal setup, we would have a fully automated loop for this evaluation. The steps for that
loop would be as follows:
An alert generation system such as Prometheus or Alertmanager posts a prompt to the
LLM's API to investigate the relevant logs. The LLM stores the log files in a location
accessible to the scoring automation.
The LLM stores the investigation result and its response somewhere accessible to the
scoring automation.
Run the scoring script file via a webhook trigger or cron job.
The scoring automation emits the score as a metric.
For the purposes of this chapter and making the example accessible, we've hardcoded the
example data and LLM evaluation. The output from DeepSeek was attained by first copying
and pasting the log into the session, combined idx_b45b8e85 with the following prompt:
From the log, tell me as concisely as possible about the node statuses.
This resulted in the text that was used in the evaluation scripts we'll run. Our first script looks
at ROUGE scores:
# Import evaluate
import evaluate

references=reference_log)
# Access ROUGE scores (no need for indexing into the result)

Running the script gives the following score:
$ python rouge_score_example.py
ROUGE-1 F1 Score: 0.22
ROUGE-L F1 Score: 0.15
For ROUGE-1 and ROUGE-L, both of these scores would be considered low. A ROUGE-1 score
would ideally be around 0.40, and a ROUGE-L score would be around 0.30. However,
DeepSeek gave exactly what was asked of it in the prompt. This difference between objective
scoring and subjective satisfaction makes ROUGE a useful, but not authoritative, metric. A
score-aware prompt would likely have resulted in a higher score. ROUGE scores should be used
in conjunction with other evaluation metrics to determine model accuracy, as their objectivity
does not account for the subjectivity of the end user.
Now let's look at a script for BERT scoring and see how DeepSeek performed. We'll run the
following script:
from bert_score import score
# Log and LLM Summary for evaluation
reference_log = ["level=info ts=2026-02-10T06:51:31.353816972Z

worker3` had their \"Ready\" condition set to \"Unknown\"."]
P, R, F1 = score(reference_log, model_summary, model_type='distilbert-base-
uncased', verbose=False)
print(f"BERTScore F1: {F1[0]:.4f}")
