43434.heading: Chapter 5 188
43434.content:
Chapter 5 188
The BERT scoring system more accurately rated the response DeepSeek gave, but it did take a
little longer to run than ROUGE. For idx_b20099e4 these scores to be ideal in production, they would need to
be 0.8 or above. However, the prompt given to DeepSeek prioritized being concise. It was
token-aware, not necessarily scoring system-aware.
Whichever scoring system you decide to adopt, if any, when you combine the score with
human review and add an additional dimension to the data (user satisfaction), it is possible to
get a more accurate understanding of how your model is performing. Over time, responses that
are considered good and their score averages can be aggregated, and the scores can become a
threshold. If the score on a response drops below where users are typically happy with the
system's responses, that would be the time to trigger a human review. You can have your
automation system emit these scores as a metric and use your observability stack to handle
deviations. After some time, you may determine that the occasional lower score isn't an issue,
but that you want to keep the threshold the same. Instead of calling humans for every response
with a low score, you might only send an alert if 10% of responses from the last hour are below
the threshold.
Here's a quick architectural diagram to help you picture this:
Figure 5.4: Turning scores into alerts
Ultimately, just as with any alert in any observed software system, the alert tuning and action
plan will be subjective. What you do in your organization may not be the same as what your
colleague does, or what is emerging as a known best practice, and that's okay. As long as you're
189 Democratizing Observability: A Primer to Self-Service Platforms
regularly evaluating and iterating to ensure what you're doing is working for your team, you're
doing it right.
The logistics of measuring response idx_7df91f87 accuracy are more challenging than simple performance
metrics. Something or someone needs to determine whether a response is accurate. How that
determination is made will depend largely on how the response is delivered. For example, if
the response is a Slack message to the team channel raising awareness of a system outage, and
human investigation reveals that it's a false positive, that would be an example of a human
review, and likely, there would be a bug fix to follow in the AI system. In situations where the
review comes from a human, such as PR reviews, whatever processes exist for measuring
accuracy will likely require some manual process, and potentially some mixture of clever
automation, such as labeling the PRs that were not accurate and running automation to count
them regularly.
However, where a PR against a GitHub repository is the expected output, you can use
automated quality gates to help ensure that at least a minimum level of accuracy exists in the

43435.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43435.heading: Chapter 5 188
43435.content:
AI output, and use the same technique of applying labels to measure when it's gone wrong. You
can then leverage CI tools such as GitHub Actions to send telemetry data to your observability
stack, allowing you to capture trends around the model's performance. With automation, the
sky is the limit; you're only limited by your own creativity and available time for creating
solutions to measure the accuracy of the output.
Finally, a third option is to have another AI agent determine whether the response is accurate.
Multi-agent AI orchestration adds some additional technical and financial implications. In
terms of level of effort, the tooling is evolving and it has become easier to support a model
where a separate AI agent acts as a validator, grader, or evaluator of the output of another
agent. You can see this as a teacher who validates and grades the work of a student. The
teacher gives feedback on what seems accurate and what doesn't. Just like humans evaluate
the work of others, the same concept can be applied to AI agents, with the result that those
agents should constantly get better.
We'll explore this a little more in Chapter 9, as ensuring you have accurate responses will assist
in building trust in your AIOps systems.
The last metric for AI observability we'll discuss in this chapter is PII leak detection. This
metric is closely related to idx_e06d682f guardrails, which we'll deep dive into during Chapter 9, but it is still
worthy of a dedicated segment now.
PII, which stands for personally identifiable information, is a protected class of information
that may be collected idx_5e3e59b7 during normal operations for a software system. Earlier, we indicated
that you'd likely place your AI agent behind an API. The method for doing this would be
through the implementation of a microservice known as the API gateway. This middleware

43436.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43436.heading: Chapter 5 190
43436.content:
Chapter 5 190
layer would handle routing all traffic to your agent, or agents in a multi-agent setup. If the
agent needs to request logs, the gateway would act as the middleman, which would process
that request and actually perform the log retrieval. A function of the API gateway could be to
validate that the response from the logging system does not contain potential PII, and to strip
it out of the body of logs if it does. The reverse flow is true; if somehow the agent became aware
of PII and tried to return it, the gateway would be able to catch and potentially sanitize that PII
from the agent's response before sending it on to the end user. An idx_45feb5cc example of such a gateway is
LiteLLM (https://docs.litellm.ai/). This is an API gateway purpose-built for LLMs and
integrates with another open source project idx_5108b2a4 from Microsoft called Presidio (https://
github.com/microsoft/presidio/) to suppress PII before it can make it to the model.
LiteLLM uses a declarative structure for this configuration, allowing you to modify YAML easily
to implement it.
Here is an example:
guardrails:
- guardrail_name: "presidio-block-guard"
litellm_params:
guardrail: presidio
mode: "pre_call"
pii_entities_config:
US_SSN: "BLOCK" # Block any request with SSN
CREDIT_CARD: "BLOCK" # Block credit card numbers

43437.heading: MEDICAL_LICENSE: "BLOCK"
43437.content:
MEDICAL_LICENSE: "BLOCK"
pii_entities_config should consist of any PII you know or have reason to suspect could exist
in your system. LiteLLM will also let you detect whether this guardrail was necessary.
Guardrail execution is an important metric, but it is idx_6d5c1cfe part of your overall security posture, so
we'll cover it more in Chapter 9. For now, let's look at how developers might expect to interact
with AIOps in an IDP.
AI is a capability of the IDP
The centralized platform becomes the centralized data hub, but the expectation remains that it
still works in service idx_b8a634cf of individual teams and their needs. The platform should provide data in a
way that is easily consumable, and the AI should help teams make the most of the data that
they have. The IDP also needs to safeguard access to that data and manage the costs associated
with the data. Where AI can be especially helpful here is in managing the quickly growing
volume of observability data.
191 Democratizing Observability: A Primer to Self-Service Platforms
How many times have you needed the observability data from 2:36 A.M. on a Tuesday six
months ago? Likely never, but you may have needed the data trends over the same six-month
period. You don't need to keep every single instance of every single metric. Using AI to do basic
data sampling can help to reduce the stored metrics down to means, medians, and modes over
time, and that time can be at whatever level of granularity makes sense for your organization.
By keeping only the data we need, and keeping the valuable information we got from the data
we no longer need, we can shrink our data stores without fearing that we'll miss out on a
critical piece of information. While we wouldn't recommend letting the AI delete data that no
longer needs to be stored, ensuring that it's available to end users who need sampling either
regularly or on demand, with the ability to write the output to a permanent locations, would
allow the platform team to use time to live or other data lifecycling features to automatically
prune old and less valuable data from the databases.
Additionally, if we believe we idx_5f640d2f may have PII in our stored logs or metrics, having an AI agent
crawl through it, sample the logs, and pull out only what's safe and statistically significant
would be faster than having a human try to script the same thing. Letting the AI access, parse,
and surface observability data to make it actionable for a development team is essentially the
perfect task for its capabilities. This brings specific value for an IDP that needs to have a unified
presentation layer that loads quickly, so end users actually want to interact with it.
While providing insights through the portal is important to give engineers quick access to all of
the data relevant to them, most software engineers don't want to spend most of their time in

43438.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43438.heading: MEDICAL_LICENSE: "BLOCK"
43438.content:
Backstage or a custom-built self-service portal. Software engineering teams want to spend
most of their time creating new services and features. They will spend most of their time
analyzing software requirement tickets, discussing the best approaches for implementation,
creating code to implement those feature requests, and committing their changes and
reviewing PRs. In the final section, we therefore look beyond the IDP and explore what types of
observability data to push into other tools developers use in their day-to-day routines.
Beyond IDP: Other places to push observability data
A successful IDP will meet users where they are. This means shipping sanitized, actionable
data to consumers in a way that integrates into their workflows, as opposed to breaking them.
Essentially, where users of the platform spend idx_0827d0fd most of their day is where data should be sent.
This could mean pushing data into Slack via webhooks, opening a Jira ticket automatically for
alerts and adding relevant data into the description, or even recording information into Git.
Historic benchmark records, test pass or fail histories, and similar data can all be recorded into
Git and compared against in the future.

43439.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43439.heading: Chapter 5 192
43439.content:
Chapter 5 192
The following are examples of what and where your observability tooling, including AI, may be
pushing data, and who might be consuming that data:
For developers: Push newly detected critical logs directly to developers via their IDE,
dev portal (Backstage), on the PR, or as a daily Slack message, instead of asking them to
learn yet another tool to find data that is relevant to them
For product owners: Push feature adoption metrics to the Jira ticket where the feature
was specified, instead of asking the business to get the data themselves from various
observability tools or dashboards
For performance engineers: Commit the top findings of a recent load test based on
observability data captured during the test to the codebase backing the CI pipeline that
triggered the test
Within your specific industry, there may be other best practices, and if you're using an
observability vendor, they may have some additional recommended best practices as well.
Understanding your security and compliance requirements is critical for knowing where you
should and should not push observability data. Observability is the art of turning data into
information. That information is idx_7c3daaa4 often need-to-know, so you will want to ensure you are
getting the right information, to the right people, in the right way. For example, it is important
to know that a user encountered a 500 error when interacting with the system, but identifying
who the user is is unimportant to getting the issue fixed and should never be included in any
data that is collected and stored.
It's important for any AI systems you're using to also understand and adhere to this principle,
which is why it's critical to put that information in instruction files. We'll talk more about
implementing guardrails and how to secure your AI systems in Chapter 9.
Remember that AI depends on instructions and input and is therefore susceptible to the
principle of garbage in, garbage out (GIGO). By idx_04df4fd8 ensuring your data is well structured and
explained, you avoid a long list of unhappy consequences. Any time an AI-enhanced tool leaks
user data, consider the following:
Was access to user idx_f52567d7 data necessary for it to do its job?
Could that data have been obfuscated?
Could that data have been better structured and explained?
Reasonable implementations should start from an understanding of the information
presented, the risks involved, and the nature of its destination. Where possible, start with the
least possible amount of access and data and increase as it becomes necessary. Don't let the
fear of missing out result in a security incident in your organization.

Provide code suggestions to fix the top performance hotspots in the code base I am currently working

me a risk analysis on which approach is better and why. These are two prompts a software engineer
would want to execute!
What sounded like a futuristic scenario a couple of months back is now a reality for some
organizations that have integrated their observability platform, code repositories, and coding
knowledge bases into the AI agents that integrate with development tools such as IDEs, Git, or
ticketing systems.
But observability-aware agents are not limited to idx_43d4fc40 development. As a Site Reliability Engineer
(SRE), I could prompt Suggest a scaling strategy based on the predicted workload patterns for the
next 7 days to ensure we keep our performance-related service-level objectives (SLOs) while not
increasing cloud spend by more than 10%. The advancements of AI and the emergence of
standards idx_762921d1 such as Model Context Protocol (MCP) or idx_0c307a6c the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol
enable AI agents to interact with platforms such as observability tools, Git, CI/CD, and
ticketing systems without creating lots of point-to-point tool integrations.
We investigate which real-life use cases the advancement in AI enables. We will focus on how
an agent that talks to observability can improve the everyday activities of software engineers,
SREs, IT Ops, or platform engineers to become more effective with observability data.

The output shows the time-saving potential for engineers. It eliminates the need to become an
expert in finding and analyzing observability data and then finding the corresponding pieces of
code to address any potential issues. It also eliminates the need for context and tool switching
as engineers can stay in their flow of work and in their tools of choice; they can keep coding in
their favorite IDE.
While the preceding output from an LLM is already impressive, it becomes more impactful if

The four phases of agentic AI
There are many idx_9dcd6f7e definitions given in this book, but let me give you one more from a public
knowledge base entry [1]:
Agentic AI builds on generative AI by enabling software agents to act with
autonomy. IDC defines it as systems that can make decisions, adapt to new
environments, and complete complex tasks with minimal human input. These
systems reason, learn from experience, and interact with their environment—often
coordinating across multiple agents—to continuously optimize outcomes.
NVIDIA, known for manufacturing the specialized computer chips that power many of the
data centers that run AI workloads, describes the four phases [2] that agentic AI goes through:
Perceive: Gather and interpret data from the environment or system.
Reason: Use LLMs and possibly retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to plan
responses.
Act: Integrate with external tools and software to execute actions.
Learn: Use feedback loops to improve future decisions through reinforcement learning.
What is relevant for this chapter is how and for which use cases an agentic AI can and should
connect with your observability platform in each individual phase.
Perceive phase
The most obvious phase idx_a5e707dc and use case is gathering data from the observability idx_e5c4293a platform in the
perceive phase. Looking back at both examples in the introduction section of this chapter. The
agent can query the observability platform to get information such as the following:
What are the top problems in my application?
What are the top security vulnerabilities?
There are many other examples of information an agent would query, such as the following:
What are the top failing API endpoints that have the biggest impact on our users?
What's the performance difference between the two deployed versions or features?
Are there logs that contain confidential data that shouldn't be there?
Are there overprovisioned clusters or workloads that can be optimized?
Are there idx_4eb36984 inefficient calls between services or to the idx_f62d95d5 database that can be optimized?

The agent can take idx_87511419 the information from the perceive phase into the reason phase and idx_29eaed53 craft a

observability tool during the reason phase, without having to rely on its own LLMs and RAG to
plan actions.
Act phase
The act phase idx_3328c3e3 would idx_e78e60b5 typically involve interaction with external tools that can make code or
configuration changes, such as proposing a code fix for the identified vulnerability or
proposing a change in the Kubernetes deployment manifests to adapt scaling or workload
sizing settings.
There are, however, use cases where agentic AI reaches out to the observability platform to
make changes there. Here are three examples:
Set up SLO-based alerting for the top three API endpoints of my service
Mark the detected problem as "in progress" or "known issue" and mute alerting for
now
Validate my release based on all observability signals you have, and give me a thumbs

The last example is common for those observability platforms that provide built-in
automation workflows to automate tasks such as automated validation of a release, a feature
flag, or even orchestrating remediation for problems. Dynatrace, New Relic, Datadog, and
probably other platforms provide similar built-in capabilities. If you have created workflows in
your observability platform that automate certain tasks, it's best for the agentic AI to simply
reuse those by triggering them, rather than replicating the individual steps.
Learn phase
Once an idx_0556fc0e action is idx_ee69cadc executed, it's time to learn whether that action had the intended effect. The
learn phase typically includes the agentic AI asking the user whether the proposed actions
solved the initial problem statement. That's valuable feedback that the agent can use the next
time a similar request comes up.

whether the root cause of the current problem might be related to a specific change. If that is

Bug tracking
A lot of information idx_957d2728 can be found in your issues and bug tracking systems. Whether this is in
Jira, GitLab, or GitHub Issues, it's a data source that can tell us whether somebody in the past
worked on a similar problem. An MCP server connected to that system can execute queries to
find bug tickets based on a similar problem description in the impacted application or services.
It can then analyze whether and how the problem was fixed in the past and provide this
information back to the developer. This idx_bf579516 saves a lot of time in identifying the next step, as it
could be that the problem was solved in the past, and we already know how to do it.
Status pages
You may idx_93ddbd4e remember October 20, 2025, as the day half the internet stood still. Why? Because
there was a major impact across the AWS US East Region. Whether it is AWS, Azure, GCP,
Salesforce, or any other third-party SaaS offering, the first thing to do is to check the status
pages of those services you are dependent on. If there is a known ongoing issue, then this could
be the root cause of your problem and will trigger a different course of action, as if all those
third-party services are running healthy. Integrating the information about status pages into
your AI agent allows for validating this additional data source. One option would be to use an
MCP server that connects to Downdetector [3], which is a service that provides real-time
problem and outage monitoring for a wide range of publicly accessible APIs.
CRM
Whether a problem idx_a75fcc59 impacts 1,000 users or just one should have no impact on how you
prioritize the problem. But on the other hand, when you have lots of fires to put out, it's
important to focus on the problem with the biggest impact. The biggest impact can mean that
a single premium user who is impacted by a new feature needs more attention than 100 non-
paying users who experience a performance degradation.
While idx_85e2e9e5 your real user monitoring (RUM) from your observability platform can tell you which
users, identified by user ID, are impacted, the CRM system can tell you how important those
users are for your business.

43448.content:
helps in prioritizing the problem at hand.
Git code and code history
If we identified that the idx_c4333a3a problem is caused by bad code, it's time to find out who wrote that
code originally or whether this code was recently changed. Looking at Git commit history is
the right place to start. An MCP server can easily analyze commit history to identify all relevant
code changes to a particular file, class, or function. When the code agent suggests code changes
to fix the problem, the agent can include the change history to ensure that things that were
fixed with a previous code commit don't break again. It also allows an agent to open up a Slack
channel with all involved developers who made code changes recently, present the evidence,
and ask for collaboration to find a solution.
Automating all idx_d3a71957 of this through an AI agent optimizes the otherwise manual tasks for a single
person to do the research manually and come up with similar conclusions.
Software catalog
Before making any idx_5052e4fe changes, it's good to know the potential impact on upstream or
downstream dependencies. If a fix includes calls to a new downstream service, then this
service will see an increase in traffic, and they must be prepared for it. If a fix includes changing
the behavior of our response, for example, changing performance behavior or a change in
service response body, then the upstream services that call us need to be informed.
Service catalogs are a good way to keep track of dependencies. They can either be managed
through idx_1e89f1d9 an internal development platform (IDP) such as Backstage, Port, Cortex, or Kratix.
Service catalogs can also be found in Configuration Management Databases (CMDBs) in
tools idx_06383f0c such as ServiceNow or BMC. Modern observability tools can also be a good source of
service catalog, assuming that you have enriched logs, metrics, and traces with metadata,
which we discussed in Chapter 3 in the Context is king section. Whatever your source is,
connecting that source through an MCP with the agentic AI allows that agent to make risk
assessments on changing the behavior through a code change. This will be additional
information presented to the engineers to make a faster, more informed decision about how to
fix the problem at hand.
As you can see, there are many tools that can be involved in an agentic AI workflow when an
engineer prompts it with the following: Analyze the current problems identified for the services I am
responsible for. Assess which problems to fix first and why. Identify the root cause, propose fixes where
necessary, and provide a risk assessment for deploying the changes.
By now, you have a good understanding of the power of agentic AI as it leverages observability
data, code insights, or ticket information through local or remote MCP servers.

Chapter 6 204
The recap on agentic AI and MCP has refreshed our memories on those important components
so that we can idx_3f7b4968 continue discussing how to best connect your observability data with the
agentic AI to maximize its impact.
Connecting observability data to your agentic AI
When prompting Tell me which problems I have in the services I am responsible for, the question is
how does the AI agent idx_83055ffe know which data it can query from idx_efd5f0e6 the observability platform to answer
this question? What is a problem anyway? Would we see this in logs or metrics? Or is there a
concept of a problem in the observability platform? How can we make sure that an agent is not
executing queries that are not efficient, resulting in high licensing costs? How can we make
sure the agent cannot access any confidential data or data not relevant to the task it's working
on? How can we make sure no confidential observability data gets exposed to other systems
that the agent talks to as well?
These are all very good and important questions to answer before moving on with a large-scale
implementation and rollout of your observability agent implementation. In this section, we
therefore focus on how to connect your observability platform, how to track usage, and how to
train the agent to become acquainted with observability to become more efficient when
executing tasks.
In this chapter, we treat our observability agent as an apprentice that we help to become a
master in observability. As in any trade, becoming a master starts with being trained on how to
use specific tools, for example, a hammer, a saw, and a screwdriver. This is followed by clear
guidance and feedback on how to become efficient with those tools and use them in
combination in order to achieve a certain goal, for example, crafting a table. We also
continuously measure the usage of tools and the outcomes to see when and whether our
apprentice reaches mastery.
As we raised the security and compliance aspect, Chapter 9 provides a more detailed
explanation of how to secure your AI and fine-tune your AI. If that's a topic of interest, look
into the sections titled Building trust in the AI and Securing the AI.
Now, back to our observability agent. We start with an apprentice that initially only
understands our written words, thanks to LLMs, but doesn't really know what to do with our
requests. We then define the tools, which are how we can access certain observability data
through an observability MCP server, for example, list current problems, and return critical log
messages. After that, we idx_b16acead provide guidance through instruction idx_50f70040 files on how to achieve a bigger
task, for example, list all the active problems and find the relevant critical logs for them. We
measure the results, refine the instructions, and give feedback on the results achieved until we

43450.heading: Chapter 6 204
43450.content:
have our master observability agent.
205 The Observability Agent: Real-Life Use Cases
Defining tools: Connecting your observability platform
through MCP
There is no need to idx_0b4141c2 go into the technical details on how to build an MCP server, as there is a lot
of documentation available online that you can follow [4]. Chances are that your observability
platform already provides an MCP server that you can either run locally or leverage as a
remotely hosted version. Many enterprises we have seen often start with the available MCP,
but sometimes decide to build their own to better control the available tools for the agents.
Another reason is to provide an MCP server with a set of tools independent of the backend
observability platform. So, when the platform in the back changes, or if there is more than one
platform used, then the MCP server acts like a transparent proxy.
Whether you build an MCP server from scratch or modify one for your own needs, there are
some considerations for the architecture and definition of the exported tools. Kudos to
Christian K., senior software engineer, who shared a lot of his learnings when building the first
open source MCP server for Dynatrace.
Start with the questions you need to answer
Put yourself in the shoes of the engineers who use an AI agent. What will they prompt, what
would an observability expert do to get the answer, and how would we make that information
queryable through the MCP? Christian's first use case was " I want to know which problems I have
in my application." The observability expert would have opened the observability tool and
looked at the currently opened alerts that the tool detected. As the terminology of his
observability uses problems instead of alerts, he decided to call the first tool of his MCP server
list_problems. That tool basically queried the API of the observability tool to return the
current list of open alerts. A short time after, other developers came to him and said that their
prompt would be Show me problems from yesterday, which required a change in the
list_problems tool to also include a timeframe parameter.
Whether it is about querying problems, incidents, alerts, metrics, logs, traces, events, synthetic
test results, SLOs, error budgets, or topology data, start by understanding the questions that
will be asked. Then, design your tools that allow the agent to query exactly that data for that
use case.
A good reference for basic tools that an observability MCP server provides is by looking at the
top vendors in the observability space and seeing what they provide. Here is a quick sample

tools, please check out the documentation of those vendors:

The preceding table is hopefully a good starting point for building your own observability MCP
server. Now, let's walk through some additional best practices and tips.
Tip: Don't mix read and write
The most common use cases for observability MCP servers are providing tools around data
access, such as get_logs, list_spans, list_problems, or execute_query. Those are all read-
access tools, meaning you are querying data from the observability tool. Another set of use
cases is around configuration or triggering actions on the observability tool, such as
create_workflow_for_notification, send_notification, or setup_slo.
The best practice is not to mix data access with other operations into a single MCP server. It's
better to provide multiple MCP servers, each targeted for its specific purpose. The reasons for
this guidance are as follows:
It avoids accidental execution of operations that modify observability configuration or
that trigger automation.
It reduces the attack surface when hackers try to do prompt injections. To read more
about this, check out the documentation on this from Invariant Labs [5].
•
•
207 The Observability Agent: Real-Life Use Cases
While it's possible for a user of an MCP server to select which tools should be active and which
ones not, it turns out that the majority just go with the default and always enable all tools.
To sum it up, if you intend to provide read and write access to your observability platform, it's a
good practice to separate those tools into separate MCP servers that must be installed
separately. You could call them Observability MCP Data Access and Observability MCP
Admin, as most write-access idx_62153e3f operations idx_1eadb22a are typically administrative!
Tip: Generic versus use case-specific
Most observability backends provide an API to execute generic queries with the query language
of the platform, such as with NRQL (New Relic), DDSQL (DataDog), DQL (Dynatrace), or
PromQL (Prometheus). For read access, it would therefore be sufficient to just offer a generic
execute_query tool, and then the agentic AI can use that tool to query any type of data that is
needed. While such a method is definitely needed, it is advisable to also think about more

43452.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43452.heading: Chapter 6 206
43452.content:
specific tools that return a specific set of data that is often requested, for example, get_logs,
list_incidents, or fetch_spans. While capturing logs can also be done through
execute_query, the get_logs tool can provide additional parameters for specific filtering on
logs, such as timespan, workload identifier, or hostname. get_logs can then craft the right
optimized query to retrieve exactly that requested data. This eliminates the need for the
agentic AI to guess the correct query in the target query language to achieve the same result.
The problem here lies in the word guess because, very often, an agentic AI doesn't come up with
the best optimized query from the start. Based on experience, those agents start with a broader
query or even queries that are not correct initially. They retry by refining the query until they
get the desired result. That refinement process not only takes time, but it also consumes
resources and often incurs additional costs, as every query API call to the backend observability
system typically comes with some type of query cost.
On the other end of the spectrum, it doesn't make sense to provide a tool for every specific use
case. For instance, it's not advisable to provide separate tools such as get_logs_from_k8s,
get_logs_from_hosts, get_logs_from_apps, and get_logs_from_serverless. While it's
possible to go that fine-grained, you need to consider whether this is really helpful, as you need
to maintain a lot of tool implementations, and there is a chance that the agent chooses the
wrong tool initially.
To sum it up, think about the questions and the top use cases your MCP server will serve. If a
common use case is to identify patterns in logs, then maybe provide a tool that is called
analyze_logs. This can execute the optimized queries to detect problematic log patterns and
return the result in a single call. This avoids a situation where an agent must execute many
different execute_query calls and then do the pattern identification based on all the data
returned. If it's more efficient to do all this within the observability platform, then do it there.

43453.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43453.heading: Chapter 6 208
43453.content:
Chapter 6 208
Tip: Local versus remote validation
When an agent is prompted with Give me an overview of all critical logs from yesterday, the agent
tries to craft a query based on the target observability platform's query language. What we
have observed is that the initial query that gets passed to the execute_query tool is often not
fully valid. We see a lot of syntax errors, as things such as yesterday might be represented in
different ways depending on the query language. The agent will overcome this problem by
updating the query based on any failure that comes back from the MCP server in a trial-and-
error fashion. And while, in the end, we get a valid result, it means that multiple round-trips to
the backend observability platform were necessary.
One way to optimize those round-trips is to add local validations into your MCP server that do
some basic checks, such as whether the query is syntactically correct, and whether the user has
permissions to access idx_be2671a0 this type of idx_e59a8b36 data. The syntax validation check alone will give the agent
immediate feedback, avoiding the additional round-trip to the backend observability platform.
This is faster, saves a network round-trip, and typically also saves costs on the backend.
Ideally, you have some observability of your MCP server and measure how many tool
executions fail due to incorrect queries or insufficient permissions. This gives you enough
evidence to add some local validation to your MCP server. We will talk more about the
observability of your MCP server in the Tracking and measuring usage and impact section later in
this chapter.
To sum it up, agents will not always get the optimal parameters for your tools on the first
attempt. If you understand the most common reasons why tool executions fail, you can add
local validation instead of leaving it all to the observability backend to validate any input. This
will greatly improve performance and save costs.
Now that we have a good understanding of how to connect our observability platform to
agents via tools idx_5db8835a exposed through an MCP server, let's dive into how to provide additional
guidance on how to use those tools.
Providing guidance: Instruction files for your AI agents
In the introduction of idx_3d55cba9 this section, we talked about idx_bfb422dd providing guidance to the AI agent to
elevate from being an apprentice to becoming a master in observability. Depending on the LLM
you use for your agents, the agent might already have some familiarity with observability and
therefore understands concepts such as logs, metrics, traces, or what a k8s cluster is. But
unless you use self-trained models with expert knowledge on the specific setup of your
observability platform, chances are that your agent really is only on an apprentice level.

43454.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43454.heading: Chapter 6 208
43454.content:
Instruction files are a way to provide guidance to agents. See them as a chance to explain the
domain knowledge to the agent without having to train a full LLM with all the insights. The
209 The Observability Agent: Real-Life Use Cases
following is a snippet from an instruction file for GitHub CoPilot giving detailed instructions to
the agent about how to help SRE and Operations teams when investigating problems and
incidents:
Figure 6.3: Agent instruction files help guide the agent with domain-specific knowledge on how to analyze
observability data

43455.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43455.heading: Chapter 6 210
43455.content:
Chapter 6 210
Without those instructions, an agent would simply start down an exploratory path of
gathering information. Exploration is a good thing, but it's time- and resource-consuming. If
you are an SRE and need a quick, deterministic answer to specific questions, the instruction file
achieves exactly that goal.
Instructions can become very detailed. The important part of the instructions is that you
specify clearly the situation, the goal, and the approach to take to achieve that goal.
Agents, by default, are only as good as the model you are using. While training your own model
is one option, you should consider using instruction files to give clear guidance on how the
agent should execute certain tasks that are asked through prompts. Make sure to read the
documentation of the agentic AI you are using. Follow the best practices on how to provide
instructions and find ways to distribute those instructions to every engineer who leverages
those agents.
Now that we know how idx_a0afd08a to improve the efficiency of our agents, we need to look into how we
can track the usage, measure performance and accuracy, and use this to optimize impact and
costs.
Optimization tip
To optimize querying and analyzing observability data, give instructions that reflect
good practices that experienced performance engineers would follow. That includes
metrics-first analysis, meaning first try to find answers in metrics as they are faster
and cheaper to query. Also, always specify a timeframe when querying data. The more
specific you make your prompt about the type of data and timeframe to analyze, the
faster and cheaper the executed queries will be. Adding this to your instruction files
ensures that your agentic AI calls your MCP server with these best practices in mind.
Tip
211 The Observability Agent: Real-Life Use Cases
Tracking and measuring usage and impact
Like with any software idx_17e0a17d service, app, or feature, it's important to track its usage, adoption, and
costs. The same goes for an MCP server. When building an MCP server that provides 10
different tools, but only 2 of them are used occasionally, the questions we need to answer are
the following:
Why are 80% of the tools not used? Shall we remove them? Or do we need to increase
the description and instruction files for agents to better leverage them?
Why is adoption low? Are there use cases that are missing? Is the data coming back of
poor quality, does it take too long, or is it too costly?
How can we get better feedback from our users about what they like and what should
be improved?
The solution to this is proper monitoring of your MCP server implementation. We need to use
the same observability best practices that we have discussed throughout this book. We need to
think about which metrics give us the insights about performance, usage, accuracy, or costs of

43456.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43456.heading: Chapter 6 210
43456.content:
the MCP server tools executions. We need to think about whether we need to add specific logs
for any troubleshooting or whether we need to look into distributed traces to better
understand the full agentic AI workflow, which also includes calling our MCP server.
Instrumenting the MCP server and beyond
You have many idx_fdffb776 options to instrument your own code. We recommend looking into
OpenTelemetry, which idx_def5540b we have covered extensively throughout Chapter 1 and Chapter 3. On
top of OpenTelemetry, there is the open source framework OpenLLMetry [6] from idx_7164d27e Traceloop.
OpenLLMetry provides OpenTelemetry-based observability for your LLM applications,
including support for MCP. It means you automatically get automated distributed traces, logs,
and metrics for all interactions with your MCP server. And it doesn't stop at your MCP.
OpenLLMetry provides insights when calling LLMs, vector DBs, or agentic frameworks such as
Anthropic, Amazon Bedrock, LangChain, LangGraph, Ollama, or OpenAI.
The following screenshot shows a sample trace published by the OpenLLMetry community on
their GitHub pull request 2829 for adding MCP observability support. The trace starts in the
agentic AI and includes idx_11448909 every call to the MCP server, including the name of the tool and the
arguments passed when it was called:
•
•
•

43457.heading: Chapter 6 212
43457.content:
Chapter 6 212
Figure 6.4: OpenLLMetry provides support for the MCP protocol to trace invocations from any agentic AI workflow
Having this detailed information in traces also allows us to extract metrics to answer the
questions raised earlier:
Which tools are executed? Which tools are not executed?
What's the performance of those tools? How many calls are failing, and why are they
failing?
When building your idx_884a0fce own MCP server, or when using MCP servers from a vendor, make sure to
instrument it so that you can better track its usage, adoption, and accuracy of results.
Analyzing the backend observability API calls
Whether it is execute_query, list_incidents, or get_logs, the MCP server will make calls to
your observability idx_ef2e4695 backend API to retrieve the request data or execute the desired operation.
It's also important to monitor those API calls as you need to answer the following questions:
Who is making calls to those APIs, and what data is retrieved?
Can the observability backend API scale to the increased demand coming in from the
MCP?
•
•
•
•
213 The Observability Agent: Real-Life Use Cases
Are there failed API calls? If so, are they caused by wrong usage of the API in a specific
version of the MCP server, or is it because of an issue in the observability backend?
Is there a way to do cost attribution of those API calls to individual users or teams?
The following screenshot idx_0dde5821 shows a dashboard that answers some of the questions raised
previously by analyzing the API calls to the backend observability API:
Figure 6.5: Analyzing observability backend API calls gives additional insights into usage, adoption, and
optimization potential, such as reducing erroneous calls
Agentic AI will change the way users interact with our software services, and this also means
that it will change the way observability data is consumed. You need to make sure that you
provide a stable and optimized observability backend that can handle the additional load
coming in through those MCP server API calls. But it's not just about handling the load; it's
also about constantly optimizing the way the MCP server is calling the backend. Therefore, go
back and revisit the Defining tools: Connecting your observability platform through MCP section,
which focuses on idx_c5ca2705 building a good list of MCP tools and teaching the agentic AI on how to best
call your MCP server to achieve optimal results for the end user.
Agentic AI observability
While observing idx_26797964 the MCP is key, observing the full agentic AI workflow is as important as just
observing the connection between the agentic AI and the observability backend.

43458.heading: Chapter 6 214
43458.content:
Chapter 6 214
Chances are that you will be integrating your observability platform into various different
agentic AIs to enable different personas in different tools to make better decisions based on
your observability data. In the next section, called Defining personas: Who is using the AI and
where?, we will talk about all those various use cases. It will become clear that we really need to
understand the end-to-end agentic AI workflow executions in order to understand usage,
adoption, and impact.
You might be using an agent in either of the following:
The IDE to support your engineers in making better coding decisions
The issue tracking system to enrich bug details with live observability data
The support ticket system to provide end user impact analysis
The CRM system to enrich customer information with the issues they ran into
The business reporting system to correlate business KPIs with technical problems
In any scenario where you are using or planning to use off-the-shelf or custom-built agents,
you should implement agentic AI observability. And this is not limited to only the use cases
where you interact with your observability backend, but should expand to all agentic AI use
cases and all the tools it connects to.
The emerging topic of AI observability probably needs a dedicated chapter or even its own
book. There is already plenty of material out there, but we wanted to make sure it also gets a
mention here. Thanks to open standards such as OpenTelemetry and OpenLLMetry, agentic
systems can be observed without too much of an effort. Check out the documentation of your
agentic AI development kit or talk to the vendor of your agentic AI solution to see how you can
get end-to-end workflow observability through OpenTelemetry sent to your observability
backend.
The following screenshot shows a idx_70934ddc distributed trace of a custom agent that leverages OpenAI
and several different tools to idx_8e16e5b4 fulfill a task. These details allow you to better understand what is
happening within an agentic workflow, which tools are called based on your prompt, where
things are slow or failing, as well as how many tokens are consumed when interacting with the
LLM as part of that workflow:

43459.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43459.heading: Chapter 6 216
43459.content:
Chapter 6 216
We are just scratching idx_da3d924b the surface here on the topic of agentic AI and LLM observability. Stay
up to date on the latest developments in that space, consult the documentation of the
frameworks and tools you are using, and strive to ingest traces, logs, and metrics into your
observability platform.
In this section, we covered what observability information should be exposed to an agent via
MCP, how to track its usage, and how to provide instructions for agents to elevate from an
apprentice to becoming masters of observability. We learned that agentic AIs are going to help
many different personas in their day-to-day work and that it's important to observe those
agents to identify their usage, internal workings, and costs. In the next section, we will take a
closer look at the idx_07fa1ac3 personas idx_118a544c and the use cases where observability data can help them make
better-informed decisions in the tools and processes they already use.
Defining personas: Who is using the AI and where?
We already got to idx_5a74dc20 know Christian, a software engineer who leverages an agentic AI in his
Visual Studio Code with prompts such as " Are there any problems with my app in production? If
yes, please investigate them, and let me know where in the code I can fix them! "
A lot of the observability-enabled use cases that get discussed at conferences or blogs focus on
how to improve the day-to-day activities of a software engineer in their IDE. But there are
many other people involved in planning, developing, testing, operating, and optimizing
software that can benefit from observability data that gets brought into their day-to-day
processes and used with tools through an AI. In this section, we will explore those use cases so
you can better understand where else observability and AI can have a major efficiency impact.
Who are your internal end users and their use cases?
If we look at the DevOps idx_25fbb5cc infinity loop that we used in Chapter 3 in the Tracking the SDLC
section, we see a lot of activities between planning, coding, deploying, and operating software.
In each phase, we have different types of engineers needing to make decisions about their next
step. In most of those steps, observability can help to make better-informed decisions. Let's
walk through some examples by looking at prompts that those individuals might want to
execute!
217 The Observability Agent: Real-Life Use Cases
Planning: What features to build, improve, or remove?
I am the product owner of our online customer self-service portal and need to plan our product
roadmap for the next 6 months to guide our engineers on what they need to work on. Analyze the
current feature usage of our online customer banking portal in production and identify the top and
least used features of that portal. Find out how much effort we currently put into maintaining all those

43460.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43460.heading: Chapter 6 216
43460.content:
features by analyzing the existing Jira tickets for those features. Then give recommendations on which
features we should remove without breaking core system functionality, which features we should
improve to increase user interactions, and give a time estimate for all those steps.
Whether done through a human or an AI agent, observability provides critical insights to the
preceding prompt, such as which features are currently used and which ones aren't, what are
critical user journeys that require certain features even though they might not be used often,
and which features have bad performance or high failure rates and therefore impact user
experience and should be optimized?
While we talk about end-user features here, the same prompt would also work for non-end-
user-facing software systems, such as APIs that you are exposing for external consumption.
Clearly, though, this prompt will save any product owner or business analyst a lot of time and
give them insights to make better decisions in their day-to-day work.
Building: How to improve the resiliency of our architecture
I am a software architect and am responsible for the cloud-native architecture of our core banking
system. Some of the services come from a vendor, but most of our services are custom-developed. All
workloads are properly tagged to distinguish them. Analyze all the problems we had in our own
software components over the past 6 months. Give me an analysis of problem areas, root causes, and
their impact on our end users. Provide suggestions on what improvements we can make to our code,
deployments, usage of existing cloud services, and architecture to reduce the risk of running into those
same problems again.
Software architects typically analyze their deployments and the dependencies between the
deployed services. They look at metrics to understand load behavior and extract dependency
information from distributed traces to understand cross-service impact. When tagging is done
properly, then all tag information is also available in the observability platform, as discussed in

43461.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43461.heading: Chapter 3 in the Context is king: the quality of observability data section.
43461.content:
Chapter 3 in the Context is king: the quality of observability data section.
While the final decision is still in the hands of the architects, getting an answer to this prompt
from an agent that analyzes the rich data in the observability platform via an MCP allows them
to make better-informed decisions.

43462.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43462.heading: Chapter 6 218
43462.content:
Chapter 6 218
Testing: What use cases are we not covering right now?
I am leading the quality engineering team, and my goal is to increase test coverage of our critical
backend APIs. I want to start by focusing on APIs that currently have no tests, and then move on to APIs
that do have tests but have still caused issues in production over the past year. Let's start with the
transfer-fund service. Identify the top 10 API calls of that service and give a recommendation on which
tests we should create and which ones need to be updated to identify those problems we have seen in the
past. Also provide some suggestions on test scenarios and test data to be used by creating a
representative dataset for each test case!
Quality engineers are often trying to catch up with all the changes and new features that
software developers put out. Leveraging AI can help them close this gap and also increase the
quality of tests executed. Ideally, you have observability enabled across your software
development life cycle, meaning idx_2a98b725 you capture logs, metrics, and traces not just in production
but also from your development and testing environments. This allows the agentic AI to
compare what has been tested and what is really happening in production. That would be the
ideal situation, as this avoids extracting this information from other tools such as the test
management system.
To refresh your memory about observability in testing, go back to Chapter 3 to the Choosing the
right metrics through proper load testing section.
This example shows yet again that agentic AI, in combination with observability, makes
quality engineers more efficient as they will be guided to focus on areas that have the biggest
impact. Nobody wants to create and maintain tests that cover the wrong things or test in the
wrong way. AI will greatly help here to improve the impact of quality engineering.
Releasing: When is a good time to release a new feature and to
whom?
I am the new release manager who recently took over from somebody who left the company. I need to
decide when the best time is to release a new feature in our customer self-service portal. Please analyze
whether there was any specific pattern of feature releases in the last 12 months for this application.
Give me an overview of which releases went well and which ones resulted in any issues. Based on the
data, give me a recommendation about when and how we should best release that feature to minimize
impact to our end users in case something goes wrong.
It's never easy to take over a role from somebody else and not have enough time to learn
everything there is to learn. There is a lot of tribal knowledge that often gets lost. When
integrating observability into your software delivery and release process, you can identify the

43463.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43463.heading: Chapter 6 218
43463.content:
impact of a release as shown in Chapter 3 in the AIOps: reducing the noise with anomaly and root
cause detection section.
219 The Observability Agent: Real-Life Use Cases
As a release manager, I can then leverage that information and make better-informed decisions
based on historical data that shows which changes, deployments, and releases of software
have caused issues and what their blast radius was.
Operating: What's the best way to mitigate production issues?
I am an SRE responsible for our critical backend services. We are preparing for Black Friday, where we
expect double the incoming traffic than we normally have. Identify all services where we have had
load-related issues in the past 12 months. Analyze traffic growth trends for those services, factor in that
traffic will double, and identify those services that don't have proper sizing defined. Then find all
runbooks for those services and analyze when they have been used and updated the last time. I want a
risk-based analysis with probabilities on which services will most likely fail, which ones need an update
to scaling rules, and where we need to update our runbooks to ensure we can react faster to any
problems that come up and stay within our SLOs!
SREs are the ones who need to ensure resiliency in production. The preceding prompt requires
a lot of information from observability, such as current and past load patterns, analyzing
problems that happened that were related to load, or incorrect sizing of the workloads. It also
talks about SLOs, which are defined in the observability platform and which we have discussed
in very much detail in Chapter 3 in the A primer on SLOs: learnings from Google's SRE handbook
section.
We hope that those idx_8b9fcb02 examples allow you to go back into your organization and start a
discussion about what decisions you need to make on a daily basis and how agentic AI with
input from observability helps you make better-informed decisions.
Once we have answered that question, we also need to ask, Where and in which tool do you want
to get this information?
From which tools do engineers interact with the agent?
If we were to only idx_afb3be1b focus on software engineers, the most likely answer to Where do you want to
interact with the agent? will be: my IDE, for example, Visual Studio Code or IntelliJ. It could also
be that you are already using some of the new agentic coding IDEs, such as Cursor, Cline, or
Amazon Q.
However, developers do not spend all their time in an IDE. In addition, all the other personas
we just discussed use various tools throughout the day, where you need to think about how to
integrate your agentic AI to deliver insights from observability to make better decisions faster.
Let's walk through a set of tools that I am sure you also have in your organization.

43464.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43464.heading: Chapter 6 220
43464.content:
Chapter 6 220
Project management and issue tracking tools
There are many tools in that space on the market. A prominent vendor is Atlassian with Jira.
Whether you use Jira or other tools to track your projects and issues, when looking at a ticket,
an agent built into that tool can immediately pull in context-aware information about the
ticket. The following screenshot shows how additional information about a performance
problem on the Gateway API was pulled in by an agent from the backend observability
platform. This eliminates the need for the person working on that ticket to log in to various
tools to find that information. In this case, the relevant information comes to the person who
needs it to decide what to do next:
Figure 6.8: The Atlassian Rovo Ops agent pulling in relevant data from the observability backend based on the
context of the ticket
It is best if you sit down with your engineers who use that set of tools and ask them what
information they typically require when working on tickets. If there is information that is
available in idx_75cb608e observability, then the best would be to bring this right into the UI, which avoids
context switching and therefore optimizes the day-to-day work.
221 The Observability Agent: Real-Life Use Cases
Collaboration and chat tools
Slack, Teams, Confluence, Miro, Asana, and Monday, to name a few, are tools that fall into the
category of collaboration and chat tools. Chances are, we find more than one of those tools in
every organization. For chat tools in particular, there is an obvious integration scenario
through a chatbot that gives easy access to observability data. For anybody who participates in
a conversation about a particular topic, or if engineers discuss a certain feature, having a
chatbot that can respond to the following prompt would greatly improve the efficiency of
those teams: Where is the latest version of our build deployed, and are there any new logs that need
our attention?
Another common use case is to pull in a chart into an existing conversation, such as Give me the
network traffic forecast for our critical services, as you can see in the following screenshot.
Figure 6.9: Prompting a bot to pull in graphs and data from observability into your chat
Tip
Analyze conversations your teams have in your collaboration tools. Identify use cases
where they start posting screenshots of dashboards or findings from distributed traces.

43465.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43465.heading: Chapter 6 222
43465.content:
Chapter 6 222
Customer service and support tools
This is a very similar idx_45b6b9c1 use case to the issue tracking system. Instead of engineers looking at their
bugs and pulling in observability data to make it easier to identify how to fix the problem
faster, we are now talking about customer success managers or customer support engineers
who work on tickets submitted by their users in case they run into a problem.
Consider the scenario where a banking customer has issues logging in to their mobile banking
app. They get on a call with customer support, who sees all the details about the customer in
their support ticketing system. An agentic AI in that system can pull in live observability data
using prompts such as Are there any other users in our system that have similar problems? The
answer could be Yes, it seems this issue impacts other users who are on the older version of our iOS
version of the app. The latest version doesn't show this issue any longer. Please suggest to the customer
to upgrade their mobile app and try again.
Having this information at the time when being on a call with a frustrated customer will
change the conversation from A customer is frustrated and wants to blame it on the support
engineer toward We have a quick solution for you to get you back on track. Anything else we can do for
you today?
Business reporting tools
Business leaders typically turn to business reporting tools to understand business success,
such as generated revenue per region or product category, the number of processed claims, or
the success rate of delivered items. When revenues drop, claims stall, or deliveries fail, the
question is why? Is nobody interested in our products? Do we need to hire more people to work
on claims? Do we need to switch our delivery service provider? Or is the answer a technical
issue, such as a global cloud outage that is currently impacting half of the internet?
Integrating observability through an AI agent into the business reporting tool gives the
business leader additional insight to better understand the situation and make a faster
decision on how to address the business-impacting situation. A prompt such as What is the
reason for the revenue drop in our sales region in Europe? could be answered with There seems to be
an issue with two of our top three payment providers in that region. Their Payment API suffers from
high failure rates and timeouts. This could be related to an ongoing network issue in the region, which
is currently impacting many of the cloud providers.
As you can see, integrating observability into your business reporting and analytics processes
will benefit your business decision-makers as they can leverage real-time information
Those are indications where a more self-service model will speed up that collaboration

43466.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43466.heading: Chapter 6 222
43466.content:
process by making it easier to get this information at the time when they need it.
223 The Observability Agent: Real-Life Use Cases
available in your observability backend about your system, but also any third-party APIs or
services your business relies on.
There are most likely many more tools you have in your organization that are currently having
a limited, siloed view. Bringing observability data into those tools, into the hands of your
engineers, product owners, customer success managers, or business leaders, allows them to
make better-informed decisions.
The final question idx_fe587d26 we want to discuss in this section is whether we can turn around how data
gets to those who need it. Does it always have to be users pulling data by executing prompts?
Or can we also push data to them at the time when they need it, without them having to ask
for it?
From manual pull prompts to automated push results
Prompting for idx_cef70ac1 observability data is most effective when you can practically do it from
anywhere and within any tool, and when the agent executing your MCP server understands
the context you are working in. This context may include which Git repository you are
currently working on, which bug you are investigating, or which customer you are interacting
with in a support ticket. But there are two things that come to mind where prompting might
not be the best approach:
What if I don't know what question to ask? How shall I know which insights I can get
to make better decisions?
What if everyone in the organization requests the same data all over again? Isn't that
inefficient?
Once we enable an organization with the ability to prompt information from their respective
tools, we can leverage the insights we can get from those interactions to answer those
questions. We get those insights by observing your MCP server and your agentic AI workflows,
as explained in the Tracking and measuring usage and impact section earlier. Once we know
which prompts are executed, by whom, at which time, and from which tools, we can identify
patterns such as the following:
What information is prompted for what purpose?
Is the same information prompted across various teams for the same reason?
What other insights are there that nobody prompts for yet?
Let's walk through three quick use cases to explain how we can use those usage insights and
convert some of the manual pull prompts into automated push results.
•
•
•
•
•

43467.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43467.heading: Chapter 6 224
43467.content:
Chapter 6 224
Use case: Push daily standup insights into Slack/MS Teams
This use case comes from an engineering team of a large software vendor that started to
leverage GitHub CoPilot in Visual Studio Code to pull in information for their daily standup. As
explained in the Providing guidance: Instruction files for your AI agents section earlier, they started
expanding their instruction files to get more details every morning for their 8 AM standup.
They wanted to know about any new error logs that were identified during the nightly tests,
any customer-impacting issues that were reported the day before that are still open, and
insights into performance hotspots they could optimize. Other development teams heard
about this and started to copy those instruction files and run the same prompts when starting
their standups.
While all this works idx_9826c53e great, it was a lot of copy-and-paste effort to keep those instruction files in
sync across development teams. Execution times also got longer as those instruction files grew,
and at some point, they realized that those queries against the MCP server were not always
efficient, resulting in unforeseen query costs or simply having to wait longer for an answer.
To optimize the prompts and make them available to any development team without having to
execute those prompts manually at the start of every standup, they decided to use some simple
automation that executed those queries against the backend observability platform every day
at 7:45 AM. The automation executed those queries for every development team that opted in
for that self-service, and it then sent the result into the respective Slack or MS Teams channel
so that each team could start their meeting on time at 8:00 AM, reading through the
information that was presented to them.
Instead of having multiple copies of instruction files, they now have a central automation
script that can be updated and maintained by all teams through a standard pull request
process. Any improvement will automatically benefit every team. The automation script itself
uses optimized queries against the observability backend and doesn't rely on well-trained
LLMs or instruction files, which also makes this approach more deterministic and typically a
bit cheaper. AI is used to take all the results of the individual queries and bring them into an
easy-to-read and understandable format before posting this as a message to their chat.
Use case: Push observability insights to pull request
Engineers who make code or configuration changes typically push them through pull requests
into the main branch so that those changes get built, applied, or deployed. The big question
after a pull request is Was this a good change or not?
While an engineer can use an AI agent built into the pull request workflow to execute prompts

43468.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43468.heading: Chapter 6 224
43468.content:
such as Are there any problems with the deployment of this pull request?, we can turn the flow of
information around and have a system set up that automatically pushes observability insights
to the pull request once that data becomes available. As an engineer, I therefore don't have to
225 The Observability Agent: Real-Life Use Cases
pull for information; instead, the relevant insights come to me as part of my pull request. There
are different ways to implement this. It could be an action that gets executed as part of the pull
request, or you implement it as an automated push once your observability platform detects
any issues. The end result, however, is the same: the engineer gets observability insights
without having to think about it.
The following idx_6f7a7498 screenshot shows automated validation of pull request changes against a set of
observability objectives. The resulting observability score is automatically posted back to the
pull request, providing fast feedback to the engineers about the quality of their proposed code
changes:
Figure 6.10: Integrating observability insights into the Git workflow brings relevant insights to the engineers where
they need it
This example reinforces a key shift in how we show the value of observability: Bring the relevant
insights to the engineers and don't ask them to find the information in various tools.
Use case: Push daily business insights via emails
Just as software engineers have their daily standups discussing current work items and asking
for help on any current blockers, business leaders often begin their day by looking at critical
business indicators to make sure they understand if there is anything that needs their
immediate attention. In our Business reporting tools section earlier, we discussed the use case
where observability data can be pulled into business reports to give leaders more contextual
information about why they may see a negative impact on their business goals.
And just like with the daily standup example for engineers, we can turn around the flow of
insights and push relevant actionable insights to business leaders.
For those of you using Microsoft 365, you probably know the Daily Digest service, which sends
you an email first thing in the morning that gives an overview of important emails that need

43469.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43469.heading: Chapter 6 226
43469.content:
Chapter 6 226
your attention, files that have been shared with you but you haven't yet looked at, or
documents where you were tagged in a comment that needs your reply.
What Microsoft does for Office 365, you can also do with your business insights extracted from
your observability data. We have seen organizations that simply set up an automation
workflow that queries information such as What are the top customer-impacting technical issues
right now and who is impacted? or What is user adoption of your latest features? or Are there any
issues with our third-party vendors, and is there a need to reach out to them?
A daily Business Insights Digest that provides business leaders the right level of information to
start their day, versus having them open multiple tools, dashboards, or reports, is what will
make them more efficient.
This brings us to the end of the section on understanding who your internal end users are,
what type of roles they have, what type of information can be extracted from observability
data, and how they can benefit from their day-to-day activities. We closed it with a suggestion
to not just make it easier to prompt this data, but also think about what type of insights from
observability we can actively push to users at the time when they need it and within the tools
they already use.
On the final stretch of this chapter, we are moving away from just delivering data via an MCP
to an agent that sits in another tool. It's great to open the world of observability to GitHub
CoPilot, Atlassian's idx_71495eeb Rovo Ops agent, AWS frontier agents, or any other agentic AI. But what if
we think about an autonomous observability agent? What would such an agent look like?
Which use cases can it orchestrate, and how would that agent connect with other agents?
Using observability agents to get from reactive to
proactive operations
It's 4:37 PM on Friday. You are idx_99a16a9f an SRE and were just added to a Slack thread with five of your
engineering colleagues, called customer-service-4733. The thread has been going on since
yesterday at 2:05 PM. It looks like at least 100 messages have already been exchanged,

The scenario described shows how powerful an agent can be when it integrates seamlessly into
existing processes. It automates analyzing existing conversations, captures additional insights
from various data sources, and comes up with recommendations on next steps.
The SRE is still the one who makes the ultimate decision, but the information provided allows
the team to make better and faster informed decisions. This helps them to stay on track and
reach their goals of ensuring resilient systems, and it gives them time to work on more
interesting things other than troubleshooting and firefighting.
Achieving goals faster is a big motivator. In the remainder of this chapter, we will look into
additional use cases, but also into different engagement models of agents. So far, we have
discussed use cases that typically started with a prompt. While this is the most common
conversation idx_a1554e9e model, we are also seeing organizations looking into fully autonomous agents
that actively join or start conversations or trigger actions to address situations before involving
human operators. This has the potential to allow teams to reach their goals even faster.
Goal-driven engineering

tracking service such as Fitbit, you know that those types of services try to keep you engaged as
well as they can. They continuously remind you to stay on your learning or fitness path so that
you have a higher chance of reaching your goals faster. And, of course, they want you to
consume more of their platform and eventually purchase their premium plans or make in-app
purchases.
There is a lot we can learn from those consumer apps and services, especially around how they
start the engagement. Typically, you open the app whenever you have time to check how many
more steps you need today to reach your daily goal or how many more points you need to make
to advance to your next learning league. But the system also actively engages with you. There
are app notifications reminding you that you have 10 more minutes to complete your hourly

Defining goals for engineering
Instead of always having to prompt an agentic AI with questions such as Can you explain that
problem to me? or What are the top performance hotspots that I should fix?, we need to think about
agents that actively notify us about things we should do so that we achieve our goals. Our
goals here would be the following:
Faster time to market: Deliver software on time without performance problems
Improve resiliency: Increase the availability of our software to meet our SLOs
Reduce risk: Never operate software with critical vulnerabilities
Optimize costs: Ensure optimal configuration of your deployments
Besides these four examples, think about your own internal engineering goals that will help
you achieve your business goals. Then, for a moment, assume that you can hire any expert in
areas you need to improve, such as someone who writes excellent code, a security expert, a
performance wizard, a master in observability, or a cloud infrastructure guru. What is it that
you want those experts to do to elevate our engineering organization to produce better output
and achieve their idx_ceaa92b2 goals faster?
Would they participate in a daily standup?
Would they participate in code reviews?
Would they do pair programming?
Would they conduct performance tests?
Would they give coding recommendations?
Now, let's see how we can implement this.
Achieving goals: Prompting Center of Excellence
While the preceding idx_530cdea4 ideas are great, the challenge typically comes with scaling this across an
organization. If you have 100 engineering teams, it's hard to hire the number of experts in the
various fields to place them within those teams.
The solution in the past has been to create Center of Excellence (CoE) teams that provide
centralized services on topics such as performance, security, FinOps, delivery, and so on. And
