The first solution to this scale challenge is that modern CoE teams take their expertise and
make it available as a self-service model. We have discussed different self-service approaches
quite extensively in our recent book Platform Engineering for Architects: Crafting modern
platforms as a product. That book explains how organizations can scale expertise beyond
individual teams by providing it through a centralized self-service platform.
Throughout this book, we have also highlighted many of those self-service scenarios. For
example, in the Collaboration and chat tools section, we discussed the use case of an engineer
requesting observability data through a prompt in a Slack conversation. CoE teams that used
to provide this data upon request by manually replying to those messages simply automated
their expertise and made it available through a self-service model.
While prompting is an important first step toward scaling the expertise that a few people have
within an organization, there idx_2f4220ea is another approach to make this even more impactful.
Scaling: From prompt to autonomous agents
What if you are not aware idx_50f6dc18 that you can ask your CoE to give you recommendations on how to
optimize your code or improve performance? What if you do not know that you have a chatbot
or an MCP server that you can prompt to help you rewrite your code to fix a vulnerability?
Ideally, expert knowledge should come to you at exactly the right time to help you make the
right next decision. It's like with your fitness tracker app: it sends you a notification 10 minutes
ahead of time to remind you about your hourly step goal, and not when it's too late.
To truly scale expertise knowledge within an organization, the next step after self-service
prompting is autonomous agents that actively reach out to the teams and engineers with
expert advice and insights so that they can achieve their goals faster.

Use case – FinOps: redistributing workloads
FinOps is a critical topic idx_8857fb05 for all organizations as it aims to optimize resource utilization to meet
both business needs while staying within financial boundaries.
FinOps teams, therefore, constantly analyze the demand for specific services or workloads and
how those demands change. If a certain service or application is now used by more users than
before, it may need an upgrade. It could also be the other way around: a service is less used
than in the past and can now run with a fraction of the initially allotted resources.
Observability can be used to identify the actual requirements of resources of a workload over
time. FinOps teams analyze historical data or use algorithms to predict future resource
utilization by considering changes in the usage behavior of upstream services. This data can
then be used to distribute those workloads to the right shared infrastructure.
Another use case relates to hardware, especially from cloud vendors, which is constantly
updated with new chipsets. Observability can tell you which workloads are GPU-intensive, and
you can use that information to move them to hardware that is optimized for those types of
workloads if performance is a key requirement.
A FinOps observability idx_48e7f129 agent can automate most of the work of a FinOps and automatically
open pull requests for the infrastructure team with newly recommended sizing.
Use case – Observability data quality checks
What if you send log idx_f72de1db files, but nobody ever looks at them? What if your services emit metrics,
but nobody ever uses them on a dashboard or for an alert? What if you have just enabled
distributed tracing and now the same exception that used to be captured in logs is also
captured in your traces?
Observability teams often look over the data that gets ingested into the backend platform. That
is done to make sure that all relevant data gets captured. But it is also done to validate that the
data that gets stored is later also used for analysis.
An observability agent can automate these observability data quality checks on a continuous
basis and either send a chat message or create a bug ticket for engineers that instructs them on
optimizing the quality of idx_38768501 their observability data. Here is an example of such a bug ticket:

Summary
In this chapter, we explored what an observability agent can look like in real life. We covered
the initial steps by allowing your engineers to use LLMs to ask questions that can be answered
by connecting your observability backend to the LLM via open protocols such as MCP.
We then discussed how to efficiently design and implement an observability MCP server by
first understanding the personas and the use cases this technology enables. We learned how
we can train agents using instruction files to improve the accuracy and quality of the delivered
responses. Finally, we discussed how, instead of prompting an LLM for specific insights, we can
build autonomous agents that actively integrate into our day-to-day processes to give us
expert opinions at scale.
In the next chapter, we again open the doors for ACME Financial Services and see where their
journey takes them as they are explore the power of agentic systems.

Let's do a quick recap of ACME Financial Services' journey so far before we continue their story
of discovery and improvement. If you recall, ACME Financial Services started its observability
improvement journey after it had completed its cloud migration and discovered that its
observability practices were failing it. They were seeing increased issues affecting customers,
an increase in resolution times, and increased employee burnout, among other issues. Most
importantly, the company's reputation was being negatively impacted, and that was making it
more difficult to win and retain customers. So the company put together a task force to figure
out how to improve the problems they were seeing.
The task force had a huge job in front of them and started by digging into the root causes of the
problems the company had been facing. Uncovering the root cause was only the beginning, as
they began investigating potential solutions. Since they hadn't been keeping track of
improvements in observability practices and tooling, they had to do a lot of research and
evaluation. After a lot of research and product evaluations, the working group decided on a
combination of new standards, new AI-capable tools, and a set of training materials. Since they
needed money for the new observability tool, they had to get approval from senior leadership.
Luckily, the team made a compelling case and got senior leadership support for their plan,
including the new observability vendor.
Investigating solutions and creating a plan was half the battle. The working group had to
implement their plan and be able to show improvements to senior leadership. They were well
prepared because of all the investigative work the working group performed, and while it took
a few years, the team was able to get their plan implemented. They were able to show
improvements in each problem area they targeted.
ACME Financial Services made enormous improvements in their observability practices, but
like many organizations, they are discovering that despite their progress, they still have more
to do. New cost pressures, unmet user needs, and the untapped potential of their existing
tooling are pushing the company toward its next evolution: an agentic platform.
In this chapter, we will cover the following topics:
Defining the end users and the pain points to solve
How an agentic platform helps
Crawl, walk, run: Breaking agentic platform projects into milestones

For this chapter, there are no technical requirements.

The observability working idx_7d0e25fc group at ACME Financial Services celebrated the completion of their
massive journey, and the impacts of their work were felt across the company. The company's

reputation was recovering, but it didn't take too long before new issues started to appear. First

incidents, mean time to resolution (MTTR), fewer idx_0694e552 resources spent debugging issues, and
saved development time by concentrating on popular and well-used features. While the

with the current and projected cost of operations, so they asked for an explanation as to why

The cost drivers
The observability working idx_9c127dff group started work on determining why the operations spend did
not decrease as they expected. The working group knew they needed data in order to focus on
the area(s) driving the largest expenditures. Since all of the changes were kept on-premises
and all deployed resources were labeled well, it was a rather simple process to gather the cost
data on the new infrastructure deployed as part of the observability improvements.
After gathering and analyzing the costs for the new infrastructure, the working group realized
that the costs for the new observability tooling were much higher than they had expected.
More compute resources were required than planned, which meant that not only were the
licensing expenses higher than expected, but the infrastructure costs to run the tool were
higher as well.
The working group also decided to do some research about costs related to observability and AI
projects. What they found surprised and dismayed them because they discovered that many AI
projects fail. They found that a McKinsey report showed only one-third of all AI projects make
it into production (https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-
insights/the-state-of-ai), which means two-thirds of AI projects are failing or stalling.
While they didn't find a single reason why those projects fail, they did find a few problems that
can cause AI projects to fail. AI needs good data in order to provide any utility. Despite the
training and work the team had put into the effort, they didn't have a clear idea of whether the
data the company was producing was of good enough quality. They thought it was possible
their data was just good enough to provide some utility while also causing a lot of wasted time,
and that could also be a cost driver.
The observability working group also realized that they would need to determine a way to
track cost savings for this initiative so they could present the benefits to senior leadership.
While they had some avenues to pursue to improve costs, it was becoming obvious that the
cost savings might not show up in the cost of operations alone. Results such as reducing
downtime, preventing outages, and even improving application development team design are
all benefits with real financial impacts that would be missed by looking at the operational cost
alone.
As a starting point, the working group decided they needed to talk with the users of the
observability tools in order to understand how the observability tools are being used and the
value they are providing. This meant getting input from the SREs and application development
teams to assess idx_ef606c1d whether the tooling helped them. Without good data, even the best SREs or
developers will struggle, and if the tooling isn't providing those groups with useful

43482.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43482.heading: Chapter 7 240
43482.content:
information, then they will be spending a lot of money on a tool and not maximizing the return
on investment.
241 ACME Financial Services: How to Move from AIOps to Agentic Platforms
A new challenge: Business process observability
A funny thing idx_9e82b1ae happened as the observability working group was gearing up to dive into the
soaring costs of their observability journey. Business leaders reached out to the working group
with a problem they hoped the observability improvements could address.
ACME Financial Services is a large and complex company that serves many different markets
with differing regulations. This means that no task is as simple as just clicking a button. The
problem the business leaders wanted to solve was to understand which applications and what
parts of the business are involved in each function the company performs.
The observability working group hadn't considered this aspect of the work they had been
driving, so they told the business leaders that they would investigate and get back to them.
They discovered that this type of observability is generally known as either business process
observability or idx_c93096cc simply business observability. They also discovered it is useful for
understanding the complex inter-operations of a company and for understanding the business
implications of problems, potential bottlenecks, and opportunities for optimization.
The team realized that this new use of the data they helped create with the observability
improvements could have a big impact on the company. Even with the improvements in
ownership metadata, there was currently still no understanding of the entire chain of events
and the applications involved in any operation the company performed. The insights from
business process observability would help the operations teams understand the business
impact of an issue. It could help teams recognize flaws in application and system designs that
could lead to more performant and resilient services. It could allow inspection of not only each
step in a process, but also which applications, and how many, are involved in each step. If done
properly, it would allow the business to understand what steps are taken for a certain business
process, such as updating mutual fund stock values or opening a new account.
It was a bonus that the additional insight this could provide would help justify the cost
associated with the observability improvements, should they be unable to bring down the
costs as much as idx_1cf89d35 senior leadership wanted. The working group figured this avenue could
provide a little bit of breathing room in their quest to reduce costs.
A new round of discussions
Once again, the observability working group undertook a series of discussions with various
teams across the business to help understand how teams were impacted by the observability

changes. They focused on how people used the observability tools and the data available to

Chapter 7 242
Feedback from the application developers
The application idx_2f6b705d development idx_4a4aa7f9 teams revealed they weren't really using the observability
tooling or data very much at all. They took the training and tried the tools when they were
rolled out, but almost every team they talked to ended up not using the tools or the data. There
were a few common reasons why this ended up being the case:
The observability tooling itself wasn't easy to navigate for people not familiar with
observability concepts and practices. The training attempted to cover this gap, but the
reality ended up being that the tool wasn't easy enough for the application developers
to navigate.
Some application developers were able to access the tool and start navigating through
some of the information, but they had difficulty translating the information in the tool
into actionable changes within the application teams.
Application developers have different kinds of tools they use to accomplish their goals.
These tools are required for them to perform their work, and attempting to push a tool
onto them when they have difficulty seeing the benefit or integrating it with their
workflows didn't work.
The end result seemed to be that the application development teams hadn't really changed
their development habits at all.
The team found these conversations were both dismaying and encouraging. They were
dismayed because they meant a lot of the work they had put into the effort wasn't being given
the chance to succeed. They were encouraging because they also meant there were still
opportunities for idx_f67009fd improvements idx_f3cfe5e5 and cost savings if they could figure out how to make the data
or the tool more usable for the application development teams.
Feedback from the SREs
The discussions idx_bcdf6212 with the SREs were enlightening in idx_352f88e8 different ways. Unlike the application
developers, the SREs were well versed in observability practices and concepts, and they didn't
have problems navigating the tool or using the data. However, the SREs highlighted that there
were a few problems with the new observability tools:
The metadata wasn't consistent. Despite the training provided on the importance of
and standards for metrics and metadata, each application team ended up

with a similar policy in the observability world idx_b5eb6d42 called sampling. In large companies such as
ACME Financial Services, it is not viable to process and store every piece of telemetry data if a
desired goal is to be financially responsible. That is why ACME Observability, and the industry
at large, recommends using sampling to reduce that storage and processing burden while still
maintaining all the data necessary to identify the root cause of incidents. The ACME

Assessing sampling
After their meeting with ACME Observability, the working group realized they had more
research to do around sampling. According to the vendor, sampling could provide significant
cost savings, but they didn't really understand how to implement it in a single application, let
alone across the entire company.
The working group researched sampling and discovered that while it is a common practice for
dealing with large amounts of telemetry data, there isn't a single, or even simple,
implementation of sampling. There are a few common strategies, such as head, tail, or random
sampling, but which strategy is best can depend on what is important for diagnosing
production issues.
The group decided to idx_60c03052 use a simple example as an exercise to understand how sampling would
help control costs. They decided on using the maximum number of connections per hour,
which could be an indicator to help scale an application. The group decided to try evaluating
two data sampling methods: head sampling and tail sampling.
Head sampling makes a decision about the metric data at the beginning of an interval, and tail
sampling makes a decision about the data after you have all the metrics for the time interval.
Their idea was that an application would only need to report the metric if the number of
connections being managed had increased when the connection was initiated. It was a simple
configuration, but at some point, the application would need to reset its internal counter to
ensure proper reporting over an hour timeframe. In their evaluation of this scenario, they
determined that latency and connection errors would probably be lost. Any sharp spikes or
drops in connections over the course of that hour would also not be accurately identified. The
group wasn't sure whether that was an acceptable trade-off for all applications. In fact, for

A platform team?
The observability working group discovered that their problem was not unique and, in fact,
was pretty common in these kinds of changes in large organizations. It is very hard to
coordinate application development teams around a set of documented standards. The more
complex the situation, the less defined the standard can be, and that leads to differences in
implementation. The solution to their problem is not just using their tooling better, but also
building their software in a repeatable, standardized way.
One of the proposed solutions to such a problem is a centralized team that provides a common
implementation of important standards and the mechanism for building and deploying
software that meets those standards. This has the benefit of putting all of the implementation
work in one team, and the results of their work are consumed by all the application teams. The
application teams don't have to worry about interpreting complex standards, and that reduces
or even eliminates the implementation differences for those core standards. In observability, it
is still important to allow application teams to provide data unique to their application, but
there is a lot of data that can be defined in a common way by a common team. The
observability working group discovered that a centralized team that performs this type of work
is often referred to idx_5b3ea627 as a platform team, and their method for doing so was through the creation
idx_8db24113 of an internal developer platform (IDP).
A big ask, a big undertaking
The observability idx_c1f9bd60 working group decided that the company would need a platform team to
design and implement common standards and to help drive application teams toward
standards-compliant implementations in their applications for their unique use cases. They
also realized that this was much easier said than done. It was one thing to create training and
rely on the application development teams to do the work, and quite another to have a
centralized team, or teams, performing that work. The latter would probably require some kind
of company reorganization and possibly some shift in responsibilities at the management
level. That is a big ask of senior leadership, and they knew that they could not make such a
request without clearly defining the work and responsibilities of that team.

Metrics and ownership data would be configured to be sent to the observability platform. The
platform team could then work with the application teams on how and when to scale their
application and provide that information to the observability platform so it can provide useful
scaling suggestions.
The platform needed to be capable and flexible, allowing teams to use it with minimal friction,
but also to expand it as needed for their specific area of business. This would mean capabilities

such as plugins to the platform, MCP servers for the observability agent, or AI skills to expand
what the agent could do.
This may not end up being how it would actually function, but the working group thought this
provided a good example of how the platform team would provide the value they were
suggesting in a way that senior leadership would be able to recognize.

Chapter 7 256
They also recognized that there were already solutions in the industry to meet these needs.
They could leverage a vendor or an open source tool such as Backstage. They included this in
their presentation to demonstrate that there were concrete, achievable paths forward,
although the final tool selection would need to be done by the implementing team.
Who is a fit for a platform team?
Now that they had an understanding of the type of work a platform team would perform, they
started looking at idx_42b37eb1 what skills the team would need in order to succeed. They sought and
received input from the SREs because a platform team seemed to straddle skills used by

Detail-oriented: The platform team would be responsible for a lot of functionality, and
any mistake could impact multiple teams. Understanding how the systems fit together
and how to create proper guardrails would be important.
Strong understanding of Kubernetes: The platform team would be closer to
Kubernetes and would create deployment standards and processes that the application
teams would be using. Since almost everything in the company was deployed on
Kubernetes, it was critical that the platform team understand how to achieve their
goals on Kubernetes and how to provide proper guardrails. The SREs highlighted that
understanding Kubernetes operators and reconciliation concepts would be a big plus.
Strong understanding of telemetry data: Since the platform team was going to be
providing standard implementations for common telemetry data (logs, metrics, and
traces), it was critical that those on the platform team understand that data and, more
importantly, how to make it useful.
Experience with mentoring others: The platform team was going to create a system
with guardrails and a common process, but they would also have to allow application

meant that not only would the platform team have to know the correct way to do
things, but they would also have to help the application teams implement their
additional use cases. This would encompass tasks such as creating training materials,
as well as being mentors and advisors to the application teams.
GitOps- and self-service-oriented: The SREs emphasized the importance of using

understand the GitOps model and be oriented toward enabling self-service actions
whenever possible.

teams to consume, which idx_a5a01c98 meant the application teams would be customers of the

Lessons from the SREs
With the proposal idx_c636dc0d well underway, the observability working idx_3acf6f0e group needed more information
from the SRES before organizing its plan into a presentation for senior leadership. They got

43502.heading: Chapter 7 258
43502.content:
Chapter 7 258
Reactive versus proactive scaling
The first topic idx_dd4c7cc7 the observability working group wanted to discuss idx_58d390ce was using observability data
to scale the Kubernetes clusters. The working group members didn't really understand how,
but they knew that the Kubernetes clusters were scaling and able to handle increased loads, so
they didn't understand how using observability data would help anything. They didn't want to
highlight this in their presentation to senior leadership if they couldn't talk to and defend the
proposed improvement.
The SREs started by explaining how the Kubernetes clusters were currently scaled. They were
generally scaled in one of two ways:
Using a Kubernetes tool called idx_b4b07a00 the Cluster Autoscaler (CAS)
Using a time-based action to increase or decrease the size of the Kubernetes cluster
The SREs explained that CAS would increase the size of a Kubernetes cluster when a Pod was
unable to be scheduled on the cluster, and scale down the cluster when it determined that
nodes were being underutilized. There are other tools that could replace CAS, such as
Karpenter or a cloud provider scaling solution, but they generally work the same way. They
scale the Kubernetes cluster only once a need is detected.
The time-based actions to scale a cluster are used when the SREs know the company will
experience an increase in traffic and therefore need more cluster resources. They explained that
this is a brute-force way to try to handle periods of time with known increased traffic. They
used trading markets as an example. Trading markets are only open during a period of time
during the day, but at night, the demand on trading systems is much lower. To account for this
in a cost effective manner, the SREs have put in place time based actions to scale up the cluster
before the trading markets open to be able to handle the surge of traffic that usually occurs at
that time, and then at the end of the trading day, they will scale down the cluster to reduce
costs since traffic drops off significantly during the evening.
The SREs then explained that the two methods they just highlighted are reactive, meaning they
can only act when defined limits are reached. Scaling a Kubernetes cluster is not
instantaneous, so even with the CAS, there is still a period of time where the system is under
stress until the new Kubernetes nodes are spun up and added to the cluster. The time-based
actions are really a poor attempt at being proactive. Through years of experience providing
services and managing traffic loads, the SREs had learned when there tends to be increased
demand within the company's offerings and had automated scaling of the Kubernetes clusters
accordingly.
While those current techniques work, they still leave a lot of room for improvement. For

43503.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43503.heading: Chapter 7 258
43503.content:
example, if there were an unexpected large spike in demand for system resources, it could take
the CAS quite some time to make the necessary resources in the cluster available. The entire
•
•
259 ACME Financial Services: How to Move from AIOps to Agentic Platforms
time that was occurring, ACME Financial Services' customers were experiencing some form of
degradation in their experience.
In another case, if there were a bank holiday, the scheduled actions could increase resources
available, and idx_06258412 therefore costs, without the associated traffic to justify the expense. The SREs
highlighted that this lack of real-time analysis was where the observability data could help
with cluster scaling. This was an area where the AI capabilities of the existing tooling, ACME
Observability, were being underutilized. The AI agent in ACME Observability would be able to
track historical utilization trends and recommend cluster size. It would also be able to predict,
based on resource consumption growth, when a cluster should scale and by how many nodes.
Both of those abilities would provide a better customer experience as well as protect against
unexpected surges in demand. The SREs differentiated this kind of functionality as being
proactive.
The last topic the SREs discussed was application scaling. Currently, the Kubernetes clusters
are using HPA to idx_7faadcf9 manage idx_088ef0a6 the number of Pods running for specific applications. This is also
reactionary and has the same limitations as the reactive cluster scaling methods. The
observability data and capabilities from ACME Observability could also help with being
proactive when scaling applications as well.
Self-service platform details
Next, the observability idx_864bde4c working group wanted to discuss the details of a self-service platform.
Based on earlier discussions with the SREs, the working group had a rough idea of what a self-
service platform was, but they weren't strong enough in the concepts to be able to explain or
defend the need or the benefit to senior leadership.
The SREs started with a basic overview of how this kind of system worked in their use cases.
They then detailed a system that held all Kubernetes cluster information in a Git repository,
and all changes required review and approval before they could be merged. Once a change was
merged to mainline, CI/CD pipelines automatically started and worked to apply the changes in
the Git repository to the Kubernetes clusters. They had alerts that notified the team if a change
had problems being applied.
The SREs said the same concepts/benefits should translate to a self-service system that could
be used by the application development teams. One difference is that issue resolution would
likely be split between the application development teams and the platform team. Based on

43504.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43504.heading: Chapter 7 258
43504.content:
the SREs' understanding of the company's deployment patterns, they gave a broad overview of
a self-service system that could be used by application teams:
All application deployment configurations would be maintained in a Git repository
A deployment would start once a change had been merged to mainline
•

43505.heading: Chapter 7 260
43505.content:
Chapter 7 260
The platform's deployment process would ensure that common metrics were
configured on the container
The application development teams would be responsible for the following:
Building application containers.
Managing any application configuration for their application.
Providing an initial set of resources for each container. Once an application was
deployed to production, the SREs would be able to adjust resources via the
configuration in the Git repository.
Some tasks could be improved by connecting the Git repository to the observability platform:
Allow ACME Observability to open change requests when resource modifications are
needed
The platform could even block deployments for applications without adequate process
data (error budget, sign-offs, and so on)
The benefits of such a system include standardization, automation of tasks, reduced
deployment complexity and variation, and a generally smooth deployment process. A
drawback to this kind of platform is that it would reduce the deployment configuration
options available to the application development teams because they would only be able to use
the deployment idx_5556aa07 configuration items that the platform team had allowed. This meant that the
platform team would have to work with the application teams to ensure there were adequate
deployment options.
In the SREs' experience, that downside was not as significant as it sounded. In the application
deployment case, the application development teams didn't generally have a strong
understanding of idx_4e766c68 Kubernetes, and removing the complexity and options could make it easier
for them to manage their applications.
Assistance with RCA
In the observability idx_da6f132a working group's earlier discussions with the SREs, they mentioned that
ACME Observability could help automate the creation of RCA. The working group wanted to
dive into how the tools could help and what kind of cost savings they might enable.
The SREs were happy to dive into this topic because creating RCAs was one of the more difficult
and time-consuming tasks they had to undertake. Ideally, RCAs wouldn't be needed because
there would be no outages, but since that was unlikely, the next best thing the SREs would like
was to automate the collection of information around an incident.
After an incident had been resolved, the SREs worked with whichever application teams were
impacted to discover what went wrong to cause the outage, with the hope of learning how to
•
•
◦
◦
◦

261 ACME Financial Services: How to Move from AIOps to Agentic Platforms
prevent it in the future. Outages can be caused by many different issues, so everyone started
with what the outage was (crashing Pod, network disruption, and so on) and then looked for
all recent changes that could have contributed to that issue. Sometimes the problem wasn't

43506.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43506.heading: Chapter 7 260
43506.content:
due to a recent application change, but due to higher or different traffic patterns triggers a
series of events that weren't expected or hadn't occurred before. It could take a lot of time and
effort to track down all the information related to an outage, analyze it, and determine what
went wrong and how to prevent it in the future.
The SREs believed the RCA process could be significantly improved with ACME Observability
being tied into all the systems in ACME Financial Services. In this scenario, ACME
Observability would know when deployments occurred, what changes went into a specific
deployment, traffic patterns, trends, and more, and could provide all that information as a
starting point for RCA. This would significantly reduce the work needed to gather the
information needed to understand what went wrong and why. The SREs even thought that, at
some point, the observability tooling could enable completely automating the creation of an
RCA.
SREs are always under strain and have limited availability, so anything that could help them
reduce their workload seemed like a big win for the members of the observability working
group. They asked the SREs to come up with some rough numbers around how much time they
spent on RCA and an estimate of how much they felt that could be reduced with the
automation that could be enabled with the observability tooling. The SREs explained this
would not be idx_26ef32d3 difficult since they used work tickets to idx_da359570 track the efforts put into creating RCAs,
which allowed them to track the work just like everything else. The RCA data would provide
another data point on reducing costs that the working group could present to senior
leadership.
Automating regulation compliance
Another feature of idx_d05955f2 ACME Observability that wasn't being used was regulation compliance.
The SREs explained that ACME Observability supported reporting compliance with various
regulations. This work was currently handled in a rather manual fashion by a regulation
compliance department. The process tended to require application teams to engage with the
compliance department when they thought a change might run afoul of a regulation. This was
less than foolproof because the application development teams didn't know the details of any
regulations. In general, there were some processes in place to help elevate architecture and
especially security design decisions to a group of senior decision makers, and that group
usually had enough knowledge to know if compliance needed to be consulted.
ACME Observability could automate compliance and help reduce the possibility of changes
that would violate a regulation from being deployed into production. Since the tool supported
reporting the level of compliance with various regulations, that data could also be queried by

43507.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43507.heading: Chapter 7 262
43507.content:
Chapter 7 262
various tools to detect whether a change would reduce compliance levels. With the company
providing services in many different regulated fields, this feature alone would reduce a
significant burden on the compliance team and help protect the company from findings of
compliance failure that would lead to significant fines and possible reputational harm.
The observability working group thought this was another potential major improvement the
tools could provide to ACME Financial Services. Anything that could cause harm to the
company's reputation was seen by senior leadership as a top priority. Automating regulatory
compliance in this way could help increase the deployment and development velocity of
application teams without increasing the potential for violating regulations. It could also
reduce the load on the idx_51b2335d compliance department and allow them to focus more on complex
questions that were not necessarily going to be understood by idx_a9999924 ACME Observability. At the very
least, any decisions the compliance department would make could be fed into ACME
Observability as guidance for the future.
Expanding left: Meeting developers where they work
The observability working idx_1d83d02d group had spent a lot of time talking to SREs and understanding
how they could improve their lives and various processes the application development teams
had to undertake. However, they still needed to solve the other half of their problem with the
observability tooling, which was that the application development teams weren't really using
it. The interface was too confusing for them, and they had a difficult time making sense of the
data, so the result was that the application developers didn't really use the tools. The working
group realized that they needed to maximize the return on the tooling to help mitigate senior
leadership's concerns over the costs.
When the observability working group evaluated tools, many of them mentioned supporting
expanding left for observability data. They dove back into ACME Observability's feature set
and documentation and looked for how it could better support the application developers.
They discovered that there were a number of ways the tool could help application developers,
and they would be enabled when more systems were connected to ACME Observability. This
was a fortuitous discovery because it fit into the work already planned in the proposal.
They also learned that it is not uncommon for application developers to shy away from
observability tooling. The tools generally are not designed in a way that integrates well with an
application developer's workflow, and because of that, they tend to be underutilized. Because
this is a common issue, there are integrations and features that can help address the problem.

43508.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43508.heading: Chapter 7 262
43508.content:
ACME Observability supported opening suggested changes in Git repositories and
commenting on developer changes if they might address or cause known issues. It also
supported plugins for software development tools that would enable the application
developers to get real-time feedback and suggestions based on the observability data. These
263 ACME Financial Services: How to Move from AIOps to Agentic Platforms
kinds of integrations provided the observability data in the tools that were commonly used by
application developers. This meant they wouldn't have to change their development
workflows in order to benefit from the observability data available to them.
This seemed a good start to addressing the problem. There would likely need to be some
training for the application idx_39f0fd87 developers, but the working group was confident that once the
application developers experienced the benefits in their development workflows, adoption
would be quick.
Observability-driven development
The observability idx_ddabedd1 working group also stumbled across the concept of observability-driven
development. This approach is part of the expanding left effort and works to improve the data
consumed by the observability tools and, therefore, improve the ability to monitor an
application. As the working group noted early in this effort, the better the data, the better the
results.
The application developers would likely see benefits just from tying various development and
observability systems together, but the effect would be amplified if the application developers
considered how to observe the internal state and actions of their applications. This is where
observability-driven development would come into play.
The working group learned that if application developers consider how to design their
applications to support being observed externally, that mentality often leads to application
designs that make it easier for the application developers to diagnose problems. In effect, the
application development teams end up helping themselves in addition to the operations
teams. It also helps application developers continually improve their applications when their
tools receive observability data, which, in turn, improves company response times as a whole.
Unlike just plugging ACME Observability into tools used by application developers, this effort
would require significant training and some changes to the application development process.
Like other development processes, incorporating observability-driven development into an
application's development cycle would require some changes to how applications are designed
and how developers test those applications. It would need to be a central part of the process
and not an afterthought. The observability working group knew they could create training, but

43509.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43509.heading: Chapter 7 262
43509.content:
they would first need to explain the benefits to senior leadership. It would be very difficult to
get this kind of change implemented with application development teams without support
from senior leadership.

43510.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43510.heading: Chapter 7 264
43510.content:
Chapter 7 264
Bringing it all together: The new proposal to senior
leadership
The observability idx_c6350875 working group finally completed its latest investigations into how to
improve observability within ACME Financial Services. What started primarily as a quest to
reduce costs grew into a much wider and more complicated proposal than the one they put
together several years ago. The group had learned that what constituted good observability
practices had changed much more than they originally thought, but that the benefits were also
much larger than they originally thought.
The working group was a little nervous about presenting the proposal to senior leadership. The
last proposal was fairly straightforward and didn't involve a whole lot of major changes within
the company. While it provided significant improvements, it did not come cheaply. Trying to
address the cost of the solution led them to discover their work was far from over. The working
group created a proposal for senior leadership that covered not just cost-cutting, but also
demonstrating the value of the tooling across the software development lifecycle as a means to
justify the investment.
It was a complex proposal with several suggestions addressing more than one area. It would
require some level of reorganization of personnel and responsibilities, as well as company-
wide policy changes, in order to achieve all the benefits they laid out. It also relied upon some
direct and indirect methods to lower costs by taking a look at the entire operations expense
rather than just the direct cost of the tooling. In order to support this approach, they also
highlighted new metrics that would be collected to track how the changes impacted various
parts of the company. The working group knew these metrics could make or break the success
of the project, because without them, it became almost impossible to assess the impact of the
work being done by the observability tooling or the platform team in financial terms.
In addition to the metrics, the working group knew they would need to get senior leadership to
expand their view on costs and savings. With the proposal integrating and affecting many
more parts of the company, the operations cost could no longer be looked at in isolation to
understand the full impact or cost savings of the proposal. This was critically important since
one of the requests from senior leadership that started the first investigation, and was more
central in the second, was around lowering operations costs.
265 ACME Financial Services: How to Move from AIOps to Agentic Platforms
A central part of this plan was the creation of a new platform team that would be responsible
for producing tools and processes that would be consumed by application development teams
across the entire company. This platform team would be responsible for implementing and

43511.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43511.heading: Chapter 7 264
43511.content:
enforcing many aspects of this proposal. Those efforts should not only reduce the load on
application development teams but also drive down costs by providing an automated and
consistent method to perform common operations.
The platform team wasn't the only big change. Application developers would be required to
learn and incorporate new design principles into their workflows. They would also need to
adjust to evaluating and requesting recommendations from the observability tooling as part of
their day-to-day workflow. The working group expected that once these changes took hold,
the application development teams would become more efficient, and it would also lead to
fewer incidents.
In addition to the company reorganization, metrics, and cost reductions, the observability
working group also made sure to highlight the potential benefits of business process
observability. They didn't know exactly how it would improve the company's systems, but they
were confident that gaining insight into all the actions for a business task would provide
immense benefit. They were confident that senior leadership would like that part of the
proposal, but they knew they needed to emphasize that it would be incredibly difficult to
achieve without the standards and common practices that would be provided by the platform
team.
The plan relied not just on the structural changes, but also on senior leadership commitment.
It would be incredibly difficult to enact the necessary changes across the company without
senior leadership pushing and supporting the efforts. This, along with the reorganization
needed for the creation of the platform team, was the biggest concern the observability
working group had as they prepared to present their plan to senior leadership.
The presentation
The observability team idx_0bf231d5 identified early on the fact that the lowest common denominator for all
the problems they wanted to solve was a lack of data normalization. They knew that a platform
engineering team could help address that through culture change while the technical pieces
were still developing. Therefore, they proposed a crawl, walk, run -style roadmap for what the
platform team would deliver and achieve. They knew they needed to prove they could beat the
statistics and continue to be among the one-third of companies that could point to successful
AI implementations.

43512.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43512.heading: Chapter 7 266
43512.content:
Chapter 7 266
Phase 1 – Crawl: Setting the standards
The first phase for the platform team's success would be to define the standards for data
normalization across the company. This was a place where the observability team had
expertise, and they recommended the CDEvents specification, which is already an emerging
standard within idx_6c1aaa04 Kubernetes (https://cdevents.dev/). The mission statement on the home
page of the specification spoke exactly to the problems ACME Financial Services needed to
solve, and on top of the specification and adoption by some of the tools already used within the
company, CDEvents provides an SDK for several different programming languages to help
teams implement the specification. This would make it easier for application teams to make
the required changes to follow the new data standards. The team was able to tie this back to
the scaling opportunities the SRE team had highlighted, and they also noted it could help
reduce the time to produce RCA.
Here, the observability team was prioritizing the SRE team users, as that was the quickest
implementation with more immediate and measurable returns on investment.
The application teams benefited as well. The SRE team would be able to do a better job
supporting their applications, and they were already well-positioned for the platform adoption
that came in Phase 2.
Phase 2 – Walk: IDP with its first golden paths
Phase 2 was not wholly dependent on the completion of Phase 1. Both could be run in parallel.
The second phase was idx_28a0ad5f where the real work would begin for the new platform team. They
needed to meet with application teams and determine what the most common workflows
were that the platform could consolidate. Once they had identified one or two use cases, this
was where they would produce the thinnest viable platform (TVP). The TVP idx_51ccfed0 had two key
focus areas:
Helping application teams repeatably deploy their applications while meeting the
standards for metrics, as well as other standardized steps for building and deploying
the applications.
Connecting to ACME Observability and surfacing actionable data to the development
teams
You know the TVP works if you can use it to build and deploy changes to the IDP. It must lead
the way, ensuring that the other teams have as smooth an experience as possible.
After the TVP, the team had identified the next most important problem to solve, which would
make the second milestone. For an organization the size of ACME Financial Services, there
must be self-service capabilities. Without them upfront, the platform cannot scale, and the
project will fail. It was highly likely they would lean on a tool such as the Backstage developer
•
•
267 ACME Financial Services: How to Move from AIOps to Agentic Platforms
portal to help them to quickly add this capability. Where tools cannot be standardized, the

43513.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43513.heading: Chapter 7 266
43513.content:
interface can, and this is one of the many key capabilities that a portal such as Backstage
provides.
Phase 2 would be characterized by many feedback loops, where the platform team made
changes, validated their success, and then either added new features or improved the existing
ones until it was possible for all application teams to leverage the platform. These regular
feedback loops were how the team could guarantee that the platform didn't just become a
piece of expensive infrastructure.
The final capability the platform needed to have in this phase was cost management
capabilities. Uncontrolled costs were the catalyst for a platform, and so they could not be left
out. One of those capabilities was that it would manage the lifecycle of the observability data.
While there was an observability vendor in play, the IDP should act as a record of truth for how
the data in that vendor was managed through integration with the vendor. It needed to verify
and enforce that every application it knew about had a data sampling strategy in use and data
retention periods defined. For example, the policy might be that raw data is only retained for
180 days, and sampled data could be retained for 36 months, but only in cold storage, which is
less expensive. By ensuring that policies and capabilities existed and also following the
policies, the platform could become an effective cost management arm.
Unlike Phase 1, Phase 2 must have clear exit criteria:
Platform adoption had hit critical mass: ~60% of teams were using the IDP, and the rest
had a path forward to using it
Self-service capabilities existed, allowing teams to accelerate their own adoption and
add features
The platform was tracking costs, exposing the cost data, and had cost management-
related capabilities
ACME Observability was integrated with AI agents in use
The platform was acting as customer zero, ensuring that the golden paths remained
accessible for the rest of the company.
Phase 3 – Run: From AI and platform to agentic platform
The final phase was the one that created the competitive edge. It was where the work that had
gone in up to then started to see the AI work as a force multiplier. That normalized data
resulted in magical scaling that met customer demand without sacrificing cost-awareness. AI
stopped being just a capability of the platform and started being central to its capabilities.
The IDP integrated with AI assistants and agents to make self-service easier, and helped with
regulatory compliance, using AI for pull request reviews to catch potential issues or changes
•
•
•
•
•

43514.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43514.heading: Chapter 7 268
43514.content:
Chapter 7 268
that may result in an unfavorable outcome. While the initial scope was to just fully utilize what
they were paying for, by applying a product mindset, they knew that they could continue to
expand as the platform continued to evolve beyond these initial phases. Here, they painted a
hopeful, but less concrete, picture that demonstrated the many possibilities for the value of the
platform to continue to be realized year over year as an agentic platform acting on behalf of the
organization.
The results of the presentation
The observability working group endured a difficult presentation with senior leadership. They
were challenged on the need for such drastic changes and the company reorganization that
would be required to support them. From senior leadership's initial position of reducing the
cost of the tooling, the proposal seemed far more expansive than was necessary.
However, as the presentation and resulting conversations progressed, senior leadership started
to see the need for the changes proposed. They especially liked the idea of metrics to be able to
track the impact of the changes, as well as addressing observability with a wider lens. As the
problems the working group uncovered became clearer to senior leadership, they slowly
started to come around to the changes they were being asked to support.
Senior leadership especially liked the parts of the plan that would expand the utility of ACME
Observability and the efforts to reduce cost. Their original ask was to investigate why the
expected cost savings hadn't materialized, but they also slowly started to realize that the scope
of the data they used to assess the effectiveness of the changes was too limited.
Unlike the first proposal from the observability working group, which was composed mostly of
minor changes and new tooling and required little of senior leadership, this proposal would
not reach its potential without significant support from senior leadership. Despite the initial
reluctance and resistance, senior leadership eventually came to accept and support the plan
presented by the observability working group. They accepted that there would not be a quick
resolution and the company was in for another multi-year journey, but they came to believe
that the end result would be a much stronger and more efficient company. They also believed
the new metrics would provide them with a much better understanding of where problems
and cost drivers existed within the company. Understanding what parts of the company are
involved in what business actions would also allow them to make better decisions.
To monitor the progress and impact of the changes, senior leadership required a dashboard to
be created with key performance indicators that they could follow. To start with, they wanted
to see the number idx_6eb79359 of deployments, the number of incidents, the percentage of deployments

43515.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43515.heading: Chapter 7 268
43515.content:
that resolved incidents, average incident MTTR, average RCA creation time, and the
applications with the largest number of incidents.
269 ACME Financial Services: How to Move from AIOps to Agentic Platforms
Time jump: What was achieved
ACME Financial Services put the observability working group's proposal into motion, but due
to the changes in responsibilities and the creation of a new team or two, it took longer to
implement than the first proposal. Once the new teams were formed and leadership and
reporting structures put in place, it still took quite a while for the self-service systems to be
built and be ready for application teams to begin using them. These efforts represented the
foundation for the new process, and they did not happen quickly. This meant that senior
leadership had to be patient but also persistent to move the effort forward. It was a sometimes
delicate affair, but senior leadership's commitment to the plan proved critical to its success.
The patience was rewarded when application teams began to use the self-service tools. They
were able to deploy new versions faster with less effort, the telemetry data was standardized
and less expensive to process, and with the increased resources available to the application
teams, they were able to implement new features and fix bugs faster. The new metrics showed
an increase in the deployment velocity for every application team that used the self-service
tools.
The application developers were initially a bit confused about how to implement the principles
of observability-driven development, but after a few false starts, they really took them to heart
and began to see benefits via a reduction in the number of incidents and better suggestions and
help from the observability tooling. Having ACME Observability connected to the tools the
application developers already used allowed them to realize significant benefits without
having to drastically change their workflows. They even started using the observability tooling
to help proactively improve their designs and avert incidents before they occurred.
The time it took to create RCAs dropped dramatically. An SRE no longer had to dig through
mountains of logs and try to correlate application behavior to a deployment time. The SRE
could ask the observability platform to find the suspected root cause of the outage. Because the
observability platform was connected to the logs, metrics, deployment system, and source
code, it was able to return information about when an application was deployed, how it caused
the outage, and even point to the commit in the code repository that was deployed when the
outage occurred. All the SRE had to do was validate the information with what was already
known and ensure that the application developers agreed. It took some time, but both the SREs

43516.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43516.heading: Chapter 7 268
43516.content:
and the application developers gained trust in the suggestions provided by the observability
tooling. The more they worked with the tools, the better and more relevant the suggestions
became. More and more suggestions were implemented, although they were still scrutinized,
which resulted in a reduction in workload for everyone.
The company achieved an understanding of the steps in their business processes that they had
never had before, thanks to their implementation of business process observability. They found

43517.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
43517.heading: Chapter 7 270
43517.content:
Chapter 7 270
and corrected several inefficient and redundant steps, which increased the performance and
reduced the complexity of a number of tasks. They found and fixed bottlenecks and were able
to assess the severity and impacts of issues before customers noticed a problem. Fixing these
problems not only made operations run smoother for customers but also fixed a number of
long-standing, unexplained issues.
The number of incidents declined, and the ones that still occurred were addressed more
efficiently. The SREs were able to focus on which incidents were most critical for maintaining
business objectives or were customer-impacting. Because of the application improvements
implemented by the development teams, more and more incidents became non-critical. This
reduced the strain on the SRE teams and helped boost consumer confidence in ACME Financial
Services, which, in turn, further helped improve the company's reputation.
Costs, which were the big driver for this effort, dropped. Not just the cost for running the tools,
but also operations costs across the whole company. The new metrics provided insights into
where bottlenecks occurred in the system, and they were addressed before they became issues.
Clusters and applications were scaled to avoid incidents. They were even able to retire the old
cluster scaling methods and rely solely on the suggestions from the observability tools. The
reduced complexity also contributed to reduced operational costs. The new metrics also
provided a much better picture of how the tools and processes impacted operational costs.
They especially showed the impacts of the AI-related functionality from the ACME
Observability tooling, which helped highlight the success of the efforts.
Summary
In this chapter, we continued following ACME Financial Services' observability journey. They
discovered that their first attempt at fixing their problems by observing their systems was
really just the foundation for what needed to be achieved. The problems could not be solved
with just tools and some minor tweaks; they required significant support and focus within the
company in order to properly address them. They discovered they had been looking at
observability through too limited a lens, which caused them to miss seeing areas where the
new tools could help improve the company. They realized the current metrics used within the
company were insufficient to assess the benefits of the changes they were making, but with
new metrics and a broader view of observability, they were able to drive down operations costs
and support that effort with data. The end result was a more cost-effective and efficient
company with improved customer loyalty and reputation.
Is there more they can accomplish? Observability and AI continue to evolve at a fast pace, and
